item.title: The Coming Risks to Russian Power
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.52
The United States has long viewed Russia as a power in terminal decline. This assessment formed in the 1980s as the Soviet Union began showing clear signs of imperial overstretch, and it congealed after the collapse of first the Warsaw Pact and then the Soviet Union itself. Washington went on to pursue a policy agenda, including NATO enlargement, that treated Russian power and interests as an afterthought, and the long-standing conflict over Ukraine turned dismissiveness into condescension. In March 2014, U.S. President Barack Obama called Russia “a regional power” that was “threatening some of its immediate neighbors, not out of strength but out of weakness.” President Donald Trump shows more fondness for Russian President Vladimir Putin than his predecessors did, but most Russia watchers in the West still dwell on Russia’s lagging technology; its failure to rescue allies in Syria, Venezuela, and Cuba; and what they see as its reduction to a vassal of mighty China. This picture of Russia as feeble and fading may suit the biases of Putin’s many critics, but it is fundamentally at odds with reality: Moscow consistently punches above its weight in global affairs. Thirty-five years after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Russia remains a nuclear superpower. As during the Cold War, NATO treats it as the benchmark threat around which the alliance plans its forces. An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted or to erode political and social stability. The effort to isolate Moscow has faltered as well. The Kremlin has skillfully promoted non-Western bodies such as BRICS, a grouping of major emerging economies, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a Eurasian political and security group. In so doing, it has extended its influence over the post-Western order now taking shape. And even though Russia’s economy is far smaller than China’s, the “no limits” partnership between Moscow and Beijing has produced a formidable coalition. This bullish assessment comes with a caveat: it relies on the international conditions that prevail today. Moscow continues to punch above its weight because it is navigating a fragmented, unpredictable world that plays to its strengths. Volatility and instability, active conflicts and arms races across several regions, economic decoupling and the retreat of globalization, the worldwide rise of nationalism and populism, the discounting of soft power and fissures in the Western alliance—all these features of the existing international order work to Moscow’s advantage. The downside risk for Russia is that today’s turmoil and uncertainty may not last. The pendulum is likely to swing back, with global disorder subsiding and the international system consolidating anew. That reversal could come when Trump leaves the White House, especially if his successor restores traditional U.S. support for the transatlantic alliance, multilateralism, and open trade. A planetary shock—accelerating climate change, an out-of-control AI system, or some other surprise—could likewise push states to set aside their current conflicts in favor of closer cooperation. When this change happens—and it will—Russia may find that its time-tested foreign policy and its once reliable but rigid institutions no longer serve it well. THRIVING IN CHAOS The centrifugal trends pulling the international system apart work to Moscow’s advantage. In a fragmented and dangerous world of strongmen, where raw power decides outcomes, Russia’s military heft remains a durable source of strength and influence. Russia is also the only power that can rival the United States in strategic nuclear weapons. China is modernizing and expanding its arsenal, but Beijing will need a long time to catch up with the two superpowers. Russia’s nuclear status has practical effects: it has deterred NATO members from deploying troops to Ukraine, and it gives Moscow powerful diplomatic leverage on arms control, strategic stability and risk reduction, nonproliferation, and the prevention of nuclear terrorism. As for its conventional capabilities, Russia retains a blue-water navy and long-range strike capabilities; only the United States can project power more widely. To be sure, the initial phase of fighting in Ukraine in February 2022 exposed serious weaknesses in the Russian army. But over the four and a half years since, the armed forces have transformed themselves, sharply improving their efficiency and combat power. Moscow now fields one of the world’s strongest militaries and, beyond that, has unique experience in next-generation ground warfare—an edge over almost any other fighting force, the United States included. Ukraine, too, has adapted its forces and tactics to new battle technologies, but it depends on Western support and may not be able to preserve those capabilities once the fighting stops. The accumulated experience of Russia’s armed forces will keep serving Moscow well in an era of frequent conventional wars. A divided, resource-scarce world also magnifies the leverage that Russia’s vast natural endowments give it. Russia is a supplier of oil, natural gas, coal, wheat, fertilizers, uranium, critical metals, diamonds, and other commodities. It regularly plays the role of dealmaker, especially now that supply, not price, is the priority. Europe, for instance, may be weaning itself off Russian fossil fuels, but China’s reliance on those supplies helps offset the asymmetries in the relationship between Moscow and Beijing. The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes during the Iran war has further strengthened Russia’s hand. Perpetual confrontation with the West does not serve Russia’s long-term development. A fiercely competitive, volatile environment also raises the value of Russia’s centralized economic and political systems. In the West, these are often derided as antiquated, inflexible, and harmful to the country’s development. Yet a strong state has helped Russia maintain social, economic, and political stability despite Western pressure and its losses in Ukraine. In an era of heightened polarization, Russia’s centralized, personalized decision-making carries clear advantages over the liberal alternative. Putin governs with little opposition, few divisions within the establishment, and scant pushback from the media, and he can pursue the kind of long-term strategic planning that unpredictable election cycles in the West rule out. The United States, meanwhile, is a divided political mess, presided over by a mercurial president and a dysfunctional Congress. Trump seems not only to respect Putin but also to envy him and his tight grip on Russia. In Britain and France, prime ministers come and go, none able to sustain public confidence. The European Union survives for now, but it makes decisions with excruciating slowness and, within its member states, faces surging support for populist parties eager to topple the bureaucrats in Brussels. As long as the international system favors rivalry over cooperation, security over prosperity, regionalization over globalization, and sovereignty over interdependence, Russia will remain in the top tier of global politics. It will even hold comparative advantages over countries with far greater commercial, financial, and technological capacities. Its rivals will be constrained by their own democratic gridlock and restless electorates. Russia cannot beat the West outright, but it can hold its own and play for a draw—until, that is, today’s competitive and fragmented order gives way to compromise, de-escalation, and stability. THE COMING CALM History moves in cycles, and the current configuration of the international system could prove fleeting. Globalization could return in a new form, and instability could give way to a long stretch of stable peace. The seemingly endless fighting in the Middle East could finally stop; Washington and Beijing might reach a sustainable trade and geopolitical compromise; the European Union may overcome its existential crisis; and a new UN secretary-general could succeed in reviving principles of multilateralism in global affairs. The reversal of the pendulum could begin as early as the coming midterm elections in the United States, if they result in a major defeat for Trump’s supporters on Capitol Hill. In such a world, some of the foreign policy assets Russia now prizes most would begin to lose their value. The softer forms of power, which Russia has long underrated, would matter more. Heavy investment in strategic and conventional forces, for instance, gives Moscow geopolitical heft, but it does nothing to help Russia plug into emerging high-value global supply chains. Were its domestic market as vast as China’s or India’s, Russia could insulate itself from the risks associated with globalization’s return. But its long-term demographic decline forecloses that option. Exporting its way out of hardship by selling even more hydrocarbons won’t work either, given the likely fall in demand for fossil fuels. Competing for large-scale foreign direct investment would be harder still. It requires high levels of interstate trust and transparency, as well as a stable and user-friendly legal framework. The country’s geography offers some advantage. With the world’s longest Arctic coastline, Russia can command a large share of the High North’s resource reserves and of the new shipping routes that will open as the climate warms. But to capitalize on its position as a transit corridor between East Asia and Western Europe, Russia would need long-term, stable partnerships with not only China but also the EU. Such relationships are hard to imagine now. Finally, without a strong civilian high-tech ecosystem, Russia could find itself far behind the United States and China in technological prowess. For over two decades, Russia’s leadership has been tightening its grip on the private sector. Its highly centralized decision-making has helped the Kremlin mobilize resources quickly and head off political and social developments that threaten the state, but it has also suffocated the entrepreneurial energy the country needs to regain its technological edge and compete in the marketplace of tomorrow. Russia’s innovation infrastructure remains rooted in the twentieth-century Soviet state-centered model. But today’s technological transformations—AI and robotics, clean energy, quantum computing, gene editing—demand new modes of interaction between states and private businesses, from global platforms down to the garage startups that often lead in key breakthroughs. BEYOND THE FORTRESS How Russia fares over the long run will depend on its ability to hedge against and prepare for another change in the world order. Its current “besieged fortress” model treats the international environment as a challenge rather than an opportunity. It can minimize immediate external risks, but it also keeps Russia from making full use of its geography, resources, and human capital. Perpetual confrontation with the United States and Europe does not serve Russia’s long-term development. The West may keep declining in power, but it will remain indispensable to Russia’s external environment—sometimes a problem for Moscow, sometimes part of the solution. Peaceful coexistence, and even limited cooperation, is the better path. Restoring ties with the EU matters most of all. These days, it is easy to forget that its member states were once Moscow’s main economic partners and its chief source of new technology and modern business practices. Given the dismal state of Russian-European relations, even a partial rapprochement will take considerable time. Once the conflict in Ukraine ends, however, the two sides could begin the slow work of repair. It is also in Russia’s own interest to do its part to uphold international legal norms, especially those coming from the United Nations and other global bodies, even when that means making concessions and giving up potential short-term gains. To be sure, a world governed by “might makes right” offers Moscow real opportunities in the short run. But over the long run, it is a dangerous game. The international balance of power is swiftly shifting, and new actors are rising. A strong international legal system—backed by all major powers, including Russia—may prove one of the few safeguards against revisionist temptations. Russia is, to the dismay of its critics, holding strong and proving itself in the current moment. But to sustain that success, it will have to look beyond short-term gains and narrow self-interest. It must be able to withstand upheaval in the international system and rapid technological change. Russia has the resources and wherewithal to determine its own course, but it is clinging too tightly to its preference for stability over change. This is understandable, given the painful memories of the 1990s, when change came as catastrophe, costing millions of Russians not just their jobs and savings but self-respect, belonging, even a reason to live. But that preference can also harden into a refusal to adapt—a calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before. item.title: China’s Purges Are Working as Designed
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.28
For two decades, scholars believed that the main reason Chinese communist rule endured into the twenty-first century—whereas every communist regime in Europe collapsed—was that it had built sturdy, long-lasting institutions. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had moved away from the unpredictable personalist dictatorship of the Mao Zedong era and established the foundations of a modern state. It set term limits on its leaders, embraced collective leadership, and increasingly promoted officials based on merit, which made it resilient enough to bounce back from the external and internal shocks that had felled other socialist systems. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, however, has spent the past decade demolishing nearly every institution that supposedly kept the party strong. He abolished presidential term limits in 2018, hollowed out collective leadership, and has declined to designate a successor. Xi has also purged high-level officials at will, especially in the most sensitive domain: the military. In January, only months after party leaders expelled nine senior military officers, the country’s Ministry of National Defense announced that General Zhang Youxia and General Liu Zhenli—until that point the People’s Liberation Army’s most senior uniformed officer and top operational commander, respectively—had been placed under investigation. Since 2022, according to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the party has formally purged three dozen generals and lieutenant generals, and many more are conspicuously missing. In Washington, many observers see these purges as evidence of China’s weakness. They see a powerful leader consumed by suspicion and obsessed with maintaining his own grip on power. If the party’s strength were indeed based on the freestanding institutions that China had built in the post-Mao era, then Xi’s purges would be a warning sign of fragility and even a potential crackup. But the party has not shown any signs of falling apart. If anything, as these purges have continued, Xi and the party appear to have only gotten stronger. Far from weakening its rule, the way the CCP cleans its ranks can explain part of what makes it durable. A purge is not an event but a process—one that the party has run in nearly identical form for a century. It regularly targets, evaluates, and forces cadres to seek clemency to retain their standing within the system. The goal is to reform them rather than get rid of them entirely, which strengthens the party by encouraging obedience and dedication to the party’s cause. CCP leaders believe it’s working, too: Xi has embraced “self-revolution,” or continuous and permanent rectification, as the means by which China will escape the unhappy fate of the Soviet Union and other socialist regimes now residing in the dustbin of history. What could threaten the party’s longevity, then, is not the count of how many officials have been purged but the one problem that such a strategy cannot solve and can even make worse: how to handle succession. A regime of self-revolution will rise and fall on that question, no matter how hard it tries to avoid internal decay. CURE THE SICKNESS, SAVE THE PATIENT China’s history of purges predates the founding of the People’s Republic, in 1949. In some cases, as has been true in similar regimes, the CCP launches violent purges to remove cadres from its ranks. The type of purge now synonymous with the actions of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union aims at eliminating someone from the party, whether through incarceration, exile, or death. The victim of such a purge does not come back. Mao employed this tactic as early as 1930, when he executed more than 700 army officers in a show of total control. But what the CCP has also done, and what is unique to its continued rule, is not a purge in the traditional sense. CCP leaders often turn to a different method of discipline: rectification. Rectification aims to keep a person inside the party, even if sometimes at a greatly diminished status. Whereas the traditional idea of a purge seeks to eliminate enemies in the ranks (the Chinese term qingdang means to “cleanse the party”), rectification aims to retain and remold cadres while keeping them in the party’s orbit. Throughout its history, the CCP has sought to rectify cadres far more frequently than it has sought to eliminate them. In December 1929, in the village of Gutian, in Fujian province, Mao put forward a resolution called “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party” that asserted the party’s control of the military. The resolution also included clues as to how the party understood internal discipline: it described its targets not as enemies but as people who had deviations in their thinking. Cadres might suffer from ailments such as having a “purely military viewpoint” (a perspective untethered from politics), promoting ultrademocracy (a political system lacking party authority), and supporting individualism. Mao’s resolution treated each of these as a sickness that could sometimes be cured through a regimen of criticism and self-criticism in front of peers. And it attached a promise to the cure: if party members submitted to the process, the CCP would retain them rather than destroy them. In the northern Chinese area of Yan’an, where Mao and his followers set up a wartime base camp starting in the mid-1930s, leaders turned rectification into doctrine. Party membership exploded from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to 800,000 by 1940, which meant that almost everyone in the organization was new and not yet trustworthy in the eyes of party leaders. The Rectification Movement of 1942–45 was the solution. Every cadre wrote an autobiography, measured his or her life against printed self-examination outlines, confessed before his or her party branch or work unit, and was examined, graded, and sorted by the party’s personnel department. In February 1942, Mao summarized the approach in a famous line: “Cure the sickness, save the patient.” Rectification aims to retain and remold cadres. None of this was gentle. The Yan’an campaign was brutal: many were tortured, and thousands died. Subsequent campaigns were often even harsher. But Mao’s approach separated Chinese communism from its nearest relatives. Stalin quickly executed unreliable cadres, and Pol Pot sent them to mass graves. In China, in many cases, the strategy was to keep cadres and try to remold them while also building permanent files detailing their every mistake. The basic procedure remains nearly identical today. A person is singled out for deviating in some way and made to write an account of his or her shortcomings. The account is checked against what his colleagues say about him and against what the organization’s records (in that individual’s personal file) already hold. The cadre is placed on a graded scale of possible sanctions, ranging from no action at one end to expulsion from the party at the other. (Most sanctions fall in the middle, including issuing a serious warning or putting someone on probation.) When a verdict on how to deal with a cadre, official, or campaign target is issued, that person, if deemed to have confessed sufficiently, is kept in the party but on terms that are revocable and conditional on the political winds. And every piece of paper the process generates goes into the cadre’s official file, permanently. It is the process used in 1952 against a village storekeeper who skimmed off the top of procured grain. It is also the process used today for China’s Politburo, whose members—the country’s most powerful men—read self-criticisms aloud to one another once a year and have their confessions written down and permanently attached to their files following the same template that was used in Yan’an. Even as Xi has expanded the scope of who can be targeted, the machinery has not changed. The ongoing case of the purged military officers under Xi likely fits this model, too. Zhang and Liu have been placed under investigation, not shot, and there is a chance that they remain on the party’s books, even if they are saddled with a thicker personal dossier and given a meaningless post or sidelined from public life altogether. In 2023, the diplomat Qin Gang, for instance, was removed from his position as foreign minister; news investigations reported that he had kept his party membership but had been reassigned to a low-level desk job at the foreign ministry’s publishing house. And even if Zhang and Liu are expelled from the party, purging remains the exception rather than the norm, as has been the party’s longstanding practice. Of the 101 generals and lieutenant generals that the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified as purged or potentially purged, only 14 had been officially kicked out of the party as of February. SINGLE FILE Rectification rarely, if ever, changes cadres’ beliefs. Eighty years of evidence, much of it the party’s own, shows cadres parroting the scripts given to them, performing the required contrition, and then reverting to their earlier behaviors the moment the campaign ends. It is a process so ritualized that participants learn to say exactly what examiners want to hear. Yet the main goal of the process is not to reform belief but to create a document to put into a dossier on file. Such a file contains objective personnel data as well as observable assessments of a cadre’s political shortcomings. It is this paper trail that enables the regime to maintain discipline even if no cadres change how they act or think. For cadres and others subject to rectification, the process sorts who is in and who has fallen out of the good graces of party leaders. As cadres constantly jockey for status, a purge is exceptional and devastating. For most party members, surviving a rectification process with minimal punishment is grounds for relief (and often accompanied by a desire to recommit to a forgiving regime) combined with a sliver of fear that the next campaign is always just around the corner. Expanded to 100 million party members, this process produces an internalized discipline in each person that strengthens the organization’s grip on power. Each cadre wakes up every day knowing the dossier exists and that it can be used against them at any time. The permanent, standardized, reopenable record of every party member’s history, associations, and vulnerabilities is also an information system that gives party leaders immense power. Autocratic rulers need information to head off threats to their power; the CCP’s personnel file system, filled with information about the party’s cadres, is an irreplaceable channel of information for China’s rulers. Most cadres are willing to go along with the party’s wishes, but for the small minority that does not express the proper attitude in the face of a discipline campaign, the party can expel them or put them in jail, heading off any threat of revolt from within. High-level defection and dissent sometimes occur, but when they do they are rarely organized and quickly fizzle out. Such record-keeping might be expected to generate resentment among party cadres, but the process is designed to spread the blame and thus insulate Beijing from any backlash. There is no single person or entity that issues a rectification verdict. Instead, party task forces (known as work teams) are mobilized to draft the verdict, colleagues from their workplace endorse it, and then a committee at a higher level of administration ratifies it. It passes through enough hands in the process that authorship is aggregated and spread so that no individual leader or party entity can be said to be responsible. Even the cadre, through his or her own self-criticism, is a co-author in the verdict. Disciplining cadres with rectification is also a coordination device. The Chinese party-state is a sprawling network of bureaucratic agencies, regional power bases, and administrative offices that have their own interests and frequently have to bargain with one another. A rectification campaign is one of the few instruments that transcends these fissures. As with the party’s other massive campaigns, such as the one-child policy, cadres understand that compliance with rectification is mandatory and a high priority for leaders. Discipline campaigns offer unambiguous carrots and sticks, including leniency for cadres who show the right attitude and professional purgatory, even exile, for those who do not. Many cadres that normally benefit from taking advantage of the fragmentation in China’s political system know to drop everything else and go along with discipline campaigns, providing Beijing with a highly visible way to impose unified priorities and strengthen party control. WHAT DISCIPLINE CANNOT SOLVE Chinese history is rife with examples of once powerful dynasties weakening and eventually falling apart. To avoid this outcome, Mao’s solution was mass mobilization: only by letting the people supervise the government, he believed, would it not slacken. Xi’s answer, offered in 2021 and elaborated since, is the party’s self-revolution. In this framework, the cure for the party’s ills can only come from inside the party, not from any external force. Ongoing party rectification campaigns require all officials to discipline themselves, and the occasional outright purge of some cadres provides undeniable proof that failure to comply has consequences. It is the first time the party has explicitly located the mechanism of its own survival inside itself. The choreography has been equally explicit. In the fall of 2014, with investigations that felled two senior military leaders underway, Xi summoned some 400 senior officers to the same hall in the village of Gutian where Mao had issued “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party.” State media called it the “new Gutian conference.” In 2024, Xi convened the military to discuss political work (that is, ideological loyalty) at Yan’an—a clear reminder that the party sees a direct line from past rectification campaigns to its present strength. Beneath the symbolism is Xi’s fear that China could end up like the Soviet Union, whose own Communist Party, Xi believes, let its internal disciplinary mechanisms atrophy and thus was the architect of its own demise. Beijing believes that the purges and rectification must continue permanently if the party is to remain in power. Whether or not the analysis of Soviet collapse is accurate, the CCP’s continued strength suggests that the party’s method of disciplining cadres may indeed explain its durability. Xi’s purges should not be measured by how many cadres they ensnared but whether they continue to produce files, verdicts, and party retention that keep the party firmly in control. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. But what strengthens the party also weakens some of China’s instruments of power. Senior military commands sit vacant or are staffed by less experienced officers, and future officers learn that the safest career record is a thin one. When forced to choose, political control is always more important to the party than operational effectiveness. This is a tradeoff that the party has been willing to make for a century and will continue to make. And China’s method of purges cannot solve the danger of succession. Rectification produces no mechanism for choosing the next ruler—if anything, by ensuring that no subordinate accumulates independent standing, it makes the emergence of a credible successor even harder. Succession, not discipline, is where the system is weak. The older generation of CCP leaders, including Mao and Deng Xiaoping, overcame the challenge of succession by drawing on their unassailable authority as revolutionaries who had fought for the party’s survival, and subsequent leaders relied on the institutions—term limits, collective leadership, and regularized succession rules—that Xi has summarily destroyed. Xi has neither, which makes the succession problem especially acute. The moment to worry about Chinese stability is not when generals disappear amid an investigation, but when the man who reads their files begins to age out of the role without an answer as to who will follow. The CCP is not going to collapse: the file system exists precisely to prevent elite fracture, and it has worked. What is likely to emerge instead is a state that is militarily weaker and politically stronger than most assessments suggest. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. Beijing’s own theorists are watching this, too, because they know that even a well-engineered system of rectification that has kept the party strong for a century has no answer for an elite power struggle over who comes next. item.title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.10
For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.” The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line. Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela. Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar. But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself. ANATOMY OF A CRISIS Iranian officials have acknowledged the country’s economic difficulties. “No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament and a key power broker, on August 21. (Bessent cited this quote as evidence that U.S. economic warfare was having its intended effect.) During a television interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian expressed frustration that some of his fellow political leaders continue to deny that sanctions are harming the country. “Some say sanctions have no effect at all; I really don’t know what to say to those people,” he remarked. The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian reflect genuine concern about Iran’s economic trajectory. The speaker and the president are understandably worried about deteriorating public opinion, given the inherent connections between general economic welfare and political legitimacy. But U.S. officials should be wary of overinterpreting these statements. Contrary to what it might seem, neither leader is suggesting that the country’s economy is on the brink of collapse. American assessments of the Iranian economy and the success of economic coercion fail to account for the ways in which sanctions have transformed Iran’s political economy, altering the distribution of economic resources in ways that reinforce its existing power structure. The Iranian leaders who are most vocal about the suffering of ordinary people are not worried about the country’s imminent economic collapse; they are dissenting against a political consensus that has long enabled Iranian elites to deliberately push the pressure of sanctions onto ordinary people. Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended. Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments of the Iranian economy miss important dynamics. Typically, the effects of sanctions are described in terms of macroeconomic indicators, including rates of growth, inflation, and currency depreciation. But these measures mainly capture price levels: the value of goods and services. They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy. To take a functional view, one must look at the dynamics at the firm and household level; they reveal why deteriorating figures in the headlines have not led to Iran’s capitulation. Iranian officials pushed the pain of sanctions onto households and firms. The fundamental dilemma for policymakers in any comprehensively sanctioned country is how to respond to balance-of-payments vulnerabilities, such as when a country runs out of the foreign currency it needs to pay for imports. There are, broadly speaking, two approaches. Policymakers can use expansionary monetary policy to fuel investment, restoring the trade surplus through a combination of higher exports and increased domestic production. Alternatively, policymakers can use monetary tightening and austerity measures to suppress import demand, restoring the trade surplus at similar export levels. When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, Russian policymakers took the first approach. They increased fiscal stimulus, driving a rapid expansion in industrial activity and manufacturing employment that created a distinct war economy. This spending was necessary to increase military production, but it also had the effect of dramatically tightening the labor market, raising real wages for ordinary Russians. That, in turn, blunted the initial effects of sanctions-related inflation. This approach eventually reached its limits, and inflation is starting to bite, but the economic strategy allowed Russia to persist in its war aims despite U.S. sanctions pressure. Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course of action. When major financial and energy sanctions imposed by the Obama administration first pushed Iran into a recession in 2012, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called for Iran to adopt a “resistance economy,” focusing on domestic capacities to counteract the sanctions pressure. But Iranian economic policymakers never managed to implement a new industrial policy or set up a new welfare system. Instead, they tolerated inflation, effectively pushing the pain of the sanctions away from the government and onto households and firms. They ran austerity budgets and refused to rationalize production or consumption through direct administration, such as by instituting quotas or price controls. The worsening economic crisis led to weakness in the labor market, allowing employers to engage in wage repression and leading to further pressure on household incomes. At first, this may seem like a policy failure. But in reality, Iranian authorities appear perfectly content to see economic activity slow. Doing so, they believe, will give them staying power in their confrontation with the United States. GOOD TIMES, BAD TIMES Microeconomic data reveal the effects of U.S. pressure on economic activity at the firm and household level. A review of Purchasing Managers’ Index data compiled by Iran’s Chamber of Commerce makes clear how the country’s economic crisis has intensified. Between 2019 and 2023, Iran’s overall economy was in contraction for two-thirds of the period thanks to Trump’s initial maximum pressure sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and disruptions related to the “Women, Life, Freedom” protests. But throughout this period, Iranian non-oil industries experienced modest growth. At the start of 2023, Iran even began to exit its long recession as the overall economy and the industrial sector grew in tandem. By March 2024, living standards were beginning to rise again, buoyed by a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes. This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes on Iran. Since then, the economic uncertainty associated with recurring military conflict has triggered a prolonged decline in industrial activity, pushing Iran into an even deeper recession. Industrial firms have reported deteriorating conditions for eight consecutive months. But that does not mean these firms are insolvent. Over the last two decades, Iranian companies have developed a practice of maintaining large inventories. This practice allows firms to mitigate the effects of sanctions on supply chains and helps shore balance sheets in a high-inflation environment in which cash loses its value but goods do not. According to filings made by companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, the average “days inventory outstanding” level among Iranian industries is around three months. In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days. These large inventories have been a source of significant economic resilience during the war. Iranian supply chains came under strain as ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled. A shift toward overland trade could not compensate for the loss of container traffic through Iran’s southern ports. But with an ample inventory of raw materials, semifinished goods, and finished products, Iranian producers could keep customers supplied—or at least customers with the means to pay. Tehran has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins, passing higher input costs onto consumers. And as the war continued, these higher prices led to demand destruction. Iranian households, embattled by years of persistent inflation, began to consume less. When they did buy, they increasingly relied on consumer credit, including new buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans. Even in special categories such as food, Iranian retailers reported diminished sales volume. The sharp drop in household consumption is clear evidence that economic welfare in Iran is declining. It is why Iranian officials have been forced to acknowledge the pain felt by ordinary people. But even so, the government has thus far failed to intervene to control rising prices. Not only have officials failed to introduce price controls—a move that successfully blunted the economic pain associated with the Iran-Iraq War 40 years ago—they have also discussed the elimination of cash transfers and energy subsidies for large portions of the population. In this respect, demand destruction has acted as a form of rationing, providing a structured way for Iranian political and economic elites to push the costs of the war and sanctions onto ordinary people. Although the government continues to face significant fiscal pressure, it has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent, Iran is still a long way from the kind of hyperinflation—typified by monthly inflation of over 50 percent—that will make the government’s strategy untenable. Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers for the real economy. In financial terms, the Iranian economy is in a worse position than at the outset of the war, but in functional terms, inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025, and supply and demand may find a new balance at a lower level of overall economic activity. Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade remains its persistent need for imports, which totaled $17 billion in the first five months of this Iranian calendar year beginning in March. That means imports will likely total around $40 billion by the end of the year, down significantly from $58 billion in the previous year and $72 billion in the year before that. The fall in import demand, driven by inflation and currency devaluation, is evidence of a deeper economic crisis. But in the near term, it will help Iranian policymakers forestall a wider economic collapse, possibly for several years. LOW POWER MODE When Bessent evoked the imagery of an “economic D-Day” in his August press conference, he failed to consider who is standing on the other side of his planned invasion. Although it may not seem like it, the success of Iranian authorities in transferring the costs of both sanctions and the war onto ordinary people represents a form of wartime mobilization. Ordinary Iranians may not wish to be mobilized in this way, but they do not have a choice. In a recent social media post, Trump asked, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” But even if ordinary Iranians were to take to the streets again to protest the financial repression they are enduring, they would once again face the brutal violence of the Islamic Republic. With multiple repressive tools at their disposal, many Iranian leaders believe that the country’s population can be made to tolerate more pain, especially if it is necessary to defeat the United States militarily. To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms. But as breathing slows in parts of Iran’s economy, ample oxygen will remain for the country’s elite. item.title: Iran’s Second Front
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.72
Seizing opportunity amid the war in Iran, the Houthis have launched a major new bid for military dominance in and around Yemen. On Tuesday, the Iranian-aligned group unleashed a wave of drones and ballistic missiles strikes on Saudi Arabia, setting fire to oil facilities in the country’s south and injuring more than 70 people. Then on Thursday, after days of heavy fighting along key frontlines inside Yemen, the Houthis routed Saudi-backed government forces along the Red Sea coast and captured the strategic port of Mokha. And on Friday, the Yemeni government reported that the Houthis had seized Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. The takeover marks a profound shift in the balance of power in Yemen, with potential consequences for the entire region. Until this week, Mokha had been home to a vital part of the anti-Houthi coalition and served as a bulwark against the rebels’ advance. With this offensive, the Houthis have shattered a status quo along the coast, upended a truce that had largely held since 2022, and set the stage for further consolidation of their control of the north. But the victory is also Iran’s, since Houthi control of both Perim Island and Mokha, which lies less than 50 miles from the Bab el Mandeb, will allow the rebels to establish themselves as the power brokers of the strait and more easily harass shipping. The timing of the Houthis’ escalation, which began with attacks on Saudi interests in July, is especially significant, given that the Red Sea has become a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for Saudi oil during the Iran war. Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened. By attacking Saudi shipping and Saudi Arabia itself, they have effectively opened a second front in the Iran war, broadening that conflict and placing further pressure on global energy and financial markets. Iranian officials have said that reaching a deal with the United States will require ending the blockade of Yemen—a shorthand for Saudi Arabia’s lifting all transit restrictions on Houthi-held territories, including the capital, Sanaa, and ending support for the Yemeni government. In this evolving regional order, Iran and its partners are trying to establish a new status quo by controlling the Middle East’s most critical maritime checkpoints. Options for addressing the Houthi challenge are moving from bad to worse. While the frontlines will likely continue to evolve, a few hard realities have been laid bare. A decisive military solution to Houthi threats is not credible. For all their public bluster, Yemeni government forces remain internally fragmented. During this week’s offensive, their backer Saudi Arabia also failed to provide close air support and other necessary assistance, suggesting continued poor coordination between the anti-Houthi coalition and Riyadh. Moreover, the Houthis’ gains also undermine the prospects for a negotiated settlement. The militant group is now likely to be even more maximalist in its demands and in its ambitions to assert control across the Red Sea. There are no easy solutions. For now, the priority for Saudi Arabia, the United States, and their Yemeni allies must be protecting other key frontlines from Houthi advances and hindering Houthi efforts to consolidate control over northern Yemen and the Bab el Mandeb. But beyond that, the anti-Houthi coalition must finally address the fissures that continue to tear it apart and agree on a credible political vision for resolving the Yemeni conflict. If it does not, there is a real risk of greater upheaval on the government side and expansion of the Houthi threat across the region. FROM THE STRAIT TO THE SEA For nearly five months after the Iran war began in late February, the Houthis mostly stayed on the sidelines. That relative calm gave way in mid-July, when the Iranians flew a Houthi delegation from Tehran to Sanaa, challenging the Yemeni government and Saudi-led coalition’s control of Yemen’s airspace. To prevent the aircraft from landing, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government bombed the Sanaa airport’s sole runway. Although the plane landed at the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah instead, the Saudi action gave the Houthis a pretext for abandoning the 2022 truce. It was at that point that the group began their bold escalation against Saudi interests and launched their new offensive against coalition forces in Yemen. The Houthi campaign is clearly designed to exploit new Saudi vulnerabilities. As Iran has throttled the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become a lifeline for the Saudi oil industry. But since the Houthis resumed their attacks in July, Saudi oil exports through the Bab el Mandeb have plummeted 95 percent. Now, by targeting infrastructure and ships near the Red Sea port complex of Yanbu, the Houthis are threatening the transit of oil exports northward through Egypt as well. Meanwhile, the U.S. war with Iran has given new fuel to the Houthis’ maximalist goals in Yemen itself. The group became frustrated by the “no war, no peace” situation that prevailed after the truce, and they blame Riyadh for slow walking a formal political settlement to the 12-year-old civil war. In reality, such a deal was obstructed by the Houthis themselves. In 2023, the UN helped negotiate a road-map agreement that would have allowed the Houthis to pay all public-sector salaries and obtain a share of oil and gas resources in return for a permanent cease-fire and the launch of a political process. It would have been a good outcome for the Houthis, who control none of the country’s hydrocarbon resources and have been shut out of the international economy. But instead of taking the offer, they began attacking Red Sea shipping to show their support for Hamas in the Gaza war—all the while assuming they could return to the table when they were ready. During the final phase of the war in Gaza, Israel and the United States caused significant military and economic damage to Houthi strongholds in Yemen. In the spring of 2025, the Trump administration undertook more than 1,000 airstrikes during Operation Rough Rider; a few months later, the Israelis targeted Houthi infrastructure and assassinated the group’s de facto prime minister and its military chief of staff. Yet these campaigns appear to have emboldened the group. By attacking global shipping, the Houthis bolstered their importance within Iran’s axis of resistance. And by engaging with these powerful militaries, the group reinforced its self-image as a major regional player that was uniquely capable of liberating the Muslim world from corrupting American and Israeli influence. Since then, the organization has intensified its effort to acquire new and more powerful military capabilities. During the Gaza war, Russia had provided the Houthis with intelligence to assist its targeting of ships. It considered providing the Houthis with advanced weapons as well, although it was ultimately dissuaded by Riyadh. Today, as described in a recent analysis in Foreign Affairs, the Houthis are harnessing diversified supply chains and shadowy financial networks while building up domestic production capacity. As a result, they have been able to strengthen their arsenal—even without direct arms transfers from Iran. Now the Houthis think they can get the Saudis to offer them even better terms than the 2023 UN-backed road map, including war reparations. As their military offensive progresses, those demands will likely continue to rise. The Houthis also face significant pressure at home to pay long-promised public-sector salaries and address increasingly desperate living conditions. More than half the population of Yemen is experiencing acute food insecurity, with six million people facing “emergency” levels of deprivation bordering on famine. RIYADH’S REDLINE Given Saudi Arabia’s heightened dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis may have calculated that the kingdom would quickly concede to their demands. Instead, Houthi actions seem to have steeled Riyadh’s resolve to confront the group. While Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman may have preferred de-escalation, or at least postponing a confrontation until a U.S.-Iranian deal reduced his kingdom’s dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis have not given the Saudis leeway to wait. With an unpredictable administration in Washington, Saudi Arabia has been preparing for confrontation by diversifying its security partnerships. On July 30, Riyadh announced a 14-country naval defense coalition for the Red Sea that included Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Sudan and Djibouti. A week later, the crown prince signed a mutual defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan at a ceremony in Mecca with the leaders of both countries at his side. The military value of these accords is unknown, and indeed, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are a first test for the latter agreement. Thus far, the results have been lackluster. According to Reuters, Pakistan warned the Iranians to rein in their Houthi allies shortly before the Houthis’ dramatic takeover of Mokha. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan has directly entered the fight in Yemen, and Islamabad has confirmed that the Mecca accord has not been invoked in response to the Yemen war. Still, for Saudi Arabia, diplomatic support is important, given the criticism Riyadh faced over a military intervention in Yemen in 2015. The Saudis have also continued to solicit support from the United States. Axios has reported that Washington gave Saudi Arabia the green light to strike the Sanaa airport, and the kingdom has asked for further U.S. support. On July 28, Riyadh teamed up with Washington to strike Iranian-backed Iraqi militias that have aligned themselves with the Houthis, a hint that Washington might join Riyadh in its military effort against the Houthis if the conflict continues to grow. Yet U.S. involvement is far from assured. Amid the demands of the Iran war, the administration has been keen to maintain a bilateral truce with the Houthis that has been in place since May 2025; many of its military assets in the Middle East are bogged down in the Strait of Hormuz, and expanding the war would be unpopular at home. While the Houthis’ seizure of Mokha and Perim Island puts greater pressure on Washington to respond, the Trump administration may be more concerned about avoiding new military entanglements ahead of the midterm elections: Axios reported that Trump declined Saudi requests to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after their advances on Thursday. Riyadh’s efforts to bolster the Yemeni government, meanwhile, have had decidedly mixed results. In January, Saudi Arabia pushed aside its longtime ally in Yemen, the United Arab Emirates, when UAE-aligned separatist forces led by the Southern Transition Council (STC) tried to assert control over all of south Yemen. Since then, the Emiratis have withdrawn from Yemen entirely, allowing Riyadh to unify government military forces under its direct command. But the Houthis’ rapid capture of Mokha raises large questions about the strength and cohesion of these forces. In battle, the unified command did not produce effective cooperation between different government-affiliated groups. As government troops from Mokha withdrew, there were even reports that they had clashed with southern forces who refused to let their northern allies enter the south with their weapons. In particular, the absence of the UAE and the dissolution of the STC have alienated an important southern constituency in the anti-Houthi coalition and deprived the coalition of a militarily capable external backer. If the Houthis are able to consolidate their gains in and around Mokha, the losses of territory could deal a powerful blow to morale among government-affiliated troops and stoke further division. DOUBLE CHOKEPOINT Iran’s greatest leverage against the United States has been its ability to shut the Strait of Hormuz. For much of the war, Saudi Arabia has been exporting three to five million barrels of oil per day via its Red Sea ports in what has become a crucial backstop for Riyadh and global oil markets. Through the Houthis, Iran can now restrict those exports as well. Tehran’s longer-term aim is to establish a daunting status quo: Houthi control over the Bab el Mandeb alongside Iranian control of Hormuz. If it could be sustained, such a strategy would make Iran and its regional partner de facto gatekeepers for trillions of dollars’ worth of trade each year. Although Tehran does not exercise command and control over the Houthis, it exerts enormous influence on the group. Iran’s decision to send the flight to Sanaa in July, setting off the current Houthi escalation, suggests the many ways that Tehran can stoke the Yemen conflict for its own ends. In turn, the Houthis’ decision to enlist Iraqi militias in their attacks on Saudi Arabia has further entangled the Yemen conflict with the Iran war. The Houthis’ growing alliances with armed groups in Somalia, Sudan, and elsewhere across the Horn of Africa also suggest the extent to which their current escalation could quickly spill over into the broader region. In the decade after Yemen’s civil war broke out in 2014, its effects reverberated into Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and finally the Red Sea. With the Iran war, the Houthis’ expanding regional ambitions and partnerships, and their combined ability with Iran to affect the global energy trade, the stage is now set for a more dangerous conflagration. This time, it could be much harder for the Houthis to preserve their earlier autonomy from Tehran. The war in Yemen has long been a battlefield for regional powers. But the latest stage could see expanding involvement from Israel, Russia, Turkey, and the United States. Rather than a battleground for regional influence, Yemen could become a platform for major-power competition centered on a critical maritime chokepoint. KNOCKING HEADS OR THROWING BOMBS Now that a dangerous cycle of escalation has started, much will hinge on what happens next. Saudi Arabia may use the recent Houthi advances to rally international support for a major campaign against the Houthis, potentially involving the United States and its new partners in the Mecca agreement. But such a response could expand the conflict without addressing the fundamental weaknesses of the anti-Houthi coalition fighting on the ground. Such an open-ended escalation is likely to favor the Houthis and further Iran’s strategy of controlling the Middle East’s chokepoints. A sustained Yemen war could also complicate U.S. efforts to reach a settlement with Iran. Alternatively, if the Saudis capitulate to the Houthis after their battlefield gains, it could deal a damning blow to the anti-Houthi coalition and further inflame Houthi regional ambitions. Yet there is still a narrow window of opportunity to prevent uncontrolled escalation and return to the negotiating table. To do so, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government—together with other regional and international partners—will need to agree on a credible plan for securing a political resolution to the Yemen conflict. The plan must address the divisions in the anti-Houthi coalition and settle the political questions that continue to tear that coalition apart while avoiding maximalist military objectives. Getting to such a settlement now will require both Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces, with support of regional and international partners, to apply effective military pressure to stem the Houthis’ advances and persuade them to accept a deal. Indeed, the Houthis themselves are under considerable economic pressure at home and stand to benefit from such talks, if they can be convinced that they cannot impose their will militarily. For a political settlement to deliver stability in Yemen, the Houthis will also have to agree to terms that address core regional and Yemeni government concerns and set out a viable governance structure. An earlier approach taken by the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen is instructive in this regard. In 2021, the Houthis walked away from negotiations and launched a major new ground offensive. The Saudis and Emiratis responded by mounting a coordinated operation that focused on getting the Houthis back to the table rather than aiming at total victory. Ultimately, the campaign helped bring about the truce months later. Any new campaign by the Saudi-led coalition today should be similarly focused on getting the Houthis to take part in negotiations. But success will first require preventing further losses on the ground and making an immediate effort to bridge divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition. It is well past time to end the failed strategy of addressing Yemen’s problems through short-term military escalation and pressure campaigns. Reviving a political settlement will not be easy or happen immediately. But the alternative is far worse: stumbling into a renewed, protracted, and increasingly regional war that, as with the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, could prove much easier to start than to end.
