item.title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.41
Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth. The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it. But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience. Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power. A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost. THE BIRTH OF A MOVEMENT In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate. The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend. Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes. The Islamic State’s overreach was ultimately its undoing. Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world. Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead. Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise. THE TIDE TURNS, EVENTUALLY After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives. Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq. The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations. Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world. No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks. Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens. The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing. OWN GOALS It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims. Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience. Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders. The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries. By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment. THE UNFINISHED FIGHT Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021. Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars. It will take constant effort to ensure that jihadis cannot rebuild. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers. This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance. Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak and security assistance fails to move the needle significantly—or if, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, Washington cuts its aid entirely—jihadi groups will remain active. The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish. For now, U.S. and allied counterterrorism campaigns and jihadis’ poor track record are keeping these groups relatively contained. But it will take continued, constant effort—intelligence cooperation with allies, drone strikes on jihadi operatives, and military training for local partners—to ensure that they cannot start rebuilding in weak states. All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States. If Washington can maintain vigilance without overextending itself, it can keep jihadism a manageable danger rather than letting it once again become a defining threat. item.title: America's Attrition Trap
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.15
Attrition is the defining feature of today’s conflicts. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have become grinding contests over which side can exhaust the other’s military capacity, economic resources, and political will. They all, of course, have unique characteristics, but their similar trajectories reflect a deeper change in how wars now unfold. Throughout the war in Ukraine, artillery crews have repeatedly had guns and could locate their targets but have lacked the shells to fire. Ukrainian engineers have found that new kinds of drones are met with Russian countermeasures within weeks, undercutting any advantage they briefly had. And in Iran, the United States degraded its adversary’s military and destroyed deeply buried nuclear facilities but failed to resolve the political problem that made the weapons a threat in the first place. Each dynamic illustrates a different gap that helps explain why states increasingly choose strategies of attrition—or find themselves trapped in them. The first is between the military capacity that countries possess on paper and the power that they can actually deploy and sustain. The second is between traditional principles of warfare and a modern battlefield on which technology makes decisive breakthroughs increasingly difficult. The third is between military means and the political ends they are intended to achieve. In combination, these mismatches push wars toward attrition. When countries cannot generate and regenerate enough military capacity to overwhelm an enemy, war becomes a test of endurance. When breakthroughs are elusive, pursuing incremental gains and the steady destruction of enemy capacity becomes attractive. And when the combatants’ political end goals are too muddy or maximalist, imposing costs indefinitely can seem like the only alternative to capitulation. For the United States, this poses a particular challenge. As American leaders increasingly seek short, decisive military operations, the United States may increasingly confront adversaries that see advantages in prolonging conflicts. The United States may not choose attrition, but it must be prepared to fight and win wars in which its adversaries do. THE LONG AND GRINDING ROAD Military power is traditionally measured by what countries possess—assets such as troops, weapons platforms, and munitions inventories. But recent wars have exposed the gap between nominal power and usable military capability. In his 2015 book, How the War Was Won, the historian Phillips O’Brien argued that even during World War II, winning the major battles that captured the popular imagination had actually become less important than dominating what he called the “super-battlefield,” the vast expanse of factories and supply lines over which military power is produced and transported. Since that war, the ability to generate and sustain military power has only become more important. Modern militaries consume materiel at an incredible clip, and their adversaries have become increasingly capable of disrupting the production and supply networks needed to replace it. When Russia invaded Ukraine again in early 2022, it appeared to possess overwhelming military superiority. Days before the invasion, the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff told lawmakers that Kyiv could fall within 72 hours of a full-scale assault; speaking to The New York Times, Ukrainian commanders said that they believed that their forces had little chance against the more than 100,000 Russian troops that had massed on their border. Yet because it could not swiftly translate its vast resources into sustained combat power at the front, Russia failed to employ its capabilities effectively and take Kyiv. But its material and manpower reserves allowed Russia to survive its early setbacks. Russia could mobilize more personnel, draw on large ammunition stocks, increase weapons production, and turn to partners such as North Korea to sustain its fight. Russia developed a theory of victory that proposed that it did not need to defeat Ukraine decisively if it could outlast it, wearing it down while waiting for Europe’s and the United States’ political commitment to weaken. Attrition gave Russia a military advantage. It also exposed a different problem among Ukraine’s powerful NATO backers: aggregate power does not necessarily translate into the capacity to sustain a prolonged, high-consumption war. Recent wars have exposed the gap between nominal power and military capability. The United States and NATO have far greater economic and military power than Russia does. Yet a war of attrition measures power differently. GDP cannot be fired from artillery tubes. Total defense spending cannot, itself, intercept missiles. The defense industries of Ukraine’s partners were not built to replace ammunition rapidly; they were organized around peacetime production. They thus struggled to convert their latent potential quickly enough into shells, interceptors, and other usable military capabilities. Russia and NATO thus encountered the capacity gap in almost opposite ways. Russia initially had capacity without commensurate effectiveness. Ukraine’s backers had effectiveness without sufficient depth to sustain a prolonged war. The conflict between U.S. and Israeli forces and Iran has presented a different iteration of this dynamic. Iran’s conventional military power could not match that of Israel or the United States, but Tehran had spent decades building the ability to compensate for its conventional inferiority by creating military capacity outside its territory. Iran’s network of proxies, sometimes called its “ring of fire,” allowed Tehran to apply pressure across multiple fronts, forcing Israel and the United States to expend interceptors and sustain high operational tempos. Iran’s use of inexpensive drones and missiles exposed the limitations of costly interceptors, expensive ships, and cutting-edge aircraft. In this strategy of attrition, Iran just needs to keep imposing costs and regenerating what is lost. ADAPT AND DIE On the eve of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, one U.S. general admired Moscow’s “learning and adaptive force.” Ukraine proved able to adapt even more quickly. But fast adaptation by both countries produced a paradox. Advantages that might have once enabled a breakthrough became temporary; neither side could sustain an advantage long enough to produce decisive results. This is the second gap. As technology changes battlefields, traditional principles for creating a military advantage—such as maneuvering forces and massing combat power—are becoming harder to apply, driving wars toward attrition. In an era of drones, massed forces can make them easier to detect and destroy; the concentrations of forces and logistics required for large-scale maneuver can be detected and targeted before a breakthrough can be achieved. The element of surprise is harder to create when the battlefield is under constant observation. Technological advancement constantly creates new opportunities, but counter-adaptation erases the advantages quickly. Quick adaptation during war is, of course, not new. But what is changing is the speed at which innovative tactics and operations can be rendered ineffective. In Ukraine, the feedback loop for learning runs directly from the battlefield to engineers and manufacturers and back again. QR codes allow troops on the ground to communicate problems such as drone malfunctions directly with support teams at the drone manufacturer, which can then alter production runs quickly. Ukrainian drone makers have described R & D cycles measured in weeks: as Russian jamming and faster drones defeat existing systems, manufacturers change frequencies, airframes, and propulsion and move the modified systems toward production. As the defense strategist Can Kasapoglu observed in July, “Unmanned systems, combat data, and human command have fused into kill chains that operate at unprecedented speed,” meaning that the war in Ukraine “has evolved from a narrow contest of platforms to a battle fought at machine speed and dictated by algorithms.” Technology is also changing how traditional principles of war are applied in the Middle East. Consider mass. Israel and the United States have used intelligence, precision weapons, and long-range strikes to mass effects without having to mass literal forces. Iran has applied the same principle differently, using large salvos of missiles and drones to overwhelm sophisticated defenses. Because both sides can persistently generate concentrated effects without concentrating forces, destroying the enemy’s ability to keep fighting becomes harder. The contest shifts toward repeated exchanges, replenishment, and endurance. In this sense, rapid adaptation can reinforce attrition. MOVING THE GOALPOSTS The third and perhaps most difficult strategic gap is that the military means being deployed in the current wars are not producing the desired political outcomes. This is true in both Russia’s war against Ukraine and in the broader Middle East confrontation involving the United States, Israel, Iran, and Iran’s regional allies and proxies. In these wars, the combatants are not pursuing limited adjustments to territorial borders or modest changes in an adversary’s behavior. The wars, instead, involve ambitious objectives that are nonnegotiable. Russia refuses to accept a Ukraine that is not in its sphere of control, and Ukraine is fighting for its right to exist as an independent state. Israel faces adversaries that reject its right to exist. The United States and Israel view an Iranian nuclear weapon as a fundamental threat to the regional security balance, while Iran sees its nuclear program and regional role as central to its security and power. Such huge stakes leave little room for compromise, making the wars deeply intractable. Attrition is inflicting high costs in blood and treasure, apparently without narrowing those political differences As 2022 approached, Ukraine was already mired in the long-running conflict that had begun in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea, and had largely stagnated; NATO had never made a decision to push Russia back to its pre-2014 borders. Following Russia’s invasion in 2022, Europe and the United States still did not make the expulsion of Russia from Ukrainian territory the explicit political objective, nor did they define an alternative political settlement. Instead, they often expressed their objectives as principles, such as supporting Ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity for “as long as it takes” and refusing to reward Russian aggression. Military strategy, however, needs to be organized around a concrete, attainable political end state to be effective. This ambiguity was understandable: defining a concrete objective and committing the military means to achieve that objective risked putting the United States and NATO on a direct collision course with Russia. But the result has been a military strategy detached from a political strategy—a determination merely to prevent Ukraine’s defeat and impose costs on Russia indefinitely. In the Middle East, a similar problem has emerged. Military force has imposed enormous costs on both Hamas and Iran, devastating their military facilities and killing their commanders. But it has not led either to capitulate. Early in Israel’s war against Hamas, Graham Allison and Amos Yadlin argued in Foreign Affairs that Israel had defeated Hamas because it had killed most of its military leaders and more than half of its fighters. But destroying an enemy’s military capacity is not the same as producing the political conditions required for a durable end to the conflict. Iran has used politics—in this case, international pressure—as a tool in its war of attrition. It has sought to degrade international support for Israel, creating a political ring of fire around its adversary. Avril Haines, the United States’s director of national intelligence under President Joe Biden, disclosed in July 2024 that Iranian government-linked actors were posing as activists online, encouraging Gaza protests, and providing financial support to protesters in the United States. International institutions, many European governments, and public opinion around the world have increased pressure on Israel, and its isolation has deepened. This has had strategic consequences. Although Israel has demonstrated that it can dominate militarily, it has struggled to translate those victories into a more favorable regional political environment. Its relationships with European and other foreign governments have deteriorated, and those divisions now complicate the international discussions over postwar arrangements in Gaza. BREAK THE MOLD For the United States, wars of attrition create a particular strategic dilemma. The Pentagon has planned for short, decisive military operations, and political leaders in Washington often promise them. Yet adversaries today have the means and incentives to deny the United States that kind of war and prolong conflicts in the hope that they can regenerate capacity, impose costs, and outlast American political will. At the same time, the United States has built a military that relies heavily on relatively small numbers of sophisticated and expensive weapons systems, an industrial base that cannot rapidly replace many of these systems, and strategies that too often leave the political conditions required for victory unresolved. U.S. defense planners are making some efforts to change this military posture, but it will take time. The danger is not that the United States cannot win a war of attrition. It is that it remains organized around the expectation that it will not have to fight one. Nearly four decades ago, the military thinker Edward Luttwak proposed a strategy of “relational maneuver,” which would focus on attacking the enemy’s internal cohesion and functioning rather than simply grinding down its forces. Recently, the Trump administration has hinted that it may be trying to adopt such a strategy in Iran. The newly launched Operation Economic Outcast aims, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it, to create an “economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe.” This broader pressure may weaken the regime or eventually cause it to collapse—if the United States finds the political will to sustain such pressure. That it will, however, cannot be assumed: rising energy prices and other economic costs will test Washington’s willingness to maintain pressure over time. The most realistic outcome in Iran may be an unresolved stalemate. Breaking this pattern will require a change in thinking in Washington. U.S. military leaders must build forces and concepts around the assumption that future wars are unlikely to be resolved quickly, while political leaders must be more realistic about whether the objectives they set can be achieved by military force alone and in a short time frame. Such adjustments will not be easy. The more dangerous possibility is that the United States will continue to drift into attritional conflicts because their price initially appears manageable, even as the human and economic costs mount. Americans may reject the notion of “forever wars.” But U.S. adversaries have every incentive to deny the United States the short, decisive conflicts it prefers. And even wars that prove relatively easy to sustain can be very difficult to end for good. item.title: Putin Will Not Yield
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.49
The war in Ukraine is causing undeniable harm across Russia. Ukraine’s deep strikes into Russian territory have added to the war’s civilian death toll; disrupted online commerce, a significant sector in a country as large as Russia; and prompted gasoline shortages. Burdened by a massive war, the Russian economy is delivering low growth rates and high inflation. In May, the prominent Russian banker Andrey Klepach offered a frank assessment in a speech published online: Russia is “falling behind. We are losing the [global] technological and economic competition.” In some respects, he added, “we are losing it to Ukraine.” In August, the state-controlled development bank where he worked fired him for this expression of disloyalty. Meanwhile, capital is quietly finding its way out of the country and deposits are being spirited away from bank accounts. None of this is good news for Russian President Vladimir Putin. After over four and a half years, Russia has been unable to convert its immense military sacrifices in Ukraine into meaningful military gains. But although Putin has no victories to present to the Russian people, he is not facing any real political precarity. One interpretation of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent visit to Moscow was that he went, in part, to convince Putin that continuing the war is futile. If Ratcliffe thought he could get Putin to desist, he was indulging in wishful thinking. Rather than inching toward a conclusion, the war is escalating. It is not forcing Putin into a dead end either politically or militarily, and to expect Russian concessions or a negotiated settlement in the near to medium term would be folly. The war, which Putin launched expecting a quick and complete victory, was not an accident. The decision to invade emanated from within the political order Putin has fashioned, a system that has been hardened by the war more than it has been transformed. The upcoming parliamentary elections that begin September 18 will certainly give the appearance of lockstep support for Putin. The reality is, of course, more complicated. But for outside observers, the key to understanding Putinism is its inner coherence, not the distance between stage-managed appearances and the actualities of public opinion. Day-to-day shifts on the frontlines in Ukraine and rhetorical expressions of domestic discontent are not among Putin’s major concerns. Despite its many costs, the war has bolstered Putinism and has been woven into the fabric of Russian statehood. SOLID STATE Analysts of Russia are understandably preoccupied by possible changes in the country’s internal trajectory—a burst of dissent, an election, a particularly destructive Ukrainian strike. Since the war began, the United States and Europe have expected its mounting costs to weigh down and even imperil Putin. Yet throughout the war, calm has reigned within Russia. A few weeks of panic directly followed the invasion of Ukraine, but after that, Russians withdrew into acceptance of the war. The 2023 mutiny by Yevgeny Prigozhin, the chief of the Wagner paramilitary company, led not to revolution but to his own untimely death. To the extent that polling can be trusted in Russia, Putin is vastly more popular than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, or President Donald Trump are in their respective countries. Ahead of the parliamentary elections, the Kremlin has barred the antiwar political party Yabloko from participating just as it was gaining support, and it has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, an antiwar political figure, to an 11-year prison term. Such repressive moves are routine in Putin’s Russia, the default operations of a governing system that long ago neutralized contests between political visions or clashes of rival parties. Not only have party politics vanished from Russia without much visible objection, there is no antiwar movement at all. Many Russians may not regard Putin’s regime as solicitous of the public good, which could explain the withdrawal of capital from the country, but the regime is also accepted as a given, a distant presence impervious to outside influence. Before the war, Putin had spent decades disabling the channels of political opposition and of political action independent from the state. Two intersecting trends have marked his quarter century in power: the steady consolidation of his rule and the increasing militarization of Russia. The Putin who became Russia’s president in 2000 could seem to be many things at once: a modernizer, a reformer, and a strongman. But no matter how he framed his leadership, his instinct for power was acute—and power, for him, was always synonymous with control. From the start, he steadily expanded his control over the state, the media, and business. By 2012, when he was elected Russia’s president for the third time, he had the controlling stake in all three sectors. Throughout the Ukraine war, calm has reigned within Russia. Putin tied his ascent to the elimination of resistance. His progress toward dominance over Russia was gradual and linear: he took over the national television networks, disempowered regions that might have had friction with Moscow, forced oligarchs to give up their political ambitions, and turned all political parties into empty vessels. Deprived of their political clout, oligarchs were reduced to his monied vassals. A drawn-out struggle against the most prominent critic of his rule, the opposition figure Alexei Navalny, culminated in Navalny’s 2024 death in detention. After 2022, most of Russia’s remaining independent media outlets, along with hundreds of thousands of antiwar citizens, fled into exile; any critics who remained in Russia faced the threat of persecution. By now, the absence of meaningful dissent is simply the status quo. Putin used his power to militarize the state and society, a trend that, in turn, augmented his hold on power. He invested heavily in defense. He made the commemoration of the World War II victory foundational to the country’s identity and encouraged the militarization of the Russian Orthodox Church. By the time he invaded Ukraine in 2022, the operation was vocally supported by Patriarch Kirill and most of the church’s clergy. Before then, Putin had launched many wars and military operations—in Chechnya, in Georgia, in Ukraine eight years earlier, and in Syria. He had avoided putting Russia on a wartime footing while making war itself a constant. And so, to Russians, war became familiar but not intrusive. From the beginning of his presidency, Putin had defined Russia in heroic terms, glorifying himself as the leader who restored it to its proper status as a respected great power. After 2022, this heroic depiction of Russia acquired a much more openly militaristic tenor. The gradual accumulation of wars that could be depicted as at least partially successful—and which did not trouble Russians’ standard of living or sense of security—contributed to Russians’ toleration of a war in Ukraine that has lasted far longer than anyone initially expected. For the past four years, the Kremlin’s mission has been to convince Russians that the war is anything but an emergency. It is a necessary state of affairs, given Russia’s many enemies, and proper, given Russia’s mission and power. STRENGTH IN HOLLOWNESS Russian politics is not an edifice without cracks. Discontent with the war is gathering beneath the frozen surface. According to polls conducted on August 9 by the Levada Institute, many Russians would prefer peace talks to an ongoing war. Some business owners and workers, especially in small and medium-sized enterprises, are frustrated by sharp tax increases. Should the economy worsen and the war cast a darker shadow on daily life, this discontent could deepen. So far, the cracks remain small. Klepach’s criticism was a modest gesture of public dissent against an edifice of power that remains more than formidable. Putin has the institutional and practical means to do what he wishes. What he wishes, most of all, is to wage war. At the center of Putin’s governing intent is subjugating Ukraine and forcing the West to accept that outcome. “Sooner or later, Ukraine will lose [its] western territories,” Putin predicted in his July speech to the navy. This was not a throwaway line. He meant that Russia is destined to control eastern Ukraine, while Poland, Hungary, and Romania will absorb the country’s west; in time, Ukraine will cease to exist. Ukraine’s nonexistence was the thesis of an essay he published seven months before the invasion. He has not moderated or mellowed over the past four years. If anything, Putinism has become more radical over time as it has become more secure; the war is a paradoxical source of the system’s self-confidence. Unable to conceive of losing, Putin feels little pressure to make concessions. He has not run out of military options and may truly believe he can win. Russia’s sizable military has enough manpower to sustain a war of attrition and enough productive capacity to generate massive amounts of missiles and drones. The country has survived being severed, via sanctions and the difficulties of cross-border travel, from Europe and the United States. The Russian economy has suffered as a result of its warped relations with the outside world, particularly its broken relationship to Europe, its natural trading partner, but Russians have no political instruments with which to act on their grievances. They are observers to decision-making that cannot be publicly scrutinized. Inside the Kremlin, Russia’s considerable wealth is an unrestricted asset for Putin. It affords him the means to reward friends, indoctrinate Russian youth, and wage war in perpetuity. Indeed, Putin might prefer an unending war, miserable as the prospect might sound, to the compromises entailed in a negotiated settlement that does not equal Ukraine’s surrender. In his July meeting with naval soldiers, he sounded as if he cannot see beyond the enormity of the war: “We should think together about how to preserve this [spirit of wartime struggle] for the future,” he observed. It would be madness for Russia to initiate a full-scale conventional war with European countries, but Moscow is intensifying its undeclared unconventional war through acts of sabotage in Europe. The war’s extension to Russian soil may even bolster support for Putin, stoking a defensive patriotism, especially among Russians who loathe “the West.” For years, Putin has inculcated the idea that “the collective West” is bent on harming Russia. Now he can claim to be vindicated. The Kremlin can present demonstrations of military power, even without a victory, as proof of Russian independence in international affairs—sovereignty, in Putin’s parlance. Europe and the United States cannot tell Russia what to do. They cannot expel Russia’s armies from Ukraine or change the Kremlin’s calculus through economic pressure. Boris Yeltsin’s Russia had struggled to avoid NATO enlargement. Putin, who regards Yeltsin and Mikhail Gorbachev before him as weak leaders, has pushed for militarization as a means of ensuring Russia’s ability to say no to Europe and the United States. His emphasis on Russia’s autonomy is not a personal whim. It undergirds his domestic popularity. Despite his place at the helm of a lavishly funded military-industrial complex, Putin is not especially skilled at strategy. There is a hollowness to his foreign policy: he has difficulty coordinating coercion with persuasion and great difficulty building relationships that have long-term legitimacy. The fall of Nicolás Maduro left Russia with little influence in Venezuela. The ouster of the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad led Damascus to curtail Russia’s military presence on the eastern Mediterranean. Russian power is ebbing in Central Asia, in Moldova, in Azerbaijan, and, lately, in Armenia (although not in Georgia), and Russia has won independence from Europe and the United States at the price of increased dependence on China—a risky bet. Nowhere is the hollowness of Russian foreign policy more visible than in Ukraine. Russia is impossibly far from the victory Putin imagined in February 2022—controlling the country’s whole territory and populace. Putin can wreak havoc in Ukraine and may be able to establish a cease-fire he can accept, but he cannot conquer Ukraine. And an unconquered Ukraine will, by fighting or by remembering the horrors of Russia’s invasion, pose an enduring strategic challenge for Russia. Putin likely assumes that Europe will tire of supporting Ukraine. But for four and a half years, the trend has clearly gone the other way. The more suffering Russia inflicts on Ukrainian civilians, the more Europe invests in Ukraine’s defense and its own. Yet all these challenges are not unmanageable for Putin. Whether Russia makes mistakes or serves Russians’ quotidian interests is secondary to his project of strengthening state power in and of itself. The conundrum of Putinism is that strategic mediocrity can enhance the regime’s durability—if not forever, then for quite a while. The more Russia is said to inhabit a hostile world, the more it finds itself wedded to an autocrat enamored of force. FOREVER WAR Contemplating the solidity of Putin’s regime, analysts sometimes entertain fantasies of a more docile successor. The Kremlin, which surely has succession plans, cannot guarantee that they will be followed in the event of Putin’s death or departure from power. Yet Putinism is relatively well positioned to survive the career of its founder. Opposition movements and revolutions demand organization. (Organization was one of Vladimir Lenin’s greatest skills, which helped him lead the only successful revolution from below in Russian history.) Inchoate discontent must contend with the vast security services that Putin and his fellow travelers have at their disposal. A successor to Putin who could retain these tools would be difficult to unseat, even if the Putin mystique is nontransferable. Policymakers in the United States and Europe must accept that Putin will persist in his war effort. A stymied economy and public skepticism are distractions from the essential story: that by now, the conditions that have made for an already long war are an organic part of Russia’s relationship to Europe, a shaping presence that will be exceptionally difficult, if not impossible, to eradicate. Putin has survived many crises: the wars in Chechnya in the late 1990s and first decade of this century; the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine (which made him look incompetent and helpless); multiple major terrorist attacks; the 2007–8 financial crash; and Prigozhin’s mutiny, among others. Arguably, most Russian elites have not obeyed the Kremlin out of deep loyalty or ideological alignment throughout Putin’s long reign. They have done so out of opportunism, and increasingly they obey out of fear. Putin is prepared to prosecute this war for years to come, not because his advisers are promising him a quick victory, although they may be. The war is embedded in Putinism, just as Putinism is embedded in the war. His governing system gives him the freedom to do what he wants, and his legacy and the war are now inseparable. Both he and Russia are in it for the long haul.
