item.title: The Other War on Terror
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.37
For years, the United States’ political dysfunction has been attributed to large-scale social and economic changes. Experts point to the failures of globalization, rising inequality, reduced social mobility, or the long aftermath of the “China shock” more than two decades ago to explain today’s extreme polarization, collapsing trust in institutions, democratic erosion, immigration backlash, and struggling middle class. Yet there is another widely overlooked factor that is equally central to understanding the United States’ current predicament: the war on terror. Typically, when policymakers and analysts speak of the global war on terror—the defining fact of international affairs for two decades—they discuss the damage done to terrorist groups, the plots that have been thwarted, the rise and fall of jihadi ideology, the many intelligence failures, and, perhaps above all, the two forever wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. These are the scorecards of contemporary counterterrorism. But left out of this framing are the profound effects of this vast war on terror on domestic politics and society. The human statistics alone tell an appalling story: more than 7,000 U.S. troops were killed in action, 53,000 were wounded, and well over 30,000 took their own lives—a staggering number. According to Brown University’s Costs of War Project, these conflicts added $8 trillion to the U.S. national debt, with trillions more projected in the future for veterans’ health care, including for the half million GIs with traumatic brain injuries and posttraumatic stress disorder. Yet even these numbers fail to show the myriad ways in which two decades of war transformed the United States. For years, the fixation on Islamist terror shaped a culture drenched in fear, as voices from politics, the media, civil society, and a swelling counterterrorism-industrial complex insisted that the country faced an existential threat. Amid this climate, the government was given broad new powers to root out and prosecute potential jihadi activity wherever it might be, and the widespread assumption that there might be another terrorist attack began to reshape American society itself. Rather than bringing the country together behind a shared—and narrowly defined—enemy, however, the result has been a dramatic decline in social cohesion. It has contributed to the demise of political bipartisanship, already weakened in previous decades. At the same time, the war on terror fueled an alarming rise in xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment and discredited the country’s political and foreign policy elites. Above all has been the uncontrolled expansion of executive power. This impetus did not begin with the war on terror; generations of American leaders and scholars have sought to increase presidential power, drawing up mechanisms that could sideline civil liberties and intertwine military and police activities. But after 9/11, these contingencies were used to give the executive branch sweeping new authority in the name of domestic security. And today, an authoritarian president is using these powers to target his political enemies. The United States, then, is overdue for a reckoning with the political legacy of the war on terror. THE POWER OF NIGHTMARES Anxiety about extended war has preoccupied American officials throughout U.S. history. In the first years after the country’s independence, James Madison, who would become the country’s fourth president, observed that “no nation can preserve its freedom in the midst of continual war.” More than a century and a half later, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower sounded the alarm about “the acquisition of unwarranted influence” by what he famously called “the military-industrial complex.” As Eisenhower forewarned, “The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.” For many of the decades since, much of that apprehension has been focused on the concentration of power in government and in the broader machinery of war. Yet during the war on terror, parts of society mobilized in parallel with the state and sought to cast a much wider net against a class of perceived enemies. Terrorist acts are typically carried out by secret actors operating within a country’s borders, and 9/11 was the ultimate case in point. The attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon—the first on U.S. soil since World War II—were carried out by foreign nationals inside the country. They were motivated by the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s particular brand of jihadi ideology, which held that major attacks on the U.S. homeland would lead Washington to withdraw support for the apostate rulers of the Muslim world. These themes—which also carried notions of proportional revenge for the number of Muslims previously killed by the United States—and the attacks themselves gave license to Islamophobes throughout American society, including in the political world and policy establishment. The most influential came from the evangelical churches: to their huge audiences, leading televangelists such as Franklin Graham, John Hagee, and Robert Jeffress described Islam as “satanic” and a “heresy from the pit of hell” and its followers as a cult of pedophiles. President George W. Bush sought to tamp down the hatred by insisting that the war on terror was not a war against Islam. But for all his protestations, many saw the war on terror as a crusade—a word that Bush himself used early on until he was told how poorly that played in the Islamic world. His message was further belied by such government actions as the detention of at least 1,200 Muslim men—many of whom were held on immigration charges but treated as high-security risks—and the severe curtailment of Muslim civil liberties by the FBI and other law enforcement in the name of addressing the terrorist threat. The fact that the 9/11 hijackers had been sustained by an efficient Muslim support network within the United States no doubt contributed to these measures, as did reasonable concerns about the potential for online radicalization. Trump blurs the lines between Islamophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment. In the decades since, the persistence of fear-mongering and the growth of anti-Muslim sentiment and hate crimes has been hard to miss. When the Obama administration sought to transfer foreign detainees captured in the war on terror from Guantánamo to facilities in the United States, Republicans depicted them as superhuman terrorists that no U.S. prison could safely secure. The plan was nixed. In 2014, when it was revealed that a jihadi’s laptop found in an Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Idlib, Syria, contained some basic information on bioweapons, members of the flourishing counterterrorism commentariat claimed that terrorists planned to cull the African Ebola virus from victims’ corpses and spray it widely in American urban centers. Candidates for high office found the terrorist threat to be the gift that never ceased giving. Political scientists at Dartmouth, where both of us have taught, recall hearing former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016, tell elderly women in a remote New Hampshire village that jihadis might take them hostage in their homes if they didn’t vote for the tough-on-terror candidate. Claims such as these were contradicted by the actual state of the threat. By 2016, it had been several years since U.S. Navy SEALS had killed bin Laden, and al-Qaeda had not managed a second attack against the United States in 15 years. The few, ostensibly Islamist-related attacks that had happened on U.S. soil were mostly lone-wolf actions, in the sense that they were not deployed and directed by al-Qaeda operatives based outside the United States. Instead, they were radicalized in place through exposure to news reporting, online propaganda, preaching, and the fellowship of like-minded individuals. (A partial exception was the 2009 Fort Hood massacre, carried out by a U.S. army major, who had corresponded with Anwar al-Awlaki, the American cleric with links to al-Qaeda who was later killed by the United States in Yemen.) In 2014, ISIS captured global attention with its claim to a caliphate and insurgency in Iraq and Syria, and it was better than al-Qaeda at recruiting followers in Europe and North America. This group carried out or claimed responsibility for bloody attacks in Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, and Spain. Several of these were devastating mass casualty attacks, but none were in the league of 9/11. Notably, ISIS’s rise in the vacuum created by the U.S. toppling of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was a result, not a cause, of the war on terror. The lack of attacks was not simply luck. Throughout these decades, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement professionals—operating far from the overheated rhetoric of the era—dealt methodically and capably with the terrorist threat. During this period, government agencies achieved a level of integration that had improved dramatically since pre-9/11 days. Foreign intelligence services and civil authorities were tightly coordinated in the effort, making it possible to know who was attempting to cross the United States’ borders. Indeed, by the time al-Qaeda struck the United States again—a 2019 shooting at a Florida naval base that killed three and injured eight—the group was a shadow of its former self. As ISIS made clear, the fading of al-Qaeda did not usher in an age of Aquarius. Yet according to solid longitudinal polling, the degree to which Americans prioritized terrorism no longer reflected quotidian reality. The unanswered and perhaps unanswerable question emerging from this period is whether the relative security Americans enjoyed in the decades after 9/11 owed more to intelligence and law enforcement and domestic security measures than to the progress of the expeditionary wars and targeted killings that were meant to root out the problem at its presumed source. Nonetheless, the question remains a vital one for those who are responsible for anticipating terrorism threats and constructing both defensive and offensive approaches to them. FOREVER WAR TO CIVIL WAR In hindsight, 2016 marked a decisive hinge point in the war on terror, when the primary question shifted from faraway military conflicts to allegedly dangerous new threats at home—and not only those from Islamists. The United States had plenty of experience with nativism before 9/11. But a decade and a half of fear-mongering produced something entirely new. Perhaps nowhere was the legacy more pernicious than in the fusing of terrorist fears with broader anti-immigration sentiment. As numerous postmortems for the 2016 presidential election made clear, stoking anti-Muslim sentiment helped mobilize the Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s base, even though economic concerns won him that close election. On the campaign trail and then in office, Trump continually blurred the lines between Islamophobia and broader anti-immigrant sentiment. One day he decried murderers, criminals, and rapists coming across the southern border; the next, he asserted that the migrant flows were cover for jihadis. Perhaps the perfect symbol of Trump’s fusion of the threat of terrorism with the challenge of illegal immigration was his repeated warnings in 2018 about a migrant caravan making its way from Central America to the U.S.-Mexican border—a caravan he claimed had “unknown Middle Easterners in it.” To be fair, the U.S. intelligence community was concerned that jihadis were exploiting chaotic conditions at the border to infiltrate the United States, but the fractured nature of interagency databases made this hard to know. In his effort to appear tougher than any competitor, Trump called for bringing back waterboarding and some unspecified technique that was “a helluva lot worse than waterboarding.” Speaking of ISIS operatives, he also said he would “take out their families.” Still more striking, candidate Trump managed to radiate Islamophobia even as he decried the post-9/11 forever wars, stymieing his Republican rivals and his eventual Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. In a way, this marked a decisive shift in the war on terror toward the American homeland. One of the two candidates for president, one of the country’s foremost politicians, was expressly lumping together a sizable American ethnic minority with external enemies. Even when the subtext of previous policy suggested suspicion of American Muslims, federal leaders never expressed explicit hostility. Trump did. Once elected, he implemented a Muslim travel ban, which he introduced just a week into his term and reformulated repeatedly until the Supreme Court finally approved it 18 months later. He also created a permissive structure for xenophobes and racists, spurring a dramatic increase in hate crimes with victims from minority groups of all kinds and accelerating the disuniting of the United States. In his second term, Trump has gone much further. In 2025, the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against alleged members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, described them as an invading force, and sent detainees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center. The Supreme Court required adequate notice to permit habeas challenges, but removals had already begun. In Florida, the government opened a remote Everglades detention compound called “Alligator Alcatraz” that might usefully be thought of as Guantánamo transplanted to U.S. soil, with its geographic isolation and removal from the domain of law. The facility shuttered after a year, but only for reasons of expense; it cost over a billion dollars per year to run. And by then, the administration was making an even more direct connection with the war on terror, as some immigrant detainees were now sent to Guantánamo itself. The Pentagon also became involved, with active-duty personnel providing logistical and operational support for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention mission. In other words, institutions created for external war, border enforcement, and domestic policing have now become components of a punitive system against immigrants who may not even have a criminal record. As a practical matter, it became a test bed for the detention of political prisoners, or, as Trump described them, “enemies of the people.” The Trump administration is not alone in using Islamophobia to drive an anti-immigrant agenda. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, for instance, has long been famous for railing against illegal immigration. But as The New York Times put it in August, citing Republican consultants, “Islam has replaced the border as a major concern” for voters. To date, Texas officials have blocked a real estate development that includes a mosque and threatened to withhold state funding from airports that provide washing stations for Muslim prayer, among other steps. Meanwhile, Republican politicians across the country have denounced the electoral successes of Muslim politicians, including Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Some have even suggested that these officials either are not American citizens or should lose their citizenship. Trump has remarked that “jihadists are being elected all over the place.” COUNTERTERRORISM-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX The sociologist Charles Tilly’s maxim that “war makes the state; the state makes war” applies not just to early modern state formation but also to how the United States’ counterterrorism efforts led to a dramatic augmentation of state powers. The war on terror propelled the United States to collect and combine information, including on its own citizens; classify individuals it considered dangerous; combine both active and reserve component military units for the purposes of population control and law enforcement; and use coercive power under a variety of emergency authorities. It also reinforced an “us against them” conception of public life in which political disagreement could be recast as disloyalty and whole minority groups treated as presumptively suspect. The perception of an enduring terrorist threat increased support for coercive policies, even among Americans otherwise resistant to authoritarian appeals. Of course, the United States faced security threats before 9/11. Yet whereas the Cold War security state depended on accurate intelligence on adversaries’ military forces and key assets, counterterrorism is focused not on large formations or fixed installations but on locating individuals hidden within large populations, both at home and in foreign societies. Defending against al-Qaeda required officials to identify suspicious people, trace money and travel, map personal networks, and act before an attack occurred. After the shock of the 9/11 attacks, Washington developed an information-sharing network that crossed the foreign and domestic divide and could search customs, immigration, intelligence, and regular law enforcement records. Joint Terrorism Task Forces set up by the FBI and state and city fusion centers created by DHS implemented this model in parallel at the local level. Their missions soon exceeded terrorism to encompass other facets of public safety. In time, national security institutions were routinely vacuuming up ordinary police information, and local law enforcement officers were combing through federal intelligence. The structure was built for finding needles in haystacks. Once built, it could search for needles of all sorts. Such capabilities made it easy to expand political control and executive power, should an elected leader choose to use them for these purposes. Top government officials could identify not only suspects but also their associations, movements, communications, and supporters, making these tools convenient for targeting individuals and groups, both real and invented, and stigmatized communities. Commercial platforms increased their reach. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)—which was founded in response to September 11—has contracted with the American software company Palantir for ImmigrationOS, a system intended to assist in the selection and apprehension of deportation targets. Artificial intelligence, and its inherent scalability, has accelerated the process by eliminating the main bottleneck to comprehensive surveillance: scarce manpower. The logic was visible during the 2020 protests in Portland, Oregon, when DHS officers monitored social media, accessed travel and immigration records, and assembled dossiers on protesters and journalists. Unidentified armed federal officers used unmarked rental vehicles to detain people and took some to holding cells in the federal courthouse without explaining what agency held them or why. The federal government’s evolution since 9/11 is reflected not just in its activities and capabilities. Its sheer mass has grown, as well. Since ICE was created in 2003, its annual budget has risen from $3.3 billion to almost $29 billion; in the same period, its corps of armed officers has grown from 3,000 to 22,000. Meanwhile, police forces across the country have transformed from lightly armed constabularies to small-scale armies. Before 9/11, the Defense Department had transferred only $27 million in hardware to local police forces. Since the attacks, the number has climbed to more than $1.6 billion. In numerous jurisdictions, police can now respond to demonstrations with mine-proof armored vehicles, camouflage, body armor, and large-caliber weaponry. The government’s target set has also expanded. In 2025, the White House issued National Security Memorandum 7, which, among other things, designated antifa—a mostly made up, decentralized, left-wing political movement opposed to white supremacy and (per its name) fascism—as a domestic terrorist organization, a status not formally recognized in the law. The memorandum directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate organized political violence carried out by those who belong to this supposed network. The offenses were “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity . . . extremism on migration, race, and gender . . . hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality.” The crimes to be investigated by the task forces largely related to protected speech. A subsequent counterterrorism strategy document in May 2026 referred specifically to the “politically motivated killings of Christians and conservatives.” The document treats hostility to Christianity as one of the diagnostic markers for identifying organized political violence, alongside anticapitalism and anti-Americanism. The Trump administration has also used counterterrorism precedents to justify the widespread use of lethal force. Beginning in 2025, the administration labeled suspected drug traffickers as narcoterrorists, giving it legal cover to use military strikes against boats and land sites in Latin America. By August 2026, its operations had killed hundreds of people, often without public evidence to establish a crime or even the basic identities of those targeted. Attacks against Iran in May 2026, meanwhile, killed much of the upper echelon of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Different legal authorities were invoked, but as with the purported drug dealers, the White House used classifications and military practices from the war-on-terror era to justify and conduct its operations. Although Israel’s preemptive and retaliatory reliance on targeted killings has drawn much attention, this mode of warfare characterized the American war on terror very nearly from its outset, including the arming of drones for this purpose; the first armed Predator flew in October 2001. During the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign within the United States, four Americans were killed and three wounded with the same impunity as the 526 targeted attacks conducted outside war zones from 2009 to 2016 during the latter phase of the war on terror. The war on terror’s focus on dangerous individuals, in other words, supplied a template that is now being applied to suspected criminals, foreign officials, heads of government, migrants, and protesters. Domestic military deployment has followed a parallel track. In 2002, Washington established U.S. Northern Command to direct homeland defense and support civil authorities. In 2025, the army created Western Hemisphere Command by combining Forces Command, Army North, and Army South under one four-star headquarters responsible for readiness, homeland defense, and operations across the Americas. Neither change erased statutory barriers to domestic military law enforcement. But both reduced the organizational distance between military forces prepared for overseas combat and missions close to home. Since June 2025, the administration has deployed National Guard personnel or active-duty Marines to six American cities. It has also assigned active-duty personnel to support ICE processing and detention facilities. These steps did not formally merge the military and DHS, but they created recurring joint operations through which domestic coercive missions could expand. Meanwhile, Trump is politicizing the armed forces, basing appointments and promotions on partisan loyalty and degrading or simply ignoring long-standing professional norms. These changes will presumably weaken the institutional barriers to the military’s political use, which concerns the missions the president assigned to military personnel, as in Los Angeles, where National Guard troops and Marines accompanied federal immigration operations. A federal district court found that troops had been systematically directed to perform law enforcement functions, including patrols and traffic control, in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act, and the administration ultimately halted these operations. But Trump has declared that they will resume on a larger scale. The homeland, he thinks, is an excellent place for U.S. armed forces to conduct battles. “We should use some of these dangerous cities as training grounds for our military,” Trump said in September 2025. “We’re under invasion from within. No different than a foreign enemy but more difficult in many ways because they don’t wear uniforms.” Urban opposition has been placed within a vocabulary of war. WHERE DOES IT END? War has not only changed the tenor of American life and enabled a vast expansion of executive power. It has also had a radicalizing effect on parts of the population, including war veterans—a phenomenon that bears echoes of the Freikorps, the groups of disbanded soldiers in Weimar Germany who, once given policing powers against the “Bolshevik” threat, quickly became a lethal paramilitary force. In her history of the white power movement, the scholar Kathleen Belew has shown how a segment of Vietnam veterans joined civilians in building a narrative of betrayal, transferring military skills and organizational forms into paramilitary politics to be redirected against enemies at home. The 1992 Ruby Ridge confrontation and the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing came from that milieu. Today, a recurrence of that pattern can be seen among veterans of Afghanistan and Iraq. Groups such as the Oath Keepers and the Three Percenters recruit current and former military personnel and police officers. Its members used military formations during the January 6 attack, and the founder of the Oath Keepers was convicted of seditious conspiracy. Of these, all had their cases dismissed, were pardoned, or had their sentences commuted by Trump. How dangerous these groups still might be is poorly understood: the Trump administration has banned contact between scholars and military personnel except in the framework of professional military education, so there is no up-to-date survey data or qualitative information on attitudes within the military about political matters. Publicly available government reporting on militias has also dried up. Given that such groups have had practical and rhetorical support from the administration in power, the threat of more violence cannot be discounted. Of course, the war on terror also had an immense role in shaping the international environment that the United States contends with today. Iran is a more capable opponent because the war in Iraq converted Hussein’s Sunni regime into one subject to Iranian influence and helped facilitate an Iranian-backed network (the “Axis of Resistance”) across the region. Islamophobia helped spur the rise of populist right-wing parties in Europe, alongside the migration crisis caused by Syria’s civil war and ISIS’s territorial gains in Syria and Iraq. In Egypt and other Arab countries, authoritarian regimes have consolidated control and gained U.S. support by arguing that they are holding the line against terrorists. And as many as 500,000 foreign civilians were killed or died as a result of the war on terror—a history that has left its own grim legacy abroad. The war on terror created a far more powerful government. In the 25 years since the 9/11 attacks, the commemorations have tended to follow a predictable pattern: recollections of the awful events of that day, the reading of names, the lighting of candles. Beyond the now ritual agreement that Iraq was a huge mistake and that Afghanistan was the neglected theater, the consequences of the United States’ reaction to those attacks—and how it has remade the country—remain surprisingly unexamined. It is well past time to give those consequences much closer attention. The 9/11 attacks accelerated the transformation of U.S. political discord from a disagreement between competing ideological coalitions into a conflict between mutually threatening social identities. Islamophobia was both an early expression of that transformation and an important mechanism through which Americans learned to define internal enemies. Over the following quarter century, this mechanism migrated from Muslims to immigrants, racial protesters, cultural minorities, and, ultimately, partisan opponents themselves. Indeed, the most important domestic political legacy of the war on terror may be that the category “terrorist” gradually shifted from the realm of political violence to a model for thinking about political opponents. Meanwhile, the war on terror created a far more powerful government. After 9/11, the United States built a state optimized for identifying threats before they materialized, relying on ubiquitous surveillance, integrated databases, watch lists, preventive policing, militarized border enforcement, expansive secrecy, remote coercive power, broad emergency authority, and a sorcerer’s apprentice national security bureaucracy. President George W. Bush constructed much of this architecture. But even as he constrained parts of it, President Barack Obama embraced much of what he inherited. Congress repeatedly ratified or declined to dismantle it. Presidential self-restraint became the independent variable in the calculation of democracy’s fate. This posed an obvious latent danger. Institutions created on the assumption that presidents would distinguish genuine national security threats from political enemies were safe only as long as presidents continued to make that distinction. When Trump entered the presidency in January 2017 with an unprecedented vision of executive power that he justified through inflammatory threat rhetoric, he could draw on a highly developed set of tools. The war on terror did not create American authoritarianism, but it certainly reduced the startup costs of an authoritarian presidency. item.title: The New Chinese Way of Cyberwar
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.34
Over the past year, the world’s attention has turned to economic chokepoints—with good reason. Iran has exercised its control over the Strait of Hormuz to gum up the global economy, and China has used its command over critical minerals to gain leverage in trade negotiations. Less consideration, however, has been paid to chokepoints in the digital domain, which could prove just as treacherous. Chinese hackers have gained and retained access to U.S. communications, energy, and transportation infrastructure. The goal of these intrusions is more than intelligence gathering; it is laying the groundwork for sabotage. Just as Iran’s closure of a vital waterway has been extremely disruptive and hard to get around, China’s penetration of critical networks could cause blackouts, make water unsafe to drink, or delay military mobilization. Indeed, the fragility of U.S. critical infrastructure was made clear this summer when Iranian hackers compromised water facilities across multiple U.S. states, causing one county to direct residents to boil water. U.S. allies are also vulnerable. China has breached hospitals in Taiwan, power grids in India, and telecommunications networks in Singapore. As I argued in an essay in Foreign Affairs last year, there is a fundamental asymmetry between China’s authoritarian approach to cyberdefense and the United States’ more democratic method. American laws and values preclude the U.S. government from monitoring private communications and critical national networks in the ways that the Chinese government does. Beijing, for its part, maintains a series of firewalls that—in addition to surveilling and censoring the Chinese people—protect Chinese networks from American offensive intrusions. And where critical infrastructure in China is centralized and controlled by the state, in the United States it is owned and operated by a diverse array of private actors with varying levels of cyberdefense. China, therefore, can use cyberweapons against the United States and its allies with greater confidence that it can withstand retaliation. Artificial intelligence is likely to exacerbate this asymmetry. Although the technology has revolutionized both offensive and defensive cyber-operations, it tends to benefit attackers more. Because AI could disproportionately benefit China, the United States has all the more reason to use the technology to improve its cyberdefenses. A year ago, using AI to defend critical infrastructure at scale was possible only in principle. Today, it is possible in practice, as advances in AI have brought down the costs of securing U.S. critical infrastructure. To root out Beijing’s digital chokepoints before they are weaponized, Washington, AI labs, and infrastructure operators need to proactively stress-test critical systems, such as plants and grids serving big cities or military bases, against cutting-edge AI models. Doing so would reveal decades of accumulated American vulnerabilities and offer a guide to how to fix them. Without such an understanding, the United States will continue to lose the cyberwar to China. A NEW FRONTIER Economies and militaries often run on digital infrastructure that wasn’t built for the tasks they carry out today, making them attractive and accessible targets for sabotage. That is, in part, why wars of the future will likely play out in the cyber-domain. The United States’ infrastructure is particularly vulnerable. Its power plants and pipelines run on decades-old hardware that was designed for physical reliability, not digital defense. They often lack the logging, encryption, or patching capabilities that create layers of protection. As American utilities modernized, their legacy equipment was wired into computer networks and cloud services for remote monitoring. This created a wealth of opportunities for hackers. Before the advent of the Internet, a saboteur might have had to plant explosives to destroy a gas pipeline. Today, a vandal might be able to shut one off by hacking into a poorly secured router sitting in a in a corporate office. To make matters worse, until recently U.S. utility companies had few incentives or requirements to shore up security. Before the advancement of AI, determining systemic risk required manual, expensive engineering analysis. And before 2021, there were few, if any, cybersecurity regulations for critical infrastructure. The Biden administration established baseline standards for pipelines, ports, airports, and water systems, such as requiring operators to implement multifactor authentication and endpoint monitoring. The United States’ infrastructure is particularly vulnerable. As AI has advanced, cyberattacks have become more dangerous. In fact, OpenAI and Anthropic admitted this summer that their models have already hacked other companies without human direction. Rogue AI could make deterring a state-sponsored cyberattack harder because it offers the aggressor plausible deniability. If a victimized country isn’t certain that a strike was directed by an adversary, or even intentional at all, it may be more hesitant to retaliate. Moreover, the United States needs to protect itself from the possibility that AI from an American company, on its own accord, attacks U.S. infrastructure. But just as AI can enhance cyberattacks, it can also make it easier to mount a cyberdefense. The technology is advanced enough to synthesize a massive amount of data to model infrastructure systems and the threats against them. A utility company could use AI to create a virtual replica of its physical systems, known as a digital twin, that uses sensors and data to mirror the behavior and performance of its real-world counterpart. A digital twin eventually learns what a system’s normal operations look like. It can pinpoint weaknesses and flag any unusual activity, potentially spotting malware. Today’s AI models have the capability to generate digital twins with varied accuracy and sophistication. Much as Waymo’s approach to testing its autonomous systems relies on millions of simulations at increasing detail and cost, a utility company building a digital twin can refine its granularity over time. If tensions heighten with an adversary, for example, the United States could model potential attacks on its own grid to figure out which vulnerabilities, if exploited, would wreak the most havoc. When the United States tried to prepare for the possibility of Russian sabotage in 2022, it could not easily determine which of its weaknesses could be used to disrupt a power grid or water facility for more than 24 hours or which investments in cybersecurity would be most effective at preventing chaos. Today, with the help of digital twins, it is possible to figure out those flaws and prioritize fixes. CARBON COPY Washington now has the technology to protect its critical systems, but it must overcome the obstacles to deploying it, including the decentralized nature of American infrastructure, the way legal liability is assigned, and the high cost of upgrading cybersecurity, which has suffered from decades of underinvestment. Throughout the United States, there are more than 4,500 public water systems, 3,000 electric utilities, and thousands of independent pipeline and telecom operators. And the private corporations and municipalities that operate most of these entities are hesitant to find and share details about their networks because revealing a flaw or unpatched vulnerability can expose them to government fines or lawsuits claiming negligence. But without such data, digital twins cannot operate accurately. The U.S. government must adopt a coordinated, national approach to building digital twins for the most critical of U.S. infrastructure systems—such as those serving ports, large populations, or military bases—and ensure those proxies are a faithful replica. The approach should change the way government and the private sector work together, leveraging the incentives that both frontier AI labs and infrastructure firms have to invest in digital twins. Over the last year, as frontier AI labs have released more powerful models, it has become increasingly difficult to generate puzzles complex enough to measure advancing AI capabilities. Digital twins of real-world infrastructure can provide a more effective testing environment for frontier models—acting as a new cyber gym. AI companies, therefore, have a reason to subsidize the building and maintenance of digital twins as they can be used to evaluate the safety of unreleased models against real systems. Infrastructure owners, in turn, would benefit by seeing their network defenses probed by state-of-the-art technology, at minimal cost. The United States needs a safe space to run such simulations. The Department of Energy, along with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, could partner with AI companies to establish a secure, air-gapped national enclave for the continuous testing of critical infrastructure. Utility owners and operators across the country could upload digital twins of their networks into this enclave and the enclave’s AI agents would constantly stress-test utility systems and offer recommendations for the highest priority cybersecurity fixes. Any unearthed bugs could inform Gold Eagle, an initiative the White House established this summer to coordinate finding and fixing vulnerabilities in U.S. networks. Patches could also be shared with allies to built trust in the American AI ecosystem and incentivize allies to use U.S. models. Rogue AI could make deterring a state-sponsored cyberattack harder. To entice utility owners and operators to participate, Congress should provide them legal safe harbor—including protections from lawsuits by the companies or people they serve—for finding weaknesses or evidence of misuse as a result of feeding data into authorized national defense AI platforms. Congress should also help cover the cost of fixing flaws or eliminating foreign footholds that are discovered by establishing a pool of money, modeled on the EPA’s funds, that would issue grants to patch immediate high-risk flaws, alongside long-term, zero-interest loans for larger utilities to undertake deep overhauls. In addition, nonprofit or private-sector programs, such as OpenAI’s Daybreak, could consider issuing grants to cover the costs. The federal government must also change how it conducts oversight. Today, it judges utility companies based on their compliance with legal standards that often lag behind advancements in hacking. A better way would be to assess utility operators on the amount of time it takes them to contain a cyberattack. Over time, these operators, for example, should be required to show, via a simulation with a digital twin, that they can isolate an attack within a reasonable time frame. Although such government efforts are worthwhile, they will take time to come to fruition. In the meantime, industries that are most at risk from the weaponization of digital chokepoints, such as hospitals and banks, should work together to press their most important suppliers to use AI to fix gaps in their cybersecurity. By coordinating through information-sharing analysis centers—organizations that act as a neighborhood watch for a particular industry and offer certain legal protections—companies can press for action through contractual means. Advancements in AI offer the United States and its allies their first real opportunity in many years to catch up to China on the cyber front. The technology to map and defend critical U.S. and allied systems is arriving faster than expected. The ultimate measure of U.S. resilience in the face of digital Chinese chokepoints will not be the raw capability of AI models but the willingness of U.S. institutions to use them—before an adversary causes a major disruption to American lives. item.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.30
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished. In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda. Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether. Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased. For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would. A MOVING TARGET In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization. Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him. By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda. More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic. THINGS FALL APART But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated. Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory. ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda. Much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments. In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead. Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed. item.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.27
In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern. Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included. In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge. FOOD, GLORIOUS FOOD It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states. These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated. Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public. Washington retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations. Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters. Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself. Food security is one of the few issues that can bring the whole world together. Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior. Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks. Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones. MORE WITH LESS The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges. The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them. The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners. But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one. Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards. REAPING AND SOWING At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership. That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests. Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it.
