item.title: Cuba’s Point of No Return
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.09
In central Havana, a giant mound of sand-colored rubble fills an entire city block. It is all that remains of the Superior Institute of Industrial Design—a stately building that in its 166 years housed a Spanish officers’ club, U.S. occupation forces after 1898, Cuba’s health ministry, and, finally, the design school. Declared uninhabitable years ago, it suffered two partial collapses in 2025. The state never sent anyone to fix it. This past February, what remained suddenly fell, entombing several squatters. When I visited in June, skinny men scaled the craggy surface, prying loose bits of brick that they carted off to build makeshift houses. Cuba, on its current trajectory, is headed for the fate of the design school: what lies ahead is an accelerating collapse of the state and economy. Unless this course is reversed soon, rebuilding the island as a stable, prosperous, and democratic place could become virtually impossible. A few months ago, a slow unraveling was not what most observers expected. Because of the tariff threat in place since February against countries supplying oil to Cuba, President Donald Trump’s warnings of military action, and reports of secret talks between Havana and Washington, many believed that either a power-sharing deal or a Venezuela-style military operation was imminent. By late May, that looked less likely. By then, according to the Miami Herald, the backchannel talks had collapsed amid opposition from Florida Republicans and Havana’s rejection of Washington’s offer: U.S. investment and petroleum in exchange for President Miguel Díaz-Canel’s removal and the privatization of Cuba’s state oil company. Havana enacted 176 economic reforms in June, which expanded space for the private sector, but this did not satisfy Washington. While allowing limited U.S. fuel and food to reach the island through private distributors, the Trump administration added new sanctions against state companies and regime officials. In August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Axios that the policy’s timeline had shifted, saying that it would take “patience and persistence” and that the regime could survive into 2028 or beyond. There are a few ways to read Rubio’s comments. One is that the administration is bluffing. It is threatening to maintain the current extraordinary sanctions pressure either to restart the stalled negotiations or to misdirect the regime ahead of a military operation. Another is that, with the United States entangled in Iran and busy managing Venezuela, Cuba has simply been demoted as a priority. The administration has put the island on life support, with just enough U.S. fuel and food allowed to reach private firms to prevent societal breakdown, but otherwise it has no new plan. Cuba policy has been set to autopilot. A third is that the administration has concluded that waiting for the one-party system to implode from within is the only viable path to regime change, even if it is long, tortuous, and uncertain. Regardless, what is not widely appreciated outside Cuba is how economic and state collapse—triggered by the regime’s unwillingness to reform and hastened by U.S. sanctions—is already remaking the island. The state, aside from its capacity for political repression, is rapidly weakening. The economy is contracting and growing more unequal, leaving a large underclass too poor to participate meaningfully in the new private sector. Social cohesion is fraying, and crime is rising, while plunging birth rates and emigration warp Cuba’s demographics. All these trends predate the foreign oil cutoff and the newest sanctions by years, if not decades, but each now appears to be accelerating. The danger is that the longer the impasse lasts, the more they will calcify into the baseline conditions for any future transition, narrowing the chances that Cuba ever becomes a well-governed country—and increasing the likelihood of an even more dysfunctional, chaotic future instead. If nothing changes soon, a transitional government could one day find itself in the same impossible position as the men atop the ruins of the design institute: trying to build something safe, habitable, and lasting out of rubble. AUTHORITARIAN ANARCHY In Havana, I heard a joke. “Only two things work in this country: the state security apparatus and the hospitals.” It was too generous to the hospitals. About state security, it was true. Repression is the only thing the Cuban state still does well. This owes less to any apparent abundance of resources than to the leadership’s entirely rational unity. The headquarters of the Directorate of Penal Institutions, which administers the country’s prison system, is as decrepit as any building in central Havana, with cardboard filling broken windows. But the generals and spy chiefs know how much they would lose from political liberalization. If the Trump administration has tried to convince some of them that there are off-ramps, it does not appear to have succeeded. So they stick together, and the state’s capacity for repression remains intact. Although Cubans I met were astonishingly willing to criticize the regime on street corners or within earshot of neighbors, and almost all did, none said that they would join a public protest, a near-certain route to detention. In case anyone forgot, police cars sat parked outside the family homes of detained protest leaders as ominous reminders; with fuel so scarce, it is telling that the regime can still find the gasoline to dispatch them. On every other dimension, however, the Cuban state is weaker than most foreign observers realize—both those on the right, who imagine an anti-American leviathan, and those on the left, who cling to the fiction of functional schools and hospitals. A better description came from a European diplomat in Havana: “authoritarian anarchy,” a state that can still stifle political expression but is increasingly unable to provide public services or to prevent disorder. Repression is the only thing the Cuban state still does well. Take public health, long one of the Cuban state’s proudest achievements. Access to the best clinics always depended on connections. But through the early 2010s, Cuba’s population-level health indicators, underpinned by well-trained doctors and generous public investment, were among Latin America’s strongest. Today, most hospitals lack essential supplies and medicines, forcing patients to buy everything from antibiotics to amputation saws on the black market. Although many doctors do their best under the circumstances, unlivable public salaries have made bribe-taking increasingly common. Graduating medical students pursue unrelated work in the emerging private sector or emigrate. The results are stark: infant mortality, once among the lowest in the region, has more than doubled since 2018, and mosquito-borne illnesses that the state had previously contained are back. Chikungunya alone infected up to a third of the population in 2025; cases of dengue and Zika have also surged. Violent crime, once almost unknown on the island, is rising sharply—another sign of the state’s haphazard retreat. Although the lack of reliable official statistics makes this hard to confirm, and although Cuba still endures far less violence than several of its neighbors, fear of robbery and assault has altered many Cubans’ daily routines. Residents of Cárdenas, a small city two hours east of Havana, stay off the streets at night. Vigilantes are allegedly behind a growing number of killings of criminal suspects there and in the city of Guantánamo (not to be confused with the nearby U.S. military base of the same name). In Havana, stories of break-ins to steal solar panels and water tanks have become common, and there is a widespread perception that police are ever more absent or bribable. Although crime is disorganized for now—driven by abject need or addiction to the cheap synthetic cannabinoid known as el químico, now everywhere on the island—it could easily cohere into something more organized. Crumbling power plants, a shortened school year, the holes Havana residents have cut into the streets to siphon off scarce public water for resale or private consumption—the hollowing of the state is visible everywhere. The long-term effects of the embargo are partly to blame, as is the cutoff of foreign oil since February. But no one forced Cuba’s leaders to devote, by 2024, 37 times as much public capital investment to tourism, real estate, and hospitality as to health and education. That was a profit-seeking gamble by a small clique of insiders, and it failed. The question now is whether the state will be able to do anything at all, including maintain public order, after several more years of breakdown. THE LONGEST ROAD The second transformation remaking Cuba, and creating dilemmas for a future transition, is economic. The economy is shrinking: it has contracted by at least 15 percent since 2020, as tourism cratered and foreign investors fled for fear of new U.S. secondary sanctions. In response, the regime has grudgingly opened space for private enterprise—not because most officials favor markets but because they have concluded that some market activity is the only way to keep the island from starving or rebelling. Since the 2021 legalization of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises, known in Spanish as MIPYMEs, these firms have come to number more than 10,000, accounting for an estimated 65 percent of all retail sales and 40 percent of total employment. June’s reforms formally expanded what private activity is permitted, although U.S. sanctions, the regime’s lack of credibility with domestic and foreign investors, and its internal divisions will likely limit their implementation. The growth of the private sector has been positive and necessary, keeping at least some shelves stocked amid the crisis and making at least part of the population less beholden to public salaries, a source of leverage for the regime. The 2021 currency unification was another necessary step. Despite its disastrous implementation, which shredded most Cubans’ purchasing power, it ended a dual-currency system that had distorted prices and masked state enterprises’ underperformance. But the specific way markets are taking root—with much of the population too poor to participate meaningfully, with no rule of law, and with the gap between winners and losers steadily widening—is pernicious for the country’s future. Several Cubans I met said they felt as if they were living through Russia’s 1990s: a period of murky deals and rigged competition that led not to broad-based prosperity but to oligarchs and mass immiseration. The word they repeated most was reparto—a divvying up of the country. Regime insiders are positioned to gain the most, and MIPYME owners have a foot in the door. Meanwhile, the young, the old, public-sector workers, and many Afro-Cubans are increasingly struggling just to eat. As one Cuban woman put it to me, “We took the longest, most painful road to Latin American capitalism.” Cuba is reproducing the worst defects of certain Central American economies—rigid class differences, cronyism, remittance dependence, and low productivity—only without their comparatively stronger growth. The widening inequality is hard to miss: even now, with blackouts regularly stretching two to three days, better-off neighborhoods have new restaurants with generators humming, lights on, live DJs, and full tables. Around them stand darkened houses, and uncollected trash piles up on the street. It didn’t have to be this way. Cuba’s population remains highly educated, even as the wages MIPYMEs can pay pull skilled professionals away from their fields. A transition today could still put a dynamic and fair market economy within reach. In two or three more years, it might not. THOSE WHO STAY The last dimension of Cuba’s collapse is the hardest to measure, but the one many Cubans told me they worry about most: what several described as “social decay.” The interlocking effects of mass emigration, rapid aging, and a growing generational divide pose enormous challenges for Cuba’s future. Since 2020, Cuba’s population has fallen by an estimated 13 to 24 percent, driven largely by an unprecedented emigration wave. Because those who left were disproportionately women of reproductive age, Cuba’s already rapid aging has accelerated. By 2050, authorities forecast, one in three Cubans will be over the age of 60, up from one in four today. That would be a significant challenge even for a country with a strong economy and a functional pension system. For Cuba, it could become an insurmountable one. Emigration has also hollowed out entire professions, emptying hospitals of health workers, schools of teachers, and even churches of priests and pastors, on a scale that Cubans have never seen before. Several middle-aged Cubans drew a contrast with the 1990s Special Period, when the loss of Soviet aid and trade shrank the economy by about 35 percent but far fewer doctors and teachers left. The island was broke then, yet hospitals and schools kept functioning. That is no longer the case. A divide has also grown between Cubans who have family abroad (and remittances with which to start businesses) and those with no such connections, disproportionately Afro-Cubans. Living without sufficient food, energy, or medicine is exacting a psychological toll as well. The young are paying the highest price, especially those whose parents are abroad and who are growing up hungrier and more excluded than earlier generations. But the cost is generalized. “This is not resilience,” a man told me in Havana, referring to the cliché that Cubans are uniquely gifted at enduring hardship. “People can adapt to anything. We transform ourselves to manage to survive this process, but it is a degradation.” THE PRICE OF DELAY When Cuba’s Caribbean and Central American neighbors began their transitions to democracy 40 to 50 years ago, few expected them to succeed. Most were far poorer, more economically dysfunctional, and more unequal than they are today. And yet they proved that unfavorable starting conditions are not destiny: most democratized and saw their economies grow and stabilize. Cuba could, too. But the longer the current stalemate lasts, the dimmer that prospect grows. Sustaining the current level of pressure may cause the regime to implode, or it may not. What it will certainly do, if it persists for another year or more, is make Cuba increasingly ungovernable—by anyone. The Trump administration may not have weighed that danger or may have judged it an acceptable cost of forcing a political opening. Strikingly, some ordinary Cubans have made the same calculation. Many I met did not believe that U.S. sanctions were primarily to blame for the current crisis. To them, whether sanctions stayed or went mattered far less than whether the regime did, since in their view it bore greater responsibility for the ruined economy. A new nationally representative survey by AmericasBarometer shows something similar: 74 percent of respondents blamed the Cuban government for the current crisis, while just 16 percent blamed the United States. All this said, the risks of sustaining the current pressure indefinitely are immense. For both countries, arguably nothing would be worse than a spiral into criminal violence and chaotic ungovernability on the island. Prolonged maximum pressure also raises the price of eventual repair, and a post-transition Cuba will have limited means of financing reconstruction. Rebuilding Cuba’s electric grid alone, degraded further with each additional blackout, will cost an estimated $8 billion. It might take the country years to regain access to financing from the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and other multilateral institutions. Given the U.S. public’s fatigue with nation building abroad, Congress is unlikely to step in to fill the gap in the meantime. The opposite course carries costs of its own. Those who propose normalization and the lifting of the embargo without meaningful political change need to be honest about what this means: accepting that Cubans, against their will, would go on living under a regime that enriches itself while keeping citizens poor enough to control. They should have no illusions that Cuba’s leaders, with fewer sanctions, will be able to rebuild state institutions, lower inequality, or restore social cohesion. The leadership’s objective is to remain in power. A third way may still be possible: a new offer of targeted sanctions relief, focused on alleviating the humanitarian crisis, in exchange for specific political and economic reforms that could weaken the regime’s control. Even if Havana has rejected such deals before, it is worth attempting. But whatever path Washington chooses, it must consider the costs of delay—already high and only rising. item.title: What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.52
What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree Ahead of January elections, Bola Tinubu is pulling out all the stops to stem insecurity. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Spending Spree Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has appointed Maj. Gen. Ibikunle Ajose as the new top army commander for the northeast, the epicenter of the country’s Islamist insurgency, after the previous leader spent less than two years in the role. The move is the latest in a series of military reforms ahead of January’s general elections, in which insecurity will be high on the list of voters’ concerns. Ajose’s appointment was part of a bigger reshuffling last week that involved 15 top generals. These redeployments, along with a major hike in military spending, are key to the government’s wider plan to stabilize bellwether regions before Nigerians head to the polls. Tinubu is seeking a second term as the candidate for the All Progressives Congress party and will face the same main challengers he came up against in 2023: former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, who is running under the African Democratic Congress (ADC), and former Anambra state Gov. Peter Obi, with the Nigeria Democratic Congress. This year, Abubakar and Obi initially joined forces to unseat Tinubu under an ADC-led opposition coalition, but the alliance fractured due to their competing ambitions. Observers are looking to see whether Obi in particular, who came in third in 2023, can translate the unprecedented backing he garnered from young Nigerian urbanites in the last election into rural support. Importantly, the public is paying close attention to how candidates intend to address widespread violence and kidnappings for ransom. A mass kidnapping of schoolchildren in Tinubu’s political heartland in the southwestern state of Oyo in May magnified the issue. More than 7,800 people were kidnapped in Nigeria between July 2025 and June 2026—a 66 percent increase from the previous year, according to a new report from risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence. Over that period, kidnappers received some $5.8 million in ransom money, three times that of the previous year. Boko Haram collected 90 percent of those payments, mainly from mass abductions. The insecurity has ripple effects across the country. For instance, many farmers have been unable to access their lands due to the threat of kidnappings, leading to food shortages and hunger, especially in the north. The “security question in Nigeria is closely connected to the economic one: An attack that closes a road, displaces farmers, or shuts a market very quickly becomes an issue of household income and food prices,” said Sekinat Ojeniyi of Africa Practice, a global risk advisory firm. On the campaign trail, Abubakar has pledged to end insecurity within one year if elected. His plan centers on cross-border military collaboration with Sahel nations and providing jobs for young people drawn to extremism. Obi has also promised to fix insecurity in one term through youth poverty alleviation and education. “You cannot create widespread poverty and expect peace,” Obi told Nigerian broadcaster Channels Television. Tinubu’s government, meanwhile, is injecting unprecedented amounts of money into defense in an attempt to address the issue. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Nigeria’s military expenditure surged 55 percent year-on-year to $2.1 billion in 2025. That figure is expected to double this year. With this money, Tinubu approved salary increases for members of the military last month. The massive investment also supports the largest expansion of the Nigerian military since the country’s civil war in the late 1960s. In July, Tinubu approved the creation of four new army divisions with a planned recruitment of 28,000 additional personnel by December. A new bill passed by Nigeria’s National Assembly in June would also allow states to establish their own police forces, putting less pressure on the federal police to secure dense forested communities that have become hideouts for extremists. “The government’s emphasis on manpower and personnel welfare makes sense, but more personnel and better pay do not automatically translate into greater security,” Ojeniyi said. “Kidnapping networks are highly adaptive and operate across state and local government boundaries, while the police, military, and intelligence agencies do not always have the same visibility or operational reach.” Meanwhile, many Nigerian and U.S. political observers have commended Tinubu for his handling of tensions with Washington, which has transformed the Trump administration’s divisive rhetoric about supposed Christian persecution in Nigeria into security cooperation. Beginning late last year, the United States deployed troops to assist with counterterrorism operations. (Most U.S. troops withdrew in July.) Although U.S. strikes in northeastern Nigeria in May killed a senior Islamic State leader, the mass abductions have continued. More than 600 people were taken from Nigeria’s north-central Niger state last month in an attack on a mosque. Although many Nigerians welcome his new security reforms, Tinubu will likely be judged on whether these last-gasp efforts a few months ahead of elections can stem the violence. The Week Ahead Wednesday, Sept. 16: The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a nomination hearing on ambassadors to Benin, Gabon, Kenya, and Togo. Wednesday, Sept. 16, to Thursday, Sept. 17: Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo meet in Geneva to discuss monitoring their cease-fire. Wednesday, Sept. 23: Morocco holds general elections. What We’re Watching Historic IPO. Africa’s richest person, Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, launched the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering on Monday, floating 4.1 billion shares in his $20 billion oil refinery on the outskirts of Lagos on the Nigerian Exchange. The rush to buy shares briefly crashed many Nigerian investment apps. The move is expected to raise about $1.6 billion, which will fund Dangote’s expansion projects across Africa. Dangote Industries said it will use the investment to double production capacity, deliver refined products across the continent, and build another refinery in Kenya. The public offer closes on Oct. 13, and Dangote is reportedly eyeing a secondary New York listing in the future. Sahrawi citizenship. The Spanish parliament’s lower house approved a bill granting citizenship to Sahrawis born before 1977, when Madrid administered Western Sahara. The legislation will now go to Spain’s Senate. It marks the latest escalation of tensions with Morocco after thousands of migrants entered Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta from Morocco in late July. Rabat claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Western Sahara, and it has occupied about 80 percent of the latter’s territory since the 1970s. More than 170,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria, which hosts the Polisario Front, a group fighting for Sahrawi independence. U.S. tech bid. The United States will lend nearly $100 million to Africell, the only mainstream U.S.-owned mobile network operator in Africa, as part of broader strategic investments to counter China in the region. Africell operates in Angola, Congo, Gambia, and Sierra Leone. The loan from the U.S. Export-Import Bank is part of Washington’s efforts to counter the expansion of China’s Huawei company in Africa. But the United States has a long way to go: Chinese firms are now baked into the continent’s tech infrastructure. For example, the three major smartphone brands in Africa—Tecno, Itel, and Infinix—are manufactured by China’s Transsion and have dominated the market for nearly two decades. Congo-Israel ties. Congo has revived plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem following President Felix Tshisekedi’s visit to the country earlier this month. Analysts consider the move an attempt to both court Israeli security support and get the United States to exert more pressure on Rwanda to stop backing the M23 rebel group in eastern Congo. Tshisekedi previously told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023 that Congo would move the embassy, three years after Tshisekedi announced that he would appoint its first ambassador to Israel in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Tshisekedi faces mounting calls in Congo to resign over his attempts to implement constitutional reforms that could pave the way for a third term in office. This Week in Health The United States has announced that it will no longer fund Namibia’s HIV program after a final $45 million disbursement for the 2027 fiscal year, ending more than two decades of aid through the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, which has provided around $1.1 billion to Namibia since it was launched under President George W. Bush in 2003. The withdrawal follows Namibia’s refusal to give the United States unrestricted access to genetic data and pathogens, which it could then share with private companies and organizations without oversight from the Namibian government as part of Trump’s America First Global Health Strategy. Namibian officials cited concerns over sovereignty, national law, and patient privacy. Since pulling out of the World Health Organization in January, the Trump administration has pursued deals that would provide commercial access to African nations’ health data. So far, Ghana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe have rejected such deals, while at least 19 nations, including Nigeria and Ethiopia, have agreed to them. “We need to reserve our data, and no one has the right to get a sovereign state to be used for other things, except for the World Health Organization cabinet,” former Namibian Health Minister Richard Kamwi said in August. FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan What We’re Reading Al-Shabab’s win. In Foreign Policy, Mohamed Gabobe reports from Mogadishu on how the U.S. withdrawal of support for the African Union peacekeeping mission in the country has severely jeopardized the remaining forces’ capacity to counter the Islamist group al-Shabab. The two-decade military intervention’s failure to quash al-Shabab—which has “has retaken nearly all the territory that it lost in a 2022-2023 Somali army campaign,” Gabobe writes—partly informed Washington’s decision. There “is no one other nation that can fill the United States’ void,” he adds. What’s in a map? On Sept. 4, the United Nations General Assembly voted to adopt a Togo-sponsored resolution to replace the traditional Mercator map with one that better represents Africa’s true size. Only the United States voted against it. In Foreign Policy, Howard W. French argues that this is just the latest example of the West being behind in understanding not just Africa’s geographic size but also its demographic weight. “Just as drawing up maps in ways that graphically diminish Africa does nothing to reduce Africa’s true dimensions, actively shunning African migrants will do nothing to change the hard demographic realities that will radically shape our collective future,” he writes. Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. item.title: The EU’s 28th State?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.37
The EU’s 28th State? European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floats making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. “We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seated on her left, von der Leyen outlined what such a future might look like, starting with an expansion of their existing free-trade agreement. Carney has been pitching such an arrangement to European officials for months. A Canadian official told The Associated Press last week that the two sides are discussing potential ties that stop just short of full membership. This could include allowing Canadian citizens to live and work in EU member states without needing a visa. An expanded partnership might also bolster collaboration in defense production, critical minerals procurement, economic security, and the development of artificial intelligence, among others. Canada wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday, adding that further discussions are expected to take place at the Canada-EU summit in October. Under EU regulations, the bloc requires unanimous approval to welcome new members. Although von der Leyen insisted on Wednesday that the Canada proposal is “not a partnership against anyone else,” the gesture comes at a time when both Canada’s and Europe’s relations with the United States under President Donald Trump are greatly strained. Last month, the White House imposed sweeping tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting “dollar for dollar” retaliatory duties on around 700 U.S. products. This was in spite of Canada being one of the United States’ largest trading partners; bilateral trade accounted for around $872.3 billion in 2025. Alongside a recent war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford as well as the U.S. president’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state, Ottawa has begun to prioritize its relationship with the EU over what it once considered its closest partner. But not everyone in Europe appears thrilled with von der Leyen’s proposal. “Of all the third countries, Canada is one of the few that we all want to get closer to right now,” an EU diplomat told the Financial Times. “But even with them, we all know we have to be careful when you start talking about trade access and preferential treatment.” Notably, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify the bloc’s 2017 free-trade deal with Canada, citing several provisions that they argue favor Canadian investors. Whether the idea ever materializes, the fact that it’s being talked about at such high levels is a sign of what Carney called the “rupture in the world order.” The Canadian premier will take the stage on Thursday to address the European Parliament. Today’s Most Read - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree - Why My Kyiv Visit Worried Me So Much by Ravi Agrawal - Only China, India, and Russia Can End the Iran War by Amir Handjani What We’re Following Guilty of war crimes. Former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Wednesday after being found guilty of orchestrating war crimes during the country’s brutal fight for independence against Serbia in the late 1990s. He continues to deny any wrongdoing and is expected to appeal the ruling. The sentence was handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a special tribunal at The Hague. According to the tribunal, Thaci oversaw the murder, torture, arbitrary detention, and abuse of alleged opponents, including ethnic minorities and perceived collaborators, while serving as the top commander of the since-disbanded Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA). “The vast majority of them were innocent civilians,” the tribunal said of Thaci’s victims. Thaci was sentenced alongside three other senior members of the ethnic Albanian KLA. Wednesday’s ruling is expected to heighten divisions between Serbians and Kosovar Albanians, the latter of whom often regard Thaci as a hero for his contribution to Kosovo’s independence. Clashes broke out between Thaci supporters and security at The Hague when protesters tried to walk to the tribunal. Incumbent Kosovar Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned Wednesday’s ruling, saying, “While the verdict may have been formally pronounced in the name of the people of Kosovo, this hollow formula must not be conflated with the will of the people.” Mecca is under fire. Saudi forces claimed on Wednesday local time to have intercepted a Houthi drone targeting the holy Muslim city of Mecca the day before. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the attempted attack crossed a “red line,” as it was “intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.” The Organization of Islamic Cooperation similarly denounced the operation as a “heinous” assault. This is the first alleged Houthi strike aimed at Mecca since fighting erupted between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in July. The Houthis denied Riyadh’s allegations, with rebel spokesperson Hazem al-Assad saying, “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.” Both sides have escalated their assaults in recent days. On Wednesday, Saudi warplanes struck Yemeni territory, and Houthi troops attacked Red Sea port cities and Saudi military bases. Such assaults have exacerbated the already tenuous global energy crisis and injected further insecurity into the war-embroiled Middle East. Seeking peace. Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo resumed peace talks in Geneva on Wednesday, alongside mediators from Qatar, Togo, and the United States. The two-day session—the seventh meeting since the two countries signed a U.S.-brokered peace accord last year—aims to address continued fighting in eastern Congo between Congolese forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels. Less than a year ago, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame signed an agreement in Washington to end the deadly conflict. However, without M23 representatives in attendance—and Kigali maintaining that it does not support the rebel group despite U.N. evidence to the contrary—Trump’s self-proclaimed “historic” peace deal did little to actually quell the fighting; just days after the December 2025 signing, around 200,000 people fled renewed violence in the region. Since then, the situation in eastern Congo has continued to deteriorate despite repeated cease-fire attempts. During this week’s talks, Kigali is expected to seek assurances that armed groups will not be allowed to operate in Congolese territory, while Kinshasa asserts that foreign security forces have no right to Congolese soil. Odds and Ends A Paris court awarded Kim Kardashian 1 euro (or $1.15) on Tuesday as compensation for being the victim of an armed robbery in 2016. Kardashian was at the Hôtel de Pourtalès for Paris Fashion Week when a gang of eight thieves, six of whom are currently in their 60s or 70s, bound the media personality with zip ties and stole more than $6 million in jewelry; the so-called grandpa robbers were found guilty of armed robbery and kidnapping, among other charges, last year. Kardashian has since described the incident as “the most terrifying experience of my life” but only requested a symbolic 1 euro in restitution. item.title: Why Existential AI Fears Have Hit a Crescendo
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.93
Why Existential AI Fears Have Hit a Crescendo And the complicated geopolitics of slowing down the technology’s development. Long before ChatGPT and Claude entered the global lexicon, there had been a steady stream of warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence. That stream has now become a flood. Late last month, OpenAI revealed a worrisome new development: Not only had one of its models broken out of its “sandbox” and hacked the company Hugging Face, it had in fact done so in secret coordination with hundreds of other OpenAI models (or “agents”). Subsequent reports revealed that OpenAI’s agents had previously infiltrated two other websites months before the Hugging Face incident. Long before ChatGPT and Claude entered the global lexicon, there had been a steady stream of warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence. That stream has now become a flood. Late last month, OpenAI revealed a worrisome new development: Not only had one of its models broken out of its “sandbox” and hacked the company Hugging Face, it had in fact done so in secret coordination with hundreds of other OpenAI models (or “agents”). Subsequent reports revealed that OpenAI’s agents had previously infiltrated two other websites months before the Hugging Face incident. The hacks exacerbated long-standing concerns around the growing cyber-capabilities of advanced AI models, including their ability to find vulnerabilities in software systems and the potential for AI-assisted bad actors to more easily disrupt poorly defended critical infrastructure such as water systems. The same day as the OpenAI report, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates published an essay warning about the “turbulent AI era” and highlighting societal risks from the technology such as widespread job losses, diminished human cognition and relationships, and use by a variety of bad actors to do harm. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve wished innovation could happen faster,” he wrote. “With AI, my feelings are more complicated.” But even those warnings were dwarfed by the highly public resignation last week of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic who previously worked at OpenAI. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote in a viral social media post announcing his resignation. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Coxon’s sentiments were echoed by several current employees at Anthropic, including Evan Hubinger, who leads the company’s research on alignment (making sure AI models are aligned with humans). “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote, adding that he estimated there was a more than 10 percent chance of that happening within the next decade. Last Thursday, Anthropic released its latest threat intelligence report containing alarming examples of misuse of its Claude models. Days later, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay of his own calling on companies to slow down the pace of AI development and for global governments to do more to rein in the technology. Some of his biggest rival executives—including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis—voiced their agreement in a rare kumbaya moment. All of this has sparked an AI panic in Washington and beyond. U.S. lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are advocating for greater oversight of artificial intelligence. It’s also made for strange bedfellows: Left-wing U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and far-right provocateur Steve Bannon both spoke at a Washington conference called the “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday and called for curbs on AI. But neither the fears nor the calls to slow down are new. The latter date back to at least 2023, when an open letter calling for a six-month pause on “giant AI experiments” received over 33,000 signatures—including Musk’s. Several similar letters and calls have followed, including one as recently as July that was signed by more than 1,300 employees of the top AI companies—including Amodei. “This has been a conversation for quite some time,” said Rumman Chowdhury, an AI researcher who served on the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s AI safety and security board under the Biden administration. “Jacob Coxon is not the first person to leave a frontier lab making similar claims,” she said, joking that AI has long slipped into an “another day, another letter” pattern without meaningful change. So why has the conversation around AI risk spiraled this time? Multiple experts Foreign Policy spoke to used the phrase “perfect storm” when answering that question, pointing to the Hugging Face hack and the revelation about the models’ ability to create a “swarm” to perform tasks together. Amodei expressed “worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet” if the current rate of AI development is maintained. There has always been a heavy degree of skepticism on the motives of AI companies warning about the existential risks of the technology that they continue to forge ahead in building. Amodei acknowledged in his essay that Anthropic gets accused of “hype, ‘doomerism’, or regulatory capture,” adding that he didn’t feel a pause was appropriate back in 2023 but advocates a slowdown now because of how far the technology’s capabilities have progressed. Coxon sought to head off some of those frequent criticisms more pointedly right after warning that AI could kill everyone. “This is not a marketing stunt,” he wrote. Amodei’s claims and the rush of industry warnings should be taken seriously, said Kat Duffy, a senior fellow for digital and cyberspace policy at the Council on Foreign Relations. “I don’t agree with people that these are necessarily PR stunts pre-IPO,” Duffy said, referring to OpenAI and Anthropic’s anticipated trillion-dollar initial public offerings. “You would say that this is incredibly dangerous and look at how good we are at controlling it, or you would say that this is incredibly powerful but it’s not really that dangerous,” she added. “Saying that this is really dangerous and we desperately need the government to jump in—it’s not clear to me why that’s in anyone’s interest as they start to go public.” However, the debate around existential risk to humanity from AI also obfuscates the many real-world harms that the technology is already causing, such as surveillance, algorithmic bias, discrimination, deepfakes, and data misuse, according to Chowdhury. “These are not the issues that are being discussed,” she said. “The regulatory structures or whatever environment that pops up around the kinds of risks that are being talked about today simply lead to a regulatory capture on a very, very narrow set of fantastical scenarios,” she added. The bigger priority, Duffy said, should be increased transparency and visibility into how AI systems are built and tested. “There is a tension between addressing what needs to happen yesterday and addressing the possibilities of catastrophic or existential risk,” she said. “If we do not go on and address the vacuum we currently have in terms of systems, collaboration, independent evaluation and vetting, shared standards, shared understanding of the problem—if we don’t have that, how on earth are we going to be able to navigate things like existential threats?” U.S. President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next week has also contributed to that “perfect storm,” Duffy said. AI is expected to be high on the agenda when the two leaders meet, with many—including Amodei—hoping for the emergence of some sort of shared mechanism to manage the technology’s most catastrophic risks. But early indications are that neither Trump nor Xi is ready to blink first. Trump spent much of Monday dismissing concerns around AI risk and the need to regulate the industry. “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social, one of five separate posts in which he shared a similar message. In that initial post, he cited Xi as announcing that “China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future.” Duffy said China’s advances actually make an argument for more governance, not less, particularly when the leading U.S. AI executives are asking for it. “China continues to close the gap between where we are in AI and where they are in AI,” she said. “Everybody can agree or disagree on exactly what that metric is, but I think there’s uniform consensus that they have been gaining, and they are the most heavily regulated AI environment in the world.” Xi has not directly weighed in on the ongoing debate thus far, but China’s state-run Global Times newspaper published an editorial on Sunday labeling Amodei’s call to slow down AI development a “Cold War playbook” for the technology that is “packed with containment provisions targeting China.” Beijing has long sought to present itself as the more responsible global player when it comes to AI development and governance but hinted on Tuesday that it would prefer doing so through the United Nations—which also convenes for its biggest annual gathering next week—rather than a bilateral agreement with Washington. “AI development and governance require the practice of true multilateralism,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Tuesday. “China always supports the UN’s role as the main channel in global AI governance, and … stands ready to join hands with all countries to build a just and equitable system.” It was a slight hedging of Guo’s statement from the previous day when asked about U.S. AI executives calling for a slowdown, when he said: “Fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only hamper efforts toward sound global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.96
What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany? German far-right populism traces back to reunification—but historians disagree about why. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. The AfD is not solely an eastern German phenomenon: Parties like it exist across the European Union, in the United Kingdom, and in the United States, too. In western Germany, the AfD breaks into double digits everywhere and even tops 20 percent in places. But its popularity is twice as high across eastern Germany—where polled rates of xenophobic sentiment are also much higher. The record result of 44 percent in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections on Sept. 6 is conceivable only in an eastern state, at least for now. One school of German historians explains the eastern mentality through the prism of the German Democratic Republic’s (GDR) fundamentally totalitarian character. Its clearest proponent is Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk, a historian affiliated with the Stasi Records Archive, the repository of the GDR’s secret police files. Kowalczuk hails from a GDR family that was closely tied to the regime, a story he tells in his book Freiheitsschock (Freedom Shock), but broke with his family and cast off the system’s Marxist-Leninist straitjacket, which cost him the opportunity to attend university. (After unification, he studied history at Humboldt University.) At 22, he joined the countrywide demonstrations that eventually chased out GDR hardliners and caused the Berlin Wall to fall. Kowalczuk emphasizes the all-encompassing totality of a state that dictated every facet of life to its subjects: “from cradle to grave,” indoctrinating and controlling through schools, party, mass organizations, and the workplace. Most historians who argue along Kowalczuk’s lines hold that the Stasi itself, through informant networks and an all-knowing, all-powerful apparatus, kept the GDR’s population of 16 million in line. Kowalczuk, however, argues that the Stasi itself was not as powerful as claimed or thought (or as portrayed in The Lives of Others): Much of its power of intimidation stemmed from its reputation, not its actual reach. In other words, eastern Germans, argues Kowalczuk, could have acted more independently and even defiantly had they had the gumption—but they didn’t. Kowalczuk argues that East Germans passively allowed themselves to be subjugated, browbeaten, restricted, and instructed by the regime. They were obedient pupils internalizing its narrow-minded, racist, authoritarian character and reproducing it in families, schools, and society. He casts eastern Germans essentially as sheep who relinquished freedom in exchange for certainty and security. In his view, the so-called peaceful revolution of 1989 wasn’t instigated by these cowed masses but by a tiny minority of dissidents and rebels—like himself. The public took to the streets only once the regime was on the run, and then portrayed themselves as freedom fighters—and victims. The newly liberated East Germans had no conception of an alternative state or society beyond that which then-West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the “reunification chancellor,” dangled before their eyes. Today’s eastern Germans, Kowalczuk says—even those born in a unified Germany—have undertaken too little to emancipate themselves from the GDR’s totalitarian mindset. They refuse to take responsibility for their own condition, demand the state provide for them, and express the same intolerance toward other cultures that the regime once did. The uncertainties that freedom presents are so unnerving that they retreat into nostalgia for the GDR—beyond even that in Goodbye, Lenin!—that idealizes its old ties to the Soviet Union and sympathizes with a dictator as ruthless as Vladimir Putin. Kowalczuk’s most direct foil is Katja Hoyer, also a GDR-born historian, though she was only 4 years old when the peaceful revolution broke out. She’s known to English-language readers through her UK bestseller Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949 – 1990, which argues that life in the GDR was more textured than Kowalczuk acknowledges. East Germans lived and loved, had birthday parties and weddings, and enjoyed vacations and families. They weren’t passive, she argues, despite the formidable security apparatus. The GDR’s film industry—during periods of liberalization—even produced quality films like the 1973 cult classic Die Legende von Paul und Paula (The Legend of Paul and Paula). Hoyer also credits GDR socialism with genuine achievements, such as women’s rights, affordable housing, and hands-on workplace participation. If unglamorous, just about everyone had a two-room apartment and, of course, a job. Rents were subsidized, healthcare free, and there was childcare for all families. Hoyer treats the relative material equality of the self-described “workers’ and farmers’ state” as a humane alternative to capitalism’s wealth gaps. “Many East Germans were proud of their achievements as social mobility provided unprecedented opportunities for the working classes,” she argues. Although Beyond the Wall stops in 1990, elsewhere Hoyer argues that eastern Germans’ lives and achievements were dismissed in the united Germany as worthless “ballast.” West German condescension and the “sink or swim” into which eastern Germans were thrown in the 1990s caused resentment to fester, and snowball, and be passed on to subsequent generations. The problem today in Germany’s eastern states, she argues, isn’t that citizens are undemocratic but that the system is less democratic than they had expected. Materially, the easterners lag behind their western brethren not least because they had no assets when communism collapsed. She has sympathy for the hardships that economic union imposed. Seen this way, the AfD vote is explicable. This party alone avoids demonizing the GDR, thus offering eastern Germans respect that none of the other parties do. The AfD may be German, Hoyer argues, but versions of it exist everywhere in Europe, including England, where she currently works. Eastern Germans’ “behaviors and characteristics have lazily been written off as a deviation from the west German norm, fostering a defiant us-against-them mentality,” she argued in 2024 in the Guardian. “This east German identity, combined with the feeling of being othered and marginalised, is a powerful thing for the AFD to exploit.” As for the racism and xenophobia, she attributes them to economic anxiety and condescension. The way to win back the easterners is to take their concerns seriously, including migration, and treat them with respect. A third prominent commentator is Dirk Oschmann, a literature professor at Leipzig University. His take in Der Osten: eine westdeutsche Erfindung (The East: A West German Invention), a 2023 work widely discussed in Germany, is close to Hoyer’s but not identical. He contends that the western Germans’ derogatory labeling of easterners as lazy, dim-witted, bigoted complaining losers is a means to deflect legitimate criticism that the West itself flubbed unification. He argues that the lock-stock-and-barrel incorporation of eastern Germany into the Federal Republic constituted a one-sided takeover. There was, for example, no constitutional convention to create the unified Germany anew. East Germany’s economy was put on equal footing with West Germany’s overnight, causing it to implode—while western companies swooped into pick up the business. The East’s factories and firms were sold off to Western buyers, who made out like bandits. West German elites stepped into leadership posts across the East: in universities, police forces, hospitals—just about everywhere. Oschmann considers Kowalczuk a proponent of this tendency by tracing everything back to the GDR itself, rather than the humiliation of unification and the travails of decades since. He explains the AfD and the power of the migration issue much as Hoyer does: as a response to grievances and disrespect. As for the East’s cultural racism, he admits its presence but calls the West’s pejorative treatment of the East a form of xenophobia or “othering.” This surfeit of analysis begs the question of whether any response from the mainstream German parties can win AfD voters to their side. Certainly, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thinks so. His remedy is to double down on restricting migration, the top reason for AfD voting. This was Merz’s answer before the Saxony-Anhalt vote and, while asylum applications have fallen by nearly half under Merz, there’s been no political payoff. Rather than vote for the copy act, 44 percent of Saxony-Anhalt’s voters cast their ballots for the original, the AfD, whose jingoism Merz chases after, while the CDU was rewarded with less than half of its previous vote share. The Social Democrats think better social safety nets will do the trick, even though AfD voters are not poor. Germany’s political establishment is clueless how to handle the AfD’s surge—and the country’s historians, sadly, offer no concrete answers either. Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.94
Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente Despite the thaw, India-China rivalry remains inevitable. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Modi, Xi Meet on BRICS Sideline Over the weekend, Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to India for the first time in seven years. Xi was in New Delhi for 24 hours to attend this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, where he held a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. An Indian Foreign Ministry statement said the two leaders pledged to strengthen commercial and cultural cooperation. A more striking readout came from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who said that the bilateral meeting covered long-term, strategic issues and that Modi and Xi reached “the most important consensus” to be partners, not rivals. Beijing hopes the meeting will advance bilateral ties “without stagnation or backsliding,” Wang added. These are positive words for a relationship between major competitors—and one that was plunged into deep crisis after a deadly 2020 border clash in the Ladakh region. But an India-China rapprochement has been playing out for nearly two years. Xi’s visit marked the culmination, not the commencement, of India-China detente. Still, the extent of the thaw shouldn’t be overstated. Historically, India-China ties have had their moments, with ample heady talk and good optics. Invariably, fresh tensions have spoiled them; the two are destined to remain rivals by history, geography, and geopolitics. In October 2024, the post-Ladakh tensions began to ease with the inking of a new border agreement. India and China subsequently made pledges to resume direct air flights and bolster commercial cooperation. In March 2025, Modi said on a podcast that cooperation with China was “essential” for global stability. Contrary to some commentary, the detente began before U.S. President Donald Trump was elected to a second term and wasn’t sparked by his policies. But Trump’s tariffs, which have hit both India and China hard, and concerns about access to U.S. markets gave both sides a strong incentive to accelerate their rapprochement and especially to deepen trade ties. However, the reality is that continued India-China rivalry is all but inevitable. Both countries are both proud civilizational states and dispute claims to around 15,000 square miles of territory—equal to the size of Greece—along their shared border. They disagree on many other major issues, from Taiwan and Tibet to surveillance. Perhaps most significantly, China is a close ally of India’s bitter rival Pakistan. Last year, the Pakistani military used Chinese weaponry in air combat operations against India for the first time. Such challenges may seem surmountable, given what the India-China relationship has going for it. This includes their rock-solid trade partnership, shared interests, and considerable cooperation in global forums (including BRICS, but also the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.) Not surprisingly, India-China ties have often enjoyed periods of warmth—but ultimately a trigger, often a border provocation, has shattered that calm. In 2017, a few years after Xi and Modi were photographed smiling on a swing together, a 73-day military standoff on the Doklam Plateau plunged relations into crisis. The Ladakh clash came just months after another Modi-Xi summit in India. Though border tensions have subsided, territorial disputes still fester and occasionally flare. To be sure, there are plenty of reasons for New Delhi and Beijing to bury the hatchet. They want to ease tensions along their fraught border, create space for deeper commercial cooperation, hedge against Trump’s unpredictability, and remove a diplomatic headache from the BRICS grouping, which both capitals badly want to succeed. Ultimately, however, so many divergences and sources of lingering mistrust preempt the possibility of full-on rapprochement. Though an extended period of cooperation is possible, it’s likely only a matter of time before the very “stagnation and backsliding” that Beijing says it wants to avoid. What We’re Following Bangladesh passes 1,000 measles deaths. More than 1,000 people in Bangladesh have now died from the measles virus since March 15, according to the latest government figures, released on Sept. 9. The country is suffering the world’s worst measles outbreak; it has logged thousands of new cases this year, including nearly 60,000 between January and June alone. Nearly 20 million children have been vaccinated in Bangladesh since a new national inoculation campaign was launched in April. Health experts attribute the ongoing crisis to underestimations of how many children needed to be vaccinated—the target figure was 18 million, but experts say that a more accurate estimate is 22.6 million. The number of measles vaccinations in Bangladesh—both first and second doses—fell between 2019 and 2023, and this year’s national campaign was the first since one from December 2020 to January 2021, during the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. A sudden change of government in August 2024 caused further vaccine interruptions. The current government, which took office in February, is working hard to ease the crisis. But it must grapple with not only the large number of children who still need to be vaccinated, but also economic stress and energy shortages that further complicate inoculation efforts. Thousands still missing in Nepal. Three weeks after a glacial collapse precipitated catastrophic floods in Nepal, more than 5,000 people remain missing. Authorities say they continue to search and are trying to provide information to families as soon as possible. But massive destruction—including 2.2 million tons of—has made search and rescue difficult. Authorities are now transitioning from search and rescue to relief and reconstruction efforts, with an eye toward the large number of people who lost their homes. The disaster leveled entire villages, submerged tunnels, and swept away hydropower facilities. Damage to roads and bridges has created additional complications. Nepal’s government said that the total estimated cost for reconstruction efforts will be $4.8 billion—around one-tenth of the country’s total nominal GDP. Sri Lanka signs labor accords with Thailand. This week, Sri Lanka and Thailand signed agreements to enable 10,000 Sri Lankans to work in the Southeast Asian country, with a focus on young workers and sectors including information technology and tourism. The Sri Lankan workers will receive equal rights and protections under Thai labor laws. The agreements address a key need for both countries: Thailand has a labor shortage, and Sri Lanka is looking to tap into a wider array of foreign labor markets. But the deal goes against a common pattern in Sri Lanka—and elsewhere in South Asia—in which young people go to the Middle East, Europe, or the United States for work. There appears to be a cultural factor at play. The Sri Lankan government believes cultural similarities between Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia will make for a smoother adjustment process—putting them in a strong position to be productive and send home remittances that are critical for the Sri Lankan economy. FP’s Most Read This Week How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan Under the Radar Last week, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said that it was not contemplating the use of military force against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Middle East. The statement came in response to speculation, fueled by a Turkish news report, that Pakistan was considering invoking the Mecca Agreement—the new mutual defense pact among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey—and joining a military operation with the Saudis against the Houthis. Houthi attacks against Saudi targets have escalated in recent days. Pakistan’s statement gives ammunition to critics of the Mecca Agreement—as well as a similar bilateral deal between Islamabad and Riyadh—who dismiss the accord as a paper tiger. In the last year, Taliban military operations have hit Pakistan has been hit multiple times; Saudi Arabia has been assaulted by the Houthis as well as direct Iranian strikes. At no time has Pakistan or Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to assist the other, though Pakistan has sent some arms and troops to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Still, the two mutual defense pacts are mainly meant to focus on deterrence, which the signatories say the United States cannot provide sufficiently in the Middle East. In Pakistan’s case, the accords are meant to help advance key foreign-policy priorities, including playing a larger role in the security architecture of the region. Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center.
