The piece noted that in 2022, “four of the top ten concert tours of 2022 were by so-called legacy acts — artists whose biggest hits came out decades ago, and who are well past the traditional retirement age.” Elton John came in at number two; The Rolling Stones at number six. It also interviewed 65-year-old Solana Beach attorney Brad Auerbach, who had recently seen shows by George Clinton (82), Elton John (75) at Petco Park; The Who, led by Roger Daltrey (78) and Pete Townshend (77), Roxy Music, and former Pink Floyd leader Roger Waters (80). Now it’s 2026. “The groups from the ‘60s, the members have passed away, or they’re too old to tour,” says O’Keefe. “The ones who are still doing it are in their final days. Eventually, you’re not going to see these people any more. I hate to sound like a marketer, but there is a market for this, and it’s nice to get paid. I was in many, many bands, some with record deals. I’ve done session work, and music for television and films. It sounds glamorous, but it really isn’t. There are more downs than ups. I got to a point where I thought: it would be really good to harness the power of these popular groups. We’re going to keep this great music alive.” O’Keefe himself was barely out of diapers when the ‘60s ended, and while he remembers his mom listening to The Fifth Dimension and The Mamas and the Papas, the stuff he came of age to was “Black Flag, REM, and The Del Fuegos.” Still, he says, “when I was learning to play music, I was inspired” by ‘60s bands like The Byrds and The Zombies. “My passion was groups that had great songs” — and re-creating those songs became the core of his vision for The Sixties Show. “When I put this together, I had this grand aspiration: a big show about the 1960s, a theater production. But our first show was in front of three people at a tiny restaurant. We had to crawl before we could run. So we didn’t have the stage sets and the multimedia.” What he had was “authenticity — from day one. We play the music note for note — exactly how it sounds on the record — and we do it without pre-recorded music. No samples, no backing tracks. We use vintage re-issue gear. That helps with the visual aesthetic, but it also gives us the tone, textures and sounds we need to re-create the songs. When we play The Byrds, it’s got to be a certain type of 12-string, and we’ve got that. We use old-style Fender amps — Twin Reverbs, Vibroluxes — that help recreate those sounds. We use Telecasters, Strats, ES-335s, Epiphone Casinos, Gibson SGs, Fender Precision Basses, Fender Jazz Basses. We’re definitely ridiculous about that stuff.” “We” refers to a carefully assembled group of musicians that includes Tom Licameli, Jim Boggia, Scott Devours, Kevin Bents, and Jeff Miller. There are Grammy winners in that list, and people who have toured with ‘60s giants like John Fogerty and The Who. “I auditioned well over 300 people,” says O’Keefe. “I was looking for people who weren’t just amazing musicians, but who understood the sensibility of how to approach this music. How did this guitar player approach it? What kind of feel did he use? How did he play it? Unless you know that, you’re not going to duplicate what’s on the record. The musicians I hire love this stuff. They understand how to play it, and they’ll do deep dives. “Thank God for the internet,” O’Keefe explains, “because now we can find out: Who produced this record? Who played on it? How did they record it? What instruments did they use? What was the board? What was the tape machine? What type of microphone? What were the EQ settings? It’s really boring for most people. But when you combine that research with putting on headphones and listening closely, you can get closer to an answer about how this stuff was recorded. There were people I wanted to bring in who said, ‘That’s too much. Why do you want to go this far?’ Well, when you see the show and hear it, you get it.” The two nods to modern necessity he mentions are “the keyboards — they’re the only way to generate the horns and string sections and exotic instruments” — and the fact that “if someone played a Les Paul on a record and we have a Telecaster in hand during the show…well, for the sake of the show, we can’t change instruments for every single song.” And it is very much a show — not, say, an evening with Wilco, wherein Jeff Tweedy can strap on a different guitar for every second song. It’s high-energy entertainment,” says O’Keefe. “There’s narration; there’s media. People can see what was happening in a particular year. There might be imagery of Martin Luther King Jr. speaking. Or interviews with people on the street in the ‘60s. It isn’t just stuff we’re throwing up there: it’s specifically related to a moment in time and to a particular song.” He stresses that it’s not a history lesson, but that’s because “we did our homework. The people in the current cast love the ’60s. They understand the sensibility of the decade and the pop culture, which goes hand in hand with the music.” Before our interview ended, O’Keefe stressed that “the show never stops growing. We’re in the initial stages of developing a run in Las Vegas. During a residency, you can have things like moving stage sets. It’s more than just a concert, and I haven’t figured out a way to completely convey that. What we always hear from people after they see us is, ‘I loved the show, but whatever I thought it was going to be, I was wrong.’”

item.title: Live Five: Safety Orange, Gregory Page, We the Commas, Jason Graham, Adams Avenue Street Fair
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.08
Safety Orange at the Holding Company September 19 Reggae rockers Safety Orange came together in 1996, founded by singer-bassist Sol Turpin, a San Diego native from Sublime tribute band 40 Oz to Freedom, with guitarist/vocalist Greg Karlo (who once played with Turpin in a Cure tribute band). Their debut full-length Life as a Fish was followed by Troll Rock High and extensive touring. A third album called State of Where I Am, released on their own Wabasa Records label (Turpin’s middle name is Wabasa), included a cover of a song by the Cure. Their single for “Better Now” was featured on Spotify’s Reggae Summer Beach playlist, and a 2022 single called “Get Outta My Way” came with a sleeve illustrated by Dead & Company gig poster artist Mark Sgarbossa. They’ve released several new songs recently including “Salt Water,” “My Town,” and “Smokin’ Love.” The Ocean Beach event includes Gun Shy and Tropical Drip. Adams Avenue Street Fair in Kensington & Normal Heights September 19 and 20 Enjoy over 75 musical acts on six stages, taking place along Adams Avenue in Kensington and Normal Heights. The 44th annual event features around ten blocks of carnival rides, beer gardens, beer tastings, festival foods, and 300 exhibitors. Kicking off at 10 am each day, attractions include special performances like the Fern Street Circus, comedy shows hosted by the Adams Avenue Theater, and full craft beer pours and specialty drinks across multiple dedicated tasting areas. Among the local acts slated to appear are The Amandas, Auz Fontaine, the Beard & the Bird, Boostive, Euphoria Brass Band, Fred Heath & the Sidewinders, Gayle Skidmore, Grampadrew, Lord Howler, Manganista, Manzanita Blues, Midnight Rivals, MohaviSoul, Please Ask For Paul, Rookie Card, Sara Petite, Scary Pierre, Sue Palmer, Tigers In Cairo, Wild Wild Wets, and Ypsitucky. Gregory Page at Pilgrim United Church of Christ September 20 The son of a traveling Armenian pop singer and a mother who was the lead singer and saxophone player in one of Britain’s first all-girl groups, roots Americana rocker Gregory Page melds traditions of folk, Celtic, jazz, ragtime, blues, swing, and French romanticism. He has performed in a wide range of iconic venues such as the London Palladium, London’s 02 Arena, and The Paradiso in Amsterdam, playing events like the Woodford Folk Festival in Australia and countless international music fests, headlining as well as opening for Bob Dylan, Leon Russell, Judy Collins, Chris Isaak, and frequent collaborator Jason Mraz. Since Page’s first solo album in 1990, he has released over 20 more and appeared as a guest on dozens of others. He performs from time to time as a member of the Rugburns (who scored a big regional hit with “Hitchhiker Joe”), as well as famed acoustic duo the Hatchet Brothers (with Frank Lee Drennen of Loam), and he’s produced music for over two dozen artists, including Jason Mraz and Tom Brosseau. He won a pair of San Diego Music Awards in 2021, taking home trophies for Album of the Year and Best Pop Album for his full-length One Hell of a Memory. We the Commas at the Belly Up Tavern The three Comma siblings who make up alt-surf R&B rockers We the Commas play what they call Surf Alternative R&B, or SARB (the name of their first EP). The band members ranged in age from 17 to 23 when they began hosting a series of weekly three-hour gigs at the Bunker House in Oceanside, as well as appearing on San Diego’s KUSI Morning Show and at a March of Dimes charity event in Balboa Park. They released their debut single “Sherry” in 2020, followed by a single and video for “Custom Made” and a debut EP called Sarb later that year. They’ve been championed by supporters such as The Head and The Heart and Young the Giant, who both shared the group’s covers online, and they've worked with A-list production talent like Rex Kudo (Post Malone, Young Thug, Lil Uzi Vert) and Charlie Handsome (Khalid, The Weeknd, Drake). They released a new single in May called “As Of late.” The Solana Beach bill includes Isabella Erardi with guests Josue Vazquez and Zach Wolf. Jason Graham at L’Auberge Del Mar September 21 “I specialize in playing fun covers in a wide variety of genres,” says indie folk artist Jason Graham, who grew up studying music and performing in the Midwest. Known for his high-energy solo sets that blend pop, rock, folk, country, and top-40 hits, he uses live looping technology to create a dynamic one-man-band experience. “I have been lucky enough to travel the world playing music on cruise ships for the past few years,” he says of the four years he spent traveling and performing with Norwegian cruise lines playing six shows a week, three to four hours a night. Now married and newly settled in San Diego, he’s become a fixture at area nightclubs, hotels, and restaurants, including the Hotel Del Coronado, Barleymash, Andaz, Union Kitchen & Tap, Cannonball, Fairmont Grand Del Mar, La Valencia Hotel, and the Bahia Resort Hotel. Comments

item.title: Live Five: Jesse Ray Smith, The Frights, Manganista, Stone Temple Pilots, My Town 2026
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.60
Jesse Ray Smith at Belly Up Tavern September 10 Jesse Ray Smith describes his sound as "heartland rock with heartbreak soul." He plays Americana music with strong touches of soul, classic rock, heartland folk, and even a bit of country. This melting pot makes sense when you consider his influences: Chris Stapleton, Bob Seger, Bruce Springsteen, The Eagles, and Van Morrison. After releasing his debut solo album in 2018, he went on to record several more releases, as well as becoming a fixture on the local solo gig scene. He's a multiple San Diego Music Award nominee, with two nods at the 2025 SDMAS, for Best Americana Artist and Best Americana Song. He released a digital album last year in two parts, Keepers Side A and Side B, and he just dropped a new single for “Love You Without Fail.” The Solana Beach bill includes Cassie B, who is heavily influenced by the funk and pop stylings of the 1970s. The Frights at Observatory North Park September 11 Surf-punkers The Frights were teens when their recording career was launched in 2013 by SOMA manager Joe Nammo, who released their debut on his Postmark label. “We did go to the same high school as Blink-182,” says Rancho Bernardo High alum Mikey Carnevale, “and every band who came out of our school wanted to sound like Blink. But it wasn’t my style.” Among their most streamed and viewed tracks is “Crust Bucket” (from their self-titled 2013 debut full-length) “Tungs” (originally featured on the album You Are Going To Hate This), “Kids” (a fan-favorite single addressing the chaos of growing up), and their 2016 track “Afraid of the Dark,” which has racked up millions of streams. They’ve gone on to play at Coachella and the BottleRock Napa Valley Festival, and have around a half dozen albums to their credit, including 2023’s Gallows Humour and 2025’s Ready When You Are. Their most recent release is an EP called Five Fucking Singles. My Town: Celebrating Decades of San Diego Music at the Holding Company September 12 and 13 Taking place over two days, the My Town festival is back to celebrate decades of San Diego music with a number of noteworthy appearances and reunions. The bill for Saturday, Sepember 12, includes punk icons The Zeros celebrating their 50th anniversary, Everready’s first show in over ten years, 1980s punk band Dum Dum Boys, 90s punk rockers The Mice (marking their first performance in around six years), Sex Pistols-Spice Girls mashup Spice Pistols, hardcore punk chick rockers Revolt Chix, Gizzards, Hour of Pearl, Substitute Gym Teacher, Holding Grudges, and Rat Tricks. Sunday September 13 features The Neighbors celebrating 34 years of hyperfast hardcore, politically aware all-vegetarian anti-war punkers Diatribe (known as the first American D-Beat, circa early 1980s), Santa Claus (1985 thrash) War Fever, Doc Hammer (named after one of the talents behind the TV cartoon show The Venture Brothers), Subversive Intent (members of The Eulogy, In Control, Meth Breath, Stay Away), Philistine (members of Waco Fuck/DEA), Moral Genocide (members from Battalion of Saints and Systematic Abuse), Aggravate (ex-Impulse), Lummux Delux (ex-Crossed Out), and Infernal Tide Riders. Manganista Record Release at the Rabbit Hole September 12 Manganista will be celebrating its new record on Escape Hatch Records. The six-track release takes two songs, “Talking to Myself” and “The Chosen One," and reimagines each three different ways. The result is one record with two songs, six tracks, and three distinctly different sides of the band’s sound. The record transforms both songs through rock, reggae, and dub versions. Side A features “Talking to Myself,” “Talking to My Stepper,” and “Talking Dub,” while Side B follows with “The Chosen One,” “Chosen Too,” and “Chosen Dub.” According to Matt Rhea, "The concept takes a cue from the 12-inch singles of the late ’70s and ’80s, when artists like Duran Duran, The Human League and other new wave and post-punk bands used the format to stretch songs into alternate mixes and extended versions. Manganista takes that tradition in its own direction, allowing the same songs to move between rock, reggae and dub across three distinct recordings." Recorded and mixed by Ben Moore at Singing Serpent, the record's alternate tracks feature guest players John Roy (sax), Brandon Niznik (bass), Don Barthelemy (drums), Matt FitzSimmons (trumpet), and Brian Wallace (flute). Stone Temple Pilots at North Island Credit Union Amphitheatre September 15 When alt-grunge icons Stone Temple Pilots open for Godsmack in Chula Vista, it will serve as a homecoming of sorts for three of the bandmembers. Guitarist Dean DeLeo, bassist Robert DeLeo, and drummer Eric Kretz co-founded the group in San Diego during the late 1980s, soon earning national and then international attention for their radio-friendly version of the sort of grunge music popularized at the time by Pearl Jam and others. In a 1994 Rolling Stone poll, STP was voted Worst New Band by critics, and Best New Band by readers. The same year, STP’s song “Plush” won a “Best Hard Rock Performance” Grammy. Previous STP singers Scott Weiland and Chester Bennington both passed away, with Jeff Gutt (known from seasons two and three of TV's X Factor) fronting the band since 2017. Their most recent studio album Perdida dropped in 2020, their second full-length to feature Gutt at the mic and the first fully-acoustic LP of the band’s career. They also recently put out a previously unreleased archival track featuring their late singer Scott Weiland: “If I Could Fly,” a demo written in 2000 that was pulled from Weiland's personal archives and given a wider release to mark the ten-year anniversary of his passing.

item.title: Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch: Paso Robles' premier agritainment and pumpkin farm
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 2.34
When autumn arrives on California’s Central Coast, the rolling hills of San Luis Obispo County (SLO) turn to a golden hue, the morning air grows crisp, and families begin searching for authentic, memorable ways to celebrate the harvest season. While Paso Robles has long been celebrated for its world-class viticulture, historical downtown square, and rich agricultural heritage, a brand-new landmark is officially opening its gates along Monterey Road: Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch. Designed from the ground up as a premier family-friendly farm destination, Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch combines time-honored harvest traditions with modern outdoor entertainment. Sprawling across scenic acreage at 5375 Monterey Road, Paso Robles, CA 93446, the ranch provides a vibrant, country-style atmosphere where local residents, regional neighbors, and travelers alike can gather, play, and create lasting autumn memories. Whether you are hunting for an oversized, display-ready giant pumpkin, testing your navigation skills in a sprawling corn maze, or letting young kids explore the custom hay fort, Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch offers a complete seasonal experience built around community and classic farm fun. For decades, families visiting the Paso Robles area during September and October had to make tough choices. A visit to one farm meant picking up pumpkins, while another location hosted a basic maze, and finding interactive play for kids meant driving to another spot entirely. Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch was founded on a simple yet ambitious vision: to bring every element of classic autumn farm fun together on a single, expansive Central Coast property. By pairing agricultural traditions with dynamic recreational activities, the ranch fills a long-standing gap in regional family tourism. Visitors do not simply drive up to buy a pumpkin off a wooden pallet; they enter an immersive, hands-on environment. From the rustle of corn leaves in the breeze to the laughter echoing off the hay fort, Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch reestablishes the farm as the cultural heart of the fall season. At Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch, every area of the property is built for engagement. The farm’s layout ensures that toddlers, school-aged children, teenagers, parents, and grandparents can all find activities tailored specifically to their idea of fall fun. The Pumpkin Patch & Pick-Your-Own Field (Giant Pumpkins) The physical and visual center of the ranch is its massive pumpkin patch. Sprawling across open farm fields, the patch offers a vibrant, country-style atmosphere for selecting seasonal produce. Guests can explore the grounds to pick and purchase from a wide assortment of options, including: Giant Pumpkins: Oversized, show-stopping specimens featured prominently as a core ranch attraction, ideal for major seasonal displays, grand porch setups, or community highlights. Standard Pumpkins: A broad selection of classic, smooth-skinned pumpkins in various sizes, perfect for traditional autumn carving, home decorating, and family jack-o'-lanterns. Decorative Gourds: A wide variety of colorful, uniquely shaped ornamental gourds and decorative seasonal produce to complete any fall home or business display. The Haunted House & Scare Maze Designed for thrill-seekers looking for after-dark autumn excitement, the haunted house and scare maze deliver Hollywood-grade set design and professional production value. Featuring dramatic lighting, fog effects, atmospheric soundscapes, and live scare actors, this attraction transforms the ranch after dark into the premier Halloween horror destination in San Luis Obispo County. The Interactive Corn Maze Step off the dirt trails and into a towering labyrinth of green and gold corn stalks. The interactive corn maze at Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch challenges explorers of all ages to navigate twists, turns, and dead ends. Designed as an engaging outdoor puzzle, the maze encourages teamwork, problem-solving, and friendly countryside competition for families and groups. Custom Hay Fort & Play Areas Engineered specifically for younger guests, the hay fort is a safe, structured play area constructed entirely from massive straw bales. Children can scale giant steps, navigate tunnels, and survey the ranch from elevated vantage points while parents relax nearby and take photos. Interactive Petting Animal Area Animals are an essential part of country life. The farm features a clean, spacious petting zoo area where children and adults can get up close, view, interact with, and learn about friendly farm animals such as miniature cows, donkeys, lamas, and pigs. The Apple Cannon Station Add a high-energy target-shooting experience to your farm visit. Guests can launch apples across open fields at fun, interactive ranch targets, combining classic harvest tradition with thrilling outdoor arcade play for kids and adults alike. Classic Farm Games Scattered across the manicured ranch grounds are classic, family-friendly outdoor games that provide non-stop entertainment between major field runs. The General Store & Ranch Bar Part lively country bar and part bustling autumn marketplace, the General Store at Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch offers a unique blend of local farm charm and professional theatrical flair. Designed with a distinct Monster City Studios touch, the store features a comfortable rustic bar environment to enjoy a drink alongside fresh farm produce, seasonal decorations, Halloween gifts, and artisan goods from Central Coast craftspeople. Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch is designed to welcome a broad range of visitors from across Paso Robles and greater San Luis Obispo County: Families with Young Children: Parents and grandparents seeking a safe, wholesome weekend outing with dedicated play structures and animal interactions. Seasonal & Fall Enthusiasts: Local residents and tourists searching for a genuine pumpkin patch experience to find high-quality home decor, giant pumpkins, and unique ornamental gourds. School & Youth Groups: Local schools, daycares, and youth organizations looking for an educational, hands-on outdoor field trip destination. Community Members & Tourists: Travelers exploring Central Coast wine country who want to pause and experience authentic local farm hospitality. Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch is conveniently located off Monterey Road, making it an easy drive from Highway 101, Templeton, Atascadero, San Luis Obispo, and surrounding coastal communities. Physical Address: 5375 Monterey Road, Paso Robles, CA 93446 Direct Phone: (805) 674-1850 Contact Email: info [at] pumpkinjacksranch.com Official Website: pumpkinjacksranch.com Whether you are planning a full family weekend outing, arranging a school field trip, or searching for the perfect giant pumpkin to anchor your porch display, Pumpkin Jack’s Ranch warmly invites you to experience the best of Central Coast autumn traditions.

item.title: Theater Review: <em>Theater People, or, The Angel Next Door</em> at Scripps Ranch Theatre
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 2.30
When North Coast Rep gave us the world premiere of Paul Slade Smith’s Theater People, or, The Angel Next Door back in 2023, they left the first part of the title off the poster. That’s understandable: “The Angel Next Door” is vastly more grabby than “Theater People,” what with the romantic promise in its elevation of the mythic Girl Next Door to heavenly status. And the angel next door is absolutely the engine of the play’s plot: the girl for whom (and about whom) a boy has written a novel manuscript so white-hot that a playwright couple has already penned a theatrical adaptation — in which they hope said girl will star. (What do you know, she’s an actress.) All that remains is for her to read and approve, and he’ll sign the publishing contract, and it’s off to Broadway. Which is why the boy and the couple are staying in the same posh Newport mansion as the actress. In fact…she’s staying right next door. Cue the madcappery. But while that’s the plot, it’s not quite what the play is about. For that, you need that first part of the title, which Scripps Ranch Theatre has bravely kept in place for its current production. Theater People plays as a playwright’s sweet, amusing Apologia Pro Vita Sua: “On the one hand, I gotta eat; on the other, just look at the magic I can make by playing let’s pretend." Hollywood types just love movies about making movies. Just look at the slew of Oscars for Argo, The Artist, Birdman, etc. Why should theater people be any different? Looking at you, Hamlet, with your play-within-a-play… It's not just the title. Mr. Smith has split himself neatly in two for this production, giving us the witty, self-indulgent, and slightly mopey Arthur Sanders and his hardworking, high-hoping wife Charlotte as the two sides of the playwright persona. (Kudos to the casting of Danny Campbell and Melissa Fernandes, who are fine as artistic types who are long past artistic differences.) As soon as they enter their room, they start setting the scene as if it were a play — which of course it is — noting the introduction of character and setting in their conversation, and wondering where they audience might be. It's all cheerfully self-conscious, right down to the comment on how there are too many doors in the room — almost certainly a nod to the astonishing quantity of open-and-shuttery in Smith’s Unnecessary Farce, given that a couple of the doors in this set never even get opened. And just as in Hamlet, there is an audience on stage as well: Olga the housemaid, who begins the play with a stony tolerance for “theater people,” and ends with…something else. Nothing about the play’s crisis or its resolution is subtle; Slade makes a theatrical exercise out of seeing how much comedy he can wring from the ex

item.title: What Nature’s Silence Said to Annie Dillard
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 3.32
“Nature’s silence is its one remark,” Annie Dillard wrote in a 1981 Atlantic essay. Dillard, who died yesterday at age 81, spent her life listening. She opens that essay, “Teaching a Stone to Talk”—which was later adapted into a collection by the same title—with the story of a man named Larry who is trying to get a rock to speak to him. “He keeps it on a shelf,” she writes, protected “by a square of untanned leather, like a canary asleep under its cloth. Larry removes the cover for the stone’s lessons.” Dillard is not sure what exactly happens at these lessons, but she respects the process: “It is a noble work, and beats, from any angle, selling shoes.” To Dillard, striving to hear the natural world was holy work too. “What have we been doing all these centuries but trying to call God back to the mountain, or, failing that, raise a peep out of anything that isn’t us?” she asks. Born in 1945 in Pittsburgh, she found inspiration in some of the places she lived. At age 28, she published Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, a Pulitzer Prize–winning nonfiction book that draws from her walks in the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia in the ’70s. Her musings on these solitary experiences in nature drew comparisons to Henry David Thoreau, who strongly influenced her work. She was also one of the first women to find a place in the male-dominated genre of wilderness writing. The writer Diana Saverin, who spent time going through an archive of Dillard’s personal writings and correspondence at Yale, once described in The Atlantic Dillard’s trepidation about how she would be received: “Before she published her book, she scribbled in her journal, wondering who would take her book seriously if its author was a ‘Virginia housewife named Annie.’” She dealt with this problem by leaving her day-to-day suburban life out of her work, so much so that some critics felt that she was exaggerating just how often she was in the wildness of nature. As Saverin noted, Dillard acknowledged that “she sometimes distorted the literal truth to achieve an artistic one.” But to Dillard, the ultimate truths revealed themselves in the time she did spend outside. In her journals, she acknowledged the “theological” sensibility in her books, and it is there on every page. “What is the difference between a cathedral and a physics lab?” she wrote in The Atlantic. “Are they not both saying Hello” to the world beyond? Throughout her life, Dillard identified, in turn, with Protestantism, Catholicism, and nothing at all. I first encountered her work in a religious-studies class at Wesleyan University, where she taught from 1979 to 2001, before my time there. Dillard was a shock to my system: Growing up as an observant but theologically confused Jew, I spent my teenage years in synagogue itchy with guilt, poring over the same words in the prayer book every Saturday and willing myself to believe. Only later did I come to understand that faith—and, perhaps more important, the very act of living—can also be found in what we see and touch and hear: even in the rustle of the wind. Dillard taught me this. “At a certain point you say to the woods, to the sea, to the mountains, the world, Now I am ready,” she wrote in 1981. “You feel the world’s word as a tension, a hum, a single chorused note everywhere the same. This is it: this hum is the silence. Nature does utter a peep—just this one.” Sometimes nature thunders, giving us no choice but to listen. Describing a total eclipse, Dillard is in awe, even afraid: “It was as though an enormous, loping god in the sky had reached down and slapped the Earth’s face.” Other times, nature’s peep can feel anticlimactic, but this quiet commands reverence. The stone never does talk to Larry, and Dillard ends that story by succumbing to her faith in the nothingness. “You take a step in the right direction to pray to this silence,” she writes. “Pray without ceasing.”

item.title: The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.94
Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge. I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens. Now the rise of the AI therapist is upon us. The growing cadre of AI mental-health services tend to avoid using words like therapist and therapy. They say that they do not replace professional help and that they can refer users to human therapists if needed. But their positioning as a therapy-like service is clear. In June, the therapy giant Talkspace launched its AI mental-health agent, Tee, “developed to help individuals navigate life’s daily mental health challenges.” Then there’s Ash, which offers to support your “emotional wellbeing,” helping you to “connect the dots between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.” Abby promises to be “warm, thoughtful, and direct” and to help you “work through the kinds of everyday emotional challenges that often go unspoken.” And Headspace’s Ebb advertises: “Stressed at work? Family drama? Trouble sleeping? Ebb can help you unpack what’s on your mind and move forward with more clarity.” When I reached Talkspace for comment, a company spokesperson told me in an email that Tee is “absolutely not a replacement for human therapy. It is a safe AI mental-health guide that can be used to talk through situations like stress, anxiety, relationships, life challenges, and personal growth.” AI therapy is a radical move, and we need to reckon with what happens when we turn to therapists who cannot feel. Therapy and AI have been intertwined since the technology’s beginnings. One of the first chatbots, Eliza, built at MIT in the mid-1960s, ran a therapy script called DOCTOR that asked users questions about their feelings and experiences—and left its creator disconcerted about his technology’s strong emotional pull. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have burst onto the scene, large swaths of the population have been using non-therapy-branded AIs for emotional and mental-health support. Two cultural forces are coming together right now: the growing embrace and destigmatization of therapy, and the idea, explicitly espoused by Silicon Valley, that AI can accomplish what patients seek. I was interested to see how these tools worked in practice, so, although I could not be a neutral observer, I signed up for Tee and attended a few sessions. After I logged in, the chatbot moved me through predetermined session stages that I could follow on my screen’s right-hand corner: Agenda Setting, Active Conversation, Core Work, Practice Plan, Session Complete. It encouraged me to talk about whatever I wanted to, but in the beginning focused on identifying a clear-cut problem, which it wanted to set as the session’s “agenda.” With the agenda set, we went back and forth a bit until the bot suggested that we “shift now from exploring the problem to building a small, realistic step forward.” Its proposed remedy was an exercise patterned on cognitive behavioral therapy that involved pausing for 90 seconds each day before I started work. These sorts of exercises can be helpful. But, in this cycle of identifying problems and fixes, we did not touch what is underneath. The chatbot was also willing to “just talk it through,” rather than offering a concrete suggestion. When we took this route, I could tell that the bot was attempting active listening—restating and asking questions about my experience, mimicking empathy. That’s a process that can help clarify thoughts, but knowing that no one was behind the dialogue, that the empathy was a technique and not a presence, left me with a sense of being poignantly unheard. Much of what matters in therapy happens in nonverbal communication. During a recent session, a patient of mine spoke flatly about upcoming social plans. Then he stopped momentarily, and his eyes softened and drifted downward. The silence that opened felt profound. After a time, I said, “I wonder what happened just there.” He took a breath and began moving into emotional territory that he had long kept out of view. Tee, meanwhile, had a different approach to silence. First, I told the chatbot about my week and how I’d been doing. It validated my emotions (“that makes sense”), asked for more detail, and around we went. But whenever I stopped typing, and might have dipped into the more meaningful recesses of myself, the chatbot in front of me was inert and lifeless. The nonverbal interplay between selves that is so important in human therapy was palpably absent. Being silent with the chatbot did not feel like an invitation to being together, but rather like a kind of deadness. I felt the strong impulse to type quickly to spur the machine back to life. There was no indication that the bot remained with me as I quietly began to feel. It is true that AI can simulate presence and empathy—sometimes fairly convincingly. That’s why people adopt chatbots as confidants and therapists in the first place. And it’s likely that future versions of the therapy bots will get better at making silence feel more meaningful. But there is a wide gulf between AI conveying I understand you and I am here with you, and AI actually being with you. Mimicking presence feels more like emotional deception. When patients trust their therapist and the therapy process, they move into a vulnerable place—and being deceived this way leads to ineffective therapy at best, and may cause harm. Most critiques of AI therapy focus on AI’s sycophancy—its failure to intervene and challenge destructive patterns of thought and action, contributing to suicides, manic episodes, and psychotic states. These critiques, while important, carry forward the old model of the therapist as a dispassionate technician. They see AI therapy as harmful because it does not act upon the patient correctly. This is a framework that the technology companies can get behind. They respond that, sure, the current chatbots have problems, but these are fixable. OpenAI and other companies have taken to publishing statistics demonstrating that their chatbots are making gains in terms of intervening with distressed users in appropriate ways. The underlying argument is that mental-health support is a set of techniques and interventions, and that once machines learn to marshal these effectively, all will be well. In my work with patients, I keep theories and techniques in mind, but the most important element of the process is striving to be fully present. If there is a North Star in this work, it is being with patients in their emotional experience in a deep and lasting way. This approach is borne out in the rich psychoanalytic literature on empathy and emotional dwelling. Trauma is most enduring when patients have felt alone in it, and one of the best pathways toward healing is coming to feel that another person remains with you in your suffering, and thus that you are no longer alone. And studies on what helps patients in therapy, across different therapeutic modalities, illustrate the importance of the human relationship and of the patient and therapist being able to express emotion. AI is an alluring alternative to traditional therapy. The barriers to entry are almost nonexistent: Gone are the friction and labor of finding a human therapist, building trust, and opening up. And AI’s promise of affordable therapy is genuinely appealing. The economics of human therapy are broken. The U.S. in particular is in profound need of insurance reform and legislation that will make therapy affordable for all. In this field as in all fields, AI is not going back into the bottle, and I imagine that it may take on useful adjunct roles in mental-health care. But AI therapy cannot meet our needs. Whatever inroads people take into AI therapy, the strongest pull, if not on the surface then as a current beneath, will be the yearning for someone who can feel with you as you move further into yourself. At the heart of AI therapy is a paradox: We embrace it out of our longing for exactly what it cannot ultimately give.

item.title: The Atrocities That Shaped the Modern Middle East
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.47
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum opens with a discussion of the seemingly forgotten attack on the Yazidi people by ISIS in 2014. Then, David is joined by the historian Simon Sebag Montefiore to discuss his new book, The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East. David and Simon discuss how much of the present-day Middle East emerged from the ruins of the Ottoman empire and the violence that took place both before and after the empire’s collapse. David and Simon discuss how, one after another, different language groups and religious groups were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether. Then, David finishes with a discussion of The Hidden Hand: The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda, by Warren Kinsella. The following is a transcript of the episode: Simon Sebag Montefiore: So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing, and if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression. David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Simon Sebag Montefiore, the acclaimed British historian and author of the new book The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East. The book discussion at the end of the show will feature The Hidden Hand by Warren Kinsella, subtitled The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda. But before either the dialogue with Simon Sebag Montefiore or the book discussion of The Hidden Hand, some opening thoughts on themes that will run all their way through today’s program. Simon Sebag’s book The Cauldron describes the transformation of the Middle East from its existence under the Ottoman empire a century and a half ago to the region of today, divided among many nations. And yet while the map of the Middle East is much more tangled than it was when the Ottomans ruled almost everything from Tunisia to Iraq—although parts of it were under foreign influence: British and French colonial rule, Italian colonial rule—a simple map, but with a complex reality. Simon Sebag describes how, one after another, different language groups, different religious groups, different groups with different histories were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether. I want to showcase just one of those acts of elimination to drive home what it is that we are talking about when we talk about the making of the modern Middle East. In August 2014, fighters of the Islamic terror group ISIS attacked the Yazidi minority in northwest Iraq. The Yazidis are a very ancient people who follow a pre-Islamic religion. There are about 600,000 of them living in northwest Iraq in August 2014. ISIS murdered some 3,000 to 5,000 of them, mostly men and older women, and captured 6,800 women and girls and turned them into sexual slaves for ISIS fighters, and spared the lives of some of the very young boys in order to recruit them and brainwash them as child soldiers fighting for ISIS. Religious and cultural sites belonging to the Yazidi people were systematically destroyed, and civilian infrastructure, especially water supplies, wrecked. Four hundred thousand of the 600,000 Yazidi were driven into exile, and few of those people have ever returned to their homes. Now, this was a true genocide. ISIS was very explicit. Their goal was to eliminate the Yazidi people, because ISIS hated their religious traditions. ISIS condemned the non-Islamic Yazidi as devil worshipers and thought that because of their non-Islamic views, they should cease to exist as a people and even as human beings. The story was a temporary big deal. People in the West were aware of the Yazidi genocide, and some of the Yazidi were given refuge, especially in Europe. But as time has passed, the story has faded from memory. It is no longer of much interest. You certainly don’t see the kind of big marches in Western countries by progressive people or other kinds of people that you’ve seen in, for example, the war that Hamas started in October of 2023. The Yazidi story doesn’t seem to matter. And I think the reason why we have a hard time holding onto it is because a lot of people who study the Middle East, especially the progressive-minded, have a kind of vision of how the Middle East should be. It’s a vision in which Arab nationalism and Islamic identity are seen as progressive, in the most literal sense—the trend of the future—and everything else is seen as kind of backward looking, and it shouldn’t be there. And so as Christian populations were either eliminated by force or driven into exile—as Simon and I will discuss, there were massacres of the Assyrian Christian population in Iraq. Much of the Christian population of Egypt has been driven into exile. The Armenians were the victim of two waves of genocide in Ottoman empire, one in the 1890s and again in the 1910s. The Kurds were subjected to murderous attack by Saddam Hussein’s Iraq and by the Iranian regime, too. And of course, there is the story of the Jews, who inhabited ancient communities in places like Alexandria and Baghdad, communities that existed before the coming of either the Arabs or of Islam to the region. And after 1945, those communities—or after 1941 in the Iraqi case—those communities were murdered, massacred, plundered, driven into exile, ceased to exist, in-gathered into the state of Israel, where the Jews who formerly lived all through the Ottoman empire have found refuge in one place. This great system of simplification was at every turn marked by atrocity, attempted genocide, the refusal of difference within the context of the Middle East. We don’t seem to find that so troubling because we have an implicit idea of who should be on top and who should not be on top. And this implicit understanding may, I think, add some context to why false accusations against Israel and the Jews have gained so much hearing. Because in a way, the Jews and the state of Israel stand out as the great exception to the trend of the Middle East. This is the one place—the one place—where a people that were a minority people under the old Ottoman empire have built a successful state that is able to be self-sufficient. And that exception to the trend everywhere else in the Middle East is seen by many as a kind of denial of the logic of history, which calls for the whole region to become all one thing under one language—or two, Turkish and Arabic—under one faith, Islam, everyone else driven to the wall. We’re going to talk a little bit about this in the program, how this happened, and we’re going to try to talk about it from an historical point of view to understand it. It is, I think, a trend to be condemned, but first, before condemning, it is a trend to be understood. And to understand why the state of Israel looms so large in our imagination, we have to pay some attention to the things that loom strangely small, like the story of the Yazidi. So horrible, so forgotten. Why? And now, my dialogue with Simon Sebag Montefiore. [Music] Frum: Simon Sebag Montefiore is a British historian of Russia and the Middle East whose books have been published in more than 40 languages. His nonfiction—he has written fiction too—his nonfiction includes: Catherine the Great and Potemkin; Stalin: The Court of the Red Tsar; and also Young Stalin, as well as the internationally best-selling Jerusalem and the history of The Romanovs: 1613–1918. He received his Ph.D. from Cambridge and is a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. He lives in London. His new book is The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East, a history of the region from the last years of the Ottoman Sultanate to the present day. Simon, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. Simon Sebag Montefiore: Lovely to be with you, David. Frum: So first, congratulations on the astonishing acclaim for The Cauldron. And thank you for making time in what has been obviously an exhausting media tour. You’ve been everywhere, so I’m so honored you would join. Montefiore: Thank you. And thanks for having me on this. I’ve always wanted to do this, so here we are finally. Frum: The Cauldron is this thrilling narrative history of the Middle East from approximately the year 1900 under the Ottoman empire to the present day, with characters that are presented very vividly: many anecdotes, many quotations from the literature of the region. The book is a tremendous linguistic achievement. And it’s an exciting read, but it’s also one that can be read not necessarily from beginning to end, but you can start from the middle and work outwards if you prefer, because it’s addressed regionally. But I want to test a thesis on you. So this is a narrative history. It’s a story, and a thrilling story. But you’re not an argumentative historian. Your own ideas are sort of present in the background but are not in the foreground. I want to try to assess what I think you’re telling us. Let me lay out what I think is your thesis, and then you can tell me whether I have it right or whether I have it wrong. May I go ahead? Montefiore: Please do. Frum: Okay. So if we start in the year 1900—let’s start a little before. Let’s start 10 years before that. Most of what is now the Middle East is ruled by the Ottoman empire. So what is now Turkey, parts of Southern Europe, what is now Iraq, what is now Syria, what is now Lebanon, what is now Israel and the West Bank. Egypt is theoretically part of the Ottoman empire, although not practically. Tunisia is theoretically part of the Ottoman empire, not practically. Libya too. And across this vast array of space, there are dominant groups, especially the Ottoman Turkish-speaking Sunni Muslims, but there are many, many minority groups in many, many cities. And it’s not an egalitarian society, it’s not a just society, and it’s not a progressive society. It’s kind of backward-looking. But still, if you’re a Greek in Smyrna, if you’re a Greek in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, if you are an Armenian in one of the cities of the empire, if you’re a Jew in Baghdad, if you’re a Yazidi peasant, an Assyrian Christian—there’s a way forward for you, both as a people and for you as individuals. And suddenly that begins to change—and you’ll know why I’m dating this back to 1890 rather than 1900—with a process that unfolds over the next decades, of brutal simplification. That’s the cauldron: the great melting. Brutal simplification. Minorities are massacred or driven into exile, and the two big dominant groups—Turkish-speaking people and Arabic-speaking people—assert greater and greater control and intolerance over the region, driving everyone else out. And that is what the cauldron is. So do I have it right? Montefiore: That’s one part of it. One part of it is an increasingly tightening nationalistic control that does ultimately lead to what is in fact the biggest kind of slow, ethnic-cleansing purge over the last 125 years, which is the destruction of and the vanishing of the Christians of the Middle East. And that is one of the parts of what you’re referring to here. One is a sort of tightening of a nationalistic control. And the other one is a driving out of anyone who doesn’t fit into that. And the Christian population—it’s such an extraordinary thing. You know, in 630 A.D., the Middle East was basically sort of 90 percent Christian, just before the Arab conquests. And then over the next sort of thousand years, 25 percent remained Christian. And so in 1900, the time you’re talking about, or 1890, you know, still 25 percent of the Middle East is Christian. And jump ahead to today, and that population has virtually vanished. It’s something like 4 percent now. Frum: Well, let’s start with one of those populations, which underwent a brutal process of murder. This is not an abstract historical process. And I’m speaking, of course, of the Armenians—and that’s why I backdated to 1890, not 1900, because the attacks on Armenians begin in the 1890s. Tell us the story of the Armenians within the Ottoman empire, and why they are so brutally treated. Montefiore: The Armenians had lived since time immemorial, since ancient times, in this region. They didn’t have a single homeland. They were spread across the Ottoman empire. But before the Ottoman empire, in the early modern period or the Middle Ages, there had been Armenian kingdoms in Eastern Anatolia. And of course, in ancient times, there had been full Armenian kingdoms in that region, and Armenian kingdoms had been buffer zones between the Persian or Parthian and the Roman Empires. They had been among the first people to convert from paganism to Christianity, and they never converted to Islam. And in the Ottoman empire, they remained a powerful community, a self-governing community that was recognized as Christian, provided they paid, like all other non-Muslim communities, the jizya—that’s the tax for people of the book. And their community was, like the Greek community, which was another large community within the Ottoman empire, also recognized. But there were spasms of violence against them whenever economics or war or famine, or there was a crisis in which one would blame the other within one’s community. But jump forward to the late 19th century. For many centuries—you put this very well in your introduction, David—but for many centuries, these minorities had been allowed to govern themselves, but they didn’t have equal rights to the ruling Ottoman Turkish Sunni Muslims. But that changed beginning in the 1830s and intensifying in the 1850s with Tanzimat. That made all Ottoman citizens equal, whether they were Christian, Greek, Armenian, Jewish. Frum: Tanzimat means “reform.” Is that right? Montefiore: It means reform. And the idea of reform was not necessarily to turn the Ottoman empire into a liberal democracy, but to make it more powerful, to exploit its peoples, to make the empire stronger. But in fact, what it did, in part, was, in part it liberated these minorities and enabled them to own land, to expand their businesses, to become wealthy. And many dynasties emerged in trade and so on that were Armenian and Greek overwhelmingly. And that caused immense jealousy amongst the Muslim population that had been the ruling class for all this time, or the ruling caste for all these centuries. And it also discombobulated the empire. And this policy only went on for about 20 years. In 1877, 1879, a new sultan attacked by Russia, fighting for the existence of his dynasty and his empire, came back. Abolished the new parliament that had been part of these Tanzimat or the climax of these Tanzimat reforms, and unleashed a new idea of Islamic empire, Islamic Ottomanism, in which the senior peoples were now the Muslims. And the sultan rebranded himself as sultan caliph of the empire. And at that point— Frum: Sultan means “power holder”; caliph means “religious leader.” Montefiore: Yeah. It meant the sort of successor to the prophet. And at this point, Abdul Hamid II, a fascinating character, started to promote a new concept in the empire where he played off different minorities against other minorities to promote essentially the Islamic nature of the state or the empire. And this involved using, for example, Kurds, who were sort of second-class Muslim citizens, to attack Armenians, who were third-class Ottoman citizens in effect. And this unleashed all sorts of notorious massacres. The Bulgarian massacres—they were also known as the Hamidian massacres after Hamid himself, the sultan. And at the same time, something else was happening. Which was the excuse for this, which was that nationalism had arrived amongst these peoples. And just as the Turks started to embrace nationalism, the Arabs started to embrace it, and the Serbs and all the Christian peoples of Europe started to embrace it, so did the Armenians. And some Armenians now started to say, like: We want a state too. Everyone else has one. Where can we have one? And they naturally found a backer in the Ottoman empire’s main enemy—which was the Russian Empire, which was the Orthodox Christian empire of the Romanovs. And so now when they looked at the Ottomans, they started to think, Not only are these people Christian Ottomans, they’re actually Christian Russian agents who are holding a dagger right at the heart of the Ottoman empire. And it was made worse because, though the Armenians were mainly concentrated in the eastern part of what is now Turkey, they actually were speckled around the whole empire. There were Armenians in Jerusalem. There were Armenians in Constantinople, the capital, and all over the empire. And therefore, they began to see them very like how Germans began to see Jews between the wars. And there hangs a tale, of course. So by the time we reach World War I—I’m jumping ahead here a bit, if I’m allowed—by the time we reach World War I and the Ottoman empire enters the war against the Allies on the side of Germany, of course Russia is on the side of the Allies and against the Ottoman empire and is, of course, backing the Armenians. And the Ottoman regime at this point has changed from the Ottomanism autocracy of Abdul Hamid II to the ultra neo-fascist, almost proto-Nazi eugenist nationalism of the Young Turks. Who were led by the three Pashas, who were the kind of triumvirate that ruled the Ottoman empire during the war, and they believed that war would be a cleansing experience for the Ottoman empire. Frum: And they attacked the Armenian communities. In the 1890s, there were Ottoman riots against Armenians in the cities. And during the war, there’s a murderous rampage against the Armenians who are not in the cities. What is the total death toll among Armenians between 1895 and 1918? Montefiore: It’s about 2 million. Frum: About 2 million. Montefiore: I mean, during World War I, 1.1 million is the usually accepted number, which is colossal. And it’s a large part of the Armenian nation. And it’s such a decisive moment because it’s because of this genocide—and by the way, this wasn’t the only genocide. They also killed 300,000 Maronite Christians in Lebanon. They also killed over 400,000 Greeks or Pontic Greeks who were on the Black Sea coast and in Ionia. They also killed several hundred thousand Assyrian Christians who lived on the borders of what is now Turkey and Iraq. And so this was a deliberate purge. And there is evidence, there are directives, there are orders from Talat Pasha and the other leaders to either massacre these people, men, women, and children, or to drive them out into the desert to starve. And it’s really the first modern genocide. Frum: And it’s a modern genocide unlike what Stalin will do to his subject peoples, where he’s trying to break economic resistance. This is ethnic elimination by—it’s maybe not a fully modern state, the Ottoman state. It’s obviously not as efficient as Germany and not as efficient as Stalin’s Russia. But it is the deliberate elimination of categories of ethnicity in order to simplify the state, to make the state more powerful. Montefiore: That’s right. And also to destroy the bacteria within, to destroy the traitors within. And so it’s decisive in various ways. One is that it ensures that the Armenian nation exists really more in diaspora than it does in formerly Armenian territories. It led the Western powers to back Armenian nationhood as well. And Armenian forces fought on the side of the Russians in the wars that followed. And in the wars that followed the fall of the Ottoman empire, they fought against the new Turkish state to try and win an Armenian state, which was designated to exist in what is now eastern Turkey. And its big backer was President Woodrow Wilson of America, who promised to rule, to govern a mandate—an American mandate—for the Armenians, which is quite a thought. Of course, this never happened. And in fact, what happened was, as David will know better than I, Wilson went back to America and failed to get any of these obligations through Congress or membership of the League of Nations that he’d created and so on. But what happened in the former Ottoman empire was that a new Turkish-nationalist maestro arose: Mustafa Kemal Pasha, who became [Mustafa Kemal] Atatürk. The master of the father of Turks, who founded a new Turkish nation, who founded a Turkish republic, and crushed the Armenians in eastern Turkey. So they never got the republic. Frum: And then drove out the Greeks from western Turkey. Montefiore: And then switched round and drove out the Greeks from western Turkey, and that’s also a fascinating part of the story. Frum: I’m going to pause you there, because there’s an element here that is going to, I think, come as a pause or something to a lot of modern readers. If you have studied Middle Eastern studies at an American university, or even more a European or British university, you’re introduced to the Middle East as a kind of inert mass. Nothing happens there unless a Western power makes it happen, and anything that happens there is a reaction to something that a Western power does. But as you were telling it, the beginning of the cycle of purging, elimination, ethnic cleansing, genocide—it’s a spontaneous local phenomenon. This is something driven by the Ottoman Turkish government and their successor, the Young Turk government, which is defining itself in new ways against its subject peoples in an effort to exert stronger control over its territory. Montefiore: That’s right. Frum: It’s not a reaction to Western neocolonialism or Western imperialism. This is something they wanted to do for their own reasons and acted on their own volition. Montefiore: Yeah. This is Ottoman Turkish imperialism. This is Ottoman Turkish genocidal massacre of their own subjects for their own purposes. And it’s a sort of proto-Nazi ideology with social Darwinism, eugenicism, and ultranationalism, and this comes from within the Middle East itself. Though, of course, they’re highly influenced, as are all the peoples of the region, by nationalism—the new drug of nationalism that seems to offer the solution to all things. Frum: Let me hit another pause button here because—and I wanted to pause before we got to Atatürk, because the First World War ends with the collapse of the Ottoman empire. It’s carved up. It loses most of its remaining European territories, and many of its holdings are then divided up into new Arab countries that either have outright Sunni majorities or else have Sunni elites, as is the case in Iraq. Most people in Iraq are not Sunni, but there’s an Arab Sunni elite, and there are then other groups. And what we now call Turkey is also a successor state. It’s carved out of the Ottoman empire, too, and it’s defined as a national state with Turkish as its language. It changes the name of its capital city from the Greek Constantinople to the kind-of-Greek Istanbul—which is also Greek, I understand, but it sounds more Turkish even though it’s Greek in origin. So we have these now-new states. And the Arab states and the new Turkish national state, they begin eliminating their minorities one by one by one. Montefiore: That’s correct. And so, you know, in Turkey, for example what happens, the new Turkish state is really defined on what we would now call, in progressive parlance, an ethno-religious basis. In the sense that Turks were Ottoman subjects who spoke Turkish, lived in what was regarded as the Turkish heartland, and were Muslim. And people who were Christian could not be Turkish. So what we see today—and it started with Atatürk’s version of Turkishness, but his was secular and this is religious. So that’s exactly right. And so they drove out the Armenians who had challenged them and tried to carve out a state in the east, and then they turned on the Greeks. And the Greeks—it was slightly a different story, because the Greeks had been promised a sort of new Byzantine Empire in what is now western Turkey. And the reason why they claimed that was because there were huge Greek Orthodox populations in western Turkey—that used to be called Ionia—that had been there for thousands of years, literally since the Trojan Wars. And they lived in cities like Smyrna, the great Greek city of Smyrna. And so now Greek armies arrived, backed by the British and the French—and this was an example of European interference in the region—they arrived to protect their own ancient local Greek populations, but also to increase their kingdom. The Greek kingdom, the Greek state. And there they encountered Atatürk and his new Turkish army. And what ensued was a brutal nation-building war of ethnic purging, population swaps. Brutal, huge battles of regular armies. The armies in this were huge. They were 150,000 strong each in these major battles, with artillery, of course, and everything. So they were real World War I battles. But this is in 1922, and the Turks won these battles, and they then drove out, massacring and driving and deporting the Greek populations of what is now western Turkey. And in 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne, which involved Britain and Greece, the populations were swapped. So all the Muslims went to Turkey, all the Christians were expelled— Frum: That sounds so antiseptic. Montefiore: It’s not that antiseptic, because there were huge massacres. Frum: It’s murder, it’s pillage, it’s people standing on docks. It’s cities on fire. Montefiore: Yeah. It’s people jumping into docks and drowning. It’s burning cities. And at the heart of it is the inferno of Smyrna, which is one of the most apocalyptic urban demolitions of all time. And this creation of the Turkish nation is so important, because it explains what we’re seeing now in the rise of Turkey as a regional power. And it explains both the militaristic Turkish nationalism. It explains also the aspiration for much more influence, the grievance that they were diminished inside these borders agreed on in 1923, and the wish to expand and re-energize the Ottoman idea. And that is what we’re seeing now with President [Recep Tayyip] Erdogan. Frum: Let me take you now to the Arabic-speaking countries, mostly Sunni, that are carved out of the Ottoman empire. Now, Egypt was notionally part of the Ottoman empire in the 19th century. It was really an independent state with a lot of British influence, some French influence. Egypt remains a reasonably cosmopolitan place after the First World War with Greek minorities, Jewish minorities. Syria has more French influence. Lebanon has a lot of French influence. Palestine, which is reserved as a Jewish homeland, is a British mandate. But there’s this new country of Iraq created, and it becomes kind of genocide central in the Arabic-speaking Middle East. Tell us about the history of Iraq from the end of the First World War to the advent of the Second World War. Montefiore: Well, that’s right. But the Egypt you described was—and it’s hard to imagine now—but Egypt was the most cosmopolitan country in the Middle East. The fellahin, the lower, you know, the peasant class, were Arab, but the merchant classes were—as you said, David—Jewish, Lebanese, Greek, Italian. And they were large populations. The Jewish population was several hundred thousand just on its own, and they were the descendants of Jews who had been settled in Egypt by Alexander the Great and the Ptolemies, so they’d been there for millennia. And the wealth of Egypt depended on this mercantile class. And then the ruling class, the landowners, were Turco-Circassians, who were the descendants of enslaved Christians who had been enslaved and kidnapped by the Ottomans and previous rulers from their villages. They were Christian children who’d been enlisted in the Ottoman or Mamluk armies, who had been stolen from their parents, who were probably murdered. And who had then been converted to Islam, manumitted, and then joined the army and founded these families, these dynasties. It’s just a fascinating story. And even in the 1920s, these people, the Turco-Circassians, were still owning and ruling Egypt. And the ruling kings of Egypt, as they became, were also Turco-Albanian dynasty, who didn’t even speak Arabic right into the 1930s, which is fascinating. So that’s Egypt. And so you’re absolutely right that these are incredibly complicated because of Ottoman countries. When you come to Syria and Lebanon, these are also multiethnic, multi-sectarian countries—as they still are, which is why their rulers to this day are desperately struggling to make them work as single countries. And the French mandate was for Greater Syria, which is now divided into Syria and Lebanon. But it’s just worth remembering how different these countries could have been. Because when one thinks of them as they were bound to be Syria and Lebanon, no, that isn’t how it worked at all. And that’s also true with Iraq. With Syria and Lebanon, the French were thinking about dividing it into five or six countries. And those countries were two Sunni ones in Aleppo and Damascus, and then a Druze one, an Alawite one at Latakia on the coast. And then they were going to devise a Christian Maronite country that the Christians would rule, who were the French allies in Lebanon. And in the end, they decided not to do this, but to divide it into two big countries: Syria and Lebanon. So then we get to Iraq. Again, one thinks of Iraq as set, but Iraq was known to the allies as Mesopotamia—“the land between the rivers” in Greek. Iraq was an old Arab name for this region, but there’d never been a country called Iraq before, just as there’d never been a country called Lebanon or Syria or Jordan. And these countries were all drawn by the Western overlords, particularly Britain and France. And Iraq was just a combination of three provinces, or vilayets, put together by the British. And the vilayets were Basra, Baghdad, and Mosul. And Mosul is where the oil was, and that’s the Kurdish area. And there was a big question as to whether Mosul would be in Iraq or not. And that’s a pretty important detail, because it’s partly the Kurdish area; it’s where the oil is. And the Turks, who we were just discussing a minute ago, wanted Mosul and believed Mosul should be in Turkey. Now, that would have really changed the situation. But the Western allies also wanted to create a state—not just for the Armenians that we were discussing, but for the Kurds. And the Kurds would have a state that was partly in what is now Turkey and partly in what is now Iraq. But that didn’t happen either, because the Kurds were betrayed by everybody. And talk about genocide; this is another genocide in the 1930s where Atatürk and the Turkish Republic bombed Kurdish revolts, destroyed Kurdish village, killed something like 40,000 to 50,000 using poison gas, bombing villages. And they crushed the Kurds for another generation. In Iraq, they hoped to get Mosul or at least to prevent a Kurdish state being created. And in the end, the British were determined that Mosul would stay in the new country they’d created of Iraq. But as you said, David, Iraq was a multiethnic, multinational, multi-sectarian country. It had a small Shia majority, a barely Sunni minority. But that minority was very educated—was the landowners, was the civil servants. And it had been favored and empowered by the Turks, who were also Sunni. And then there were huge minorities of Kurds, small Christian sects, the Chaldeans, and Assyrians. And when I say “small,” they were a million people, so they weren’t that tiny. Non-Muslim sects like the Yazidis and Turkmen and all sorts of other minorities. Assyrians who were Christian. Frum: And Jews in Baghdad. Montefiore: And Jews in Baghdad. And a third of Baghdad was Jewish. Yeah. And many of the great families there like the Sassoons, most famously, who later went to England and became the sort of richest family in England, basically. The Sassoons, “the Rothschilds of the East,” they were known as. They were an incredibly prosperous minority, and they dominated the city in many ways. And the most kind of privileged of them ran huge business empires and also served the Pashas who ran Baghdad and— Frum: And between 1919 and 1942, there’s just attack after attack on each of these groups: on the Assyrian Christians, on the Kurds, on the Jews. And they are murdered and driven into exile. Montefiore: That’s exactly what happened. One of the big outrages is in the early ’30s, when they turn on the Christian Assyrians and massacre them. The Assyrians flee the country. And it’s really the first sign in Iraq that these new nation-states created for the Arabs are actually contradicting the multiethnic kind of cosmopolitan nature of these regions, that had been, perhaps in some ways, at various moments—and one mustn’t generalize—better ruled by empires with capitals far away. And so the climax for the Jews comes in 1941 with the Farhud, which is a terrifying pogrom. But in these pogroms against the Jews in 1941, influenced by specifically Nazi propaganda and perpetrated by a self-consciously Nazi-influenced militia, it was an episode more like October the 7, you know—where women were raped and then their bodies mutilated. Body parts were paraded through the town. And it really took place at an interesting moment when the British were about to retake Baghdad, and a pro-Nazi government was just in the process of being overthrown in 1941. And in that interim period, they decided they were going to get the Jews, and they went round the town marking the doors of every Jewish house. And so when the Farhud started, when the pogrom started, they knew exactly the houses, and they could see the mark on the door. Which is just a sort of chilling detail, isn’t it, David? David Frum: Yeah. I want to bring now the story up to the present in our last few minutes. One of the things I think that you will hear said a lot on modern university campuses by advocacy groups of various kinds is—they’ll tell the story of this Edenic Middle East before the Jews got there, before the Jews came to the state of Israel. And they will ask, Why aren’t the Jews comfortable to live in a multiethnic, multinational state with an Arab majority? What could possibly go wrong in such a situation? And I wanted to give people a tour of that. The story of the Middle East from the weakening of the Ottoman empire, as you say, in the late 19th century, beginning with the attacks on the Armenians, most bloodily in the 1890s and continuing, is: You either have a state, or you’re dead. Those are your choices in the Middle East. Montefiore: That’s right, and that is one of the themes of the book. And one of the themes of the book is to confront all of these Edenic myths, which even a cursory look at the facts and the history will show you is entirely legendary and has never existed. You know, it starts with the myth that the Ottoman empire was this kind of wonderful kumbaya, tolerant, poetry-spouting kind of a multicultural society. And that was never true. It was a conquest society built on the enslavement and kidnapping of Christian children. This isn’t some sort of story, by the way. This is how the Ottoman empire, it was how it was so successful. This tribute of children—which the Ottoman empire took from Christian villages in the Caucasus, in the Crimea, in southern Ukraine, and also in the Balkans—was how it was provided with talented, energetic manpower. And the women went into the harems. The boys went into the army or the civil service. And the women in the harems. The most lucky of them became queens. They became the wives of actual sultans. And Hürrem Sultan, known as Roxelana, for example, the blonde or red-haired Ukrainian girl—who incidentally was the most powerful Ukrainian in world history, I would argue—she became Suleiman the Magnificent’s wife, mother of his successor. And she was typical, but of the luckiest of those. But for the boys, they became soldiers. They were forcefully converted to Islam. Once they were about to become officers, they were manumitted—in other words, freed from slavery—and then they were able to work up the military. And they were the army of the Ottoman empire that conquered this vast empire from the borders of Libya all the way to the borders of Iran. So that’s the first thing about the Ottoman empire. The second thing is: There was tolerance, provided you accepted the total supremacy of Islam and Sultan. And if you in any way challenged that political and religious supremacy, you were slaughtered. The history of the Ottoman empire is filled with massacres of minorities and Jews at regular intervals. And this goes on right into the 19th century, well before we get to the 1890s, where David started this discussion. But, you know, a typical example is in 1860; 25,000 Christians were massacred in Damascus in the 1860 event, which was one of the occurrences that brought the Western powers into the Ottoman empire. And we’ve seen how the Ottoman Empire ended, with a proto-Nazi genocide of entire races. And then you get into the creation of these states. If we look into the second half of the 20th century—where Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon, they all became independent—again, you see a similar pattern. Dictators from one sect or another protected and promoted their own group. Saddam Hussein, for example, protected the Sunni majority, even though he was from a very poor Tikriti peasant family, and brutally crushed the Shiites and the Kurds. And ultimately, to come back to your theme, this culminated in the attempted genocide of the Kurdish nation in Iraq. So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing. And if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression. And that is the process by which, in my book, you’ll see over a century and a quarter we go from this wonderful efflorescence of sects and ethnicities. You go to this bleaker and bleaker and bleaker environment, and the Christians virtually vanish. So that in 2000, like 25 years ago, you still had a million Christians in Iraq. After the Islamist insurgency during the Iraq War, now there are 115,000 Christians in Iraq. So 900,000 of them have gone. So this is the picture. Frum: And this process of consolidation also leads to economic and technological failure. So Egypt—the cosmopolitan Egypt you describe of the 19th century—there was a large stock market in Alexandria. Egypt was a food exporter. Cotton exporter. Montefiore: Huge cotton industry. Frum: A big, big destination for foreign investment. The Suez Canal. And then after the Second World War, Egypt, a newly nationalist, newly Arabized Egypt, expels its Greeks, Italians, Jews, of course. And imposes state control over the economy and becomes an ever-more poverty-stricken country, dependent evermore not on investment, but on aid. Montefiore: That’s right. Frum: That’s the story of every region. And this story is told as one that the West did to the Middle East, not as a story something the Middle East did to itself Montefiore: Agree. That is one of the major themes of the book. And you do have to question whether the nation-state itself was—as an ideology, as a state architecture—suited to this region at all. Frum: Well, let’s talk about one particular nation-state, which is the one that gets almost all the airtime, and that is the nation-state of Israel. Built over a century of gradual development, created by a vote of the United Nations in 1947. In 1947, there is a war of independence. The Arab population is pushed out of what will become Israel, or chooses to leave. In some cases leaves voluntarily. And then Jewish populations all over the rest of the Middle East are expelled in hundreds of thousands, and come to Israel. And a nation-state is built there that is actually economically capable, technologically capable, militarily capable. And this becomes the last and most intolerable provocation, that there is one nation-state that actually is suited to the region when other nation-states don’t work. Montefiore: That’s right. And also, I mean, there are other ways to look at Israel.
